speaker: MENENIUS
text: Pray you, who does the wolf love?

speaker: SICINIUS
text: The lamb.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Ay, to devour him, as the hungry plebeians
would the noble Martius.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: He’s a lamb indeed, that baas like a bear.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
He’s a bear indeed, that lives like a lamb.
You two are old men; tell me one thing that I shall
ask you.

speaker: BOTH
text: Well, sir.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
In what enormity is Martius poor in, that
you two have not in abundance?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: He’s poor in no one fault, but stored with all.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Especially in pride.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: And topping all others in boasting.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
This is strange now. Do you two know how
you are censured here in the city, I mean of us o’
th’ right-hand file, do you?

speaker: BOTH
text: Why, how are we censured?

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Because you talk of pride now, will you not
be angry?

speaker: BOTH
text: Well, well, sir, well?

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Why, ’tis no great matter; for a very little
thief of occasion will rob you of a great deal of patience.
Give your dispositions the reins, and be
angry at your pleasures, at the least, if you take it
as a pleasure to you in being so. You blame Martius
for being proud.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: We do it not alone, sir.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
I know you can do very little alone, for
your helps are many, or else your actions would
grow wondrous single. Your abilities are too infantlike
for doing much alone. You talk of pride. O,
that you could turn your eyes toward the napes
of your necks and make but an interior survey of
your good selves! O, that you could!

speaker: BOTH
text: What then, sir?

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Why, then you should discover a brace of
unmeriting, proud, violent, testy magistrates, alias
fools, as any in Rome.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Menenius, you are known well enough, too.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
I am known to be a humorous patrician and
one that loves a cup of hot wine with not a drop of
allaying Tiber in ’t; said to be something imperfect
in favoring the first complaint, hasty and tinder-like
upon too trivial motion; one that converses
more with the buttock of the night than with the
forehead of the morning. What I think I utter,
and spend my malice in my breath. Meeting two
such wealsmen as you are—I cannot call you
Lycurguses—if the drink you give me touch my
palate adversely, I make a crooked face at it. I cannot
say your Worships have delivered the matter
well when I find the ass in compound with the
major part of your syllables. And though I must
be content to bear with those that say you are reverend
grave men, yet they lie deadly that tell you
have good faces. If you see this in the map of my
microcosm, follows it that I am known well enough
too? What harm can your bisson conspectuities
glean out of this character, if I be known well
enough, too?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Come, sir, come; we know you well enough.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
You know neither me, yourselves, nor anything.
You are ambitious for poor knaves’ caps
and legs. You wear out a good wholesome forenoon
in hearing a cause between an orange-wife
and a faucet-seller, and then rejourn the controversy
of threepence to a second day of audience.
When you are hearing a matter between party and
party, if you chance to be pinched with the colic,
you make faces like mummers, set up the bloody
flag against all patience, and, in roaring for a
chamber pot, dismiss the controversy bleeding,
the more entangled by your hearing. All the peace
you make in their cause is calling both the parties
knaves. You are a pair of strange ones.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Come, come. You are well understood to be a
perfecter giber for the table than a necessary
bencher in the Capitol.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Our very priests must become mockers if
they shall encounter such ridiculous subjects as
you are. When you speak best unto the purpose, it
is not worth the wagging of your beards, and your
beards deserve not so honorable a grave as to
stuff a botcher’s cushion or to be entombed in an
ass’s packsaddle. Yet you must be saying Martius is
proud, who, in a cheap estimation, is worth all
your predecessors since Deucalion, though peradventure
some of the best of ’em were hereditary
hangmen. Good e’en to your Worships. More of
your conversation would infect my brain, being
the herdsmen of the beastly plebeians. I will be
bold to take my leave of you.
How now, my as fair as noble ladies—and the
moon, were she earthly, no nobler—whither do
you follow your eyes so fast?

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
Honorable Menenius, my boy Martius approaches.
For the love of Juno, let’s go!

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Ha? Martius coming home?

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
Ay, worthy Menenius, and with most prosperous
approbation.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Take my cap, Jupiter, and I thank thee!
Hoo! Martius coming
home?

speaker: VALERIA , VIRGILIA
text: Nay, ’tis true.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
Look, here’s a letter from him.
The state hath another, his wife another,
and I think there’s one at home for you.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
I will make my very house reel tonight. A
letter for me?

speaker: VIRGILIA
text: Yes, certain, there’s a letter for you; I saw ’t.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
A letter for me? It gives me an estate of
seven years’ health, in which time I will make a lip
at the physician. The most sovereign prescription
in Galen is but empiricutic and, to this preservative,
of no better report than a horse drench. Is he not
wounded? He was wont to come home wounded.

speaker: VIRGILIA
text: O no, no, no!

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text: O, he is wounded, I thank the gods for ’t.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
So do I too, if it be not too much. Brings he
victory in his pocket, the wounds become him.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
On ’s brows, Menenius. He comes the third
time home with the oaken garland.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Has he disciplined Aufidius soundly?

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
Titus Lartius writes they fought together,
but Aufidius got off.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
And ’twas time for him too, I’ll warrant him
that. An he had stayed by him, I would not have
been so ’fidiused for all the chests in Corioles and
the gold that’s in them. Is the Senate possessed of
this?

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
Good ladies, let’s go.—Yes, yes, yes. The
Senate has letters from the General, wherein he
gives my son the whole name of the war. He hath
in this action outdone his former deeds doubly.

speaker: VALERIA
text:
In troth, there’s wondrous things spoke of
him.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Wondrous? Ay, I warrant you, and not without
his true purchasing.

speaker: VIRGILIA
text: The gods grant them true.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text: True? Pow waw!

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
True? I’ll be sworn they are true. Where is
he wounded? God save your
good Worships! Martius is coming home; he has
more cause to be proud.—Where is he wounded?

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
I’ th’ shoulder and i’ th’ left arm. There will
be large cicatrices to show the people when he
shall stand for his place. He received in the repulse
of Tarquin seven hurts i’ th’ body.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
One i’ th’ neck and two i’ th’ thigh—there’s
nine that I know.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
He had, before this last expedition, twenty-five
wounds upon him.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Now it’s twenty-seven. Every gash was an
enemy’s grave. Hark, the
trumpets!

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
These are the ushers of Martius: before him
he carries noise, and behind him he leaves tears.
Death, that dark spirit, in ’s nervy arm doth lie,
Which, being advanced, declines, and then men die.

speaker: HERALD
text:
Know, Rome, that all alone Martius did fight
Within Corioles’ gates, where he hath won,
With fame, a name to Martius Caius; these
In honor follows “Coriolanus.”
Welcome to Rome, renownèd Coriolanus.

speaker: ALL
text: Welcome to Rome, renownèd Coriolanus!

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
No more of this. It does offend my heart.
Pray now, no more.

speaker: COMINIUS
text: Look, sir, your mother.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
O,
You have, I know, petitioned all the gods
For my prosperity.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
Nay, my good soldier, up.
My gentle Martius, worthy Caius, and
By deed-achieving honor newly named—
What is it? Coriolanus must I call thee?
But, O, thy wife—

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
My gracious silence, hail.
Wouldst thou have laughed had I come coffined home,
That weep’st to see me triumph? Ah, my dear,
Such eyes the widows in Corioles wear
And mothers that lack sons.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Now the gods crown thee!

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: And live you yet? O, my sweet lady, pardon.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
I know not where to turn. O, welcome home!—
And, welcome, general.—And you’re welcome all.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
A hundred thousand welcomes! I could weep,
And I could laugh; I am light and heavy. Welcome.
A curse begin at very root on ’s heart
That is not glad to see thee! You are three
That Rome should dote on; yet, by the faith of men,
We have some old crab trees here at home that will not
Be grafted to your relish. Yet welcome, warriors!
We call a nettle but a nettle, and
The faults of fools but folly.

speaker: COMINIUS
text: Ever right.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Menenius ever, ever.

speaker: HERALD
text: Give way there, and go on!

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Your hand and yours.
Ere in our own house I do shade my head,
The good patricians must be visited,
From whom I have received not only greetings,
But with them change of honors.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
I have lived
To see inherited my very wishes
And the buildings of my fancy. Only
There’s one thing wanting, which I doubt not but
Our Rome will cast upon thee.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Know, good mother,
I had rather be their servant in my way
Than sway with them in theirs.

speaker: COMINIUS
text: On, to the Capitol.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
All tongues speak of him, and the blearèd sights
Are spectacled to see him. Your prattling nurse
Into a rapture lets her baby cry
While she chats him. The kitchen malkin pins
Her richest lockram ’bout her reechy neck,
Clamb’ring the walls to eye him. Stalls, bulks, windows
Are smothered up, leads filled, and ridges horsed
With variable complexions, all agreeing
In earnestness to see him. Seld-shown flamens
Do press among the popular throngs and puff
To win a vulgar station. Our veiled dames
Commit the war of white and damask in
Their nicely-gauded cheeks to th’ wanton spoil
Of Phoebus’ burning kisses. Such a pother,
As if that whatsoever god who leads him
Were slyly crept into his human powers
And gave him graceful posture.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
On the sudden
I warrant him consul.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Then our office may,
During his power, go sleep.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
He cannot temp’rately transport his honors
From where he should begin and end, but will
Lose those he hath won.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: In that there’s comfort.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Doubt not
The commoners, for whom we stand, but they
Upon their ancient malice will forget
With the least cause these his new honors—which
That he will give them make I as little question
As he is proud to do ’t.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
I heard him swear,
Were he to stand for consul, never would he
Appear i’ th’ marketplace nor on him put
The napless vesture of humility,
Nor showing, as the manner is, his wounds
To th’ people, beg their stinking breaths.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: ’Tis right.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
It was his word. O, he would miss it rather
Than carry it but by the suit of the gentry to him
And the desire of the nobles.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
I wish no better
Than have him hold that purpose and to put it
In execution.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: ’Tis most like he will.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
It shall be to him then as our good wills,
A sure destruction.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
So it must fall out
To him, or our authority’s for an end.
We must suggest the people in what hatred
He still hath held them; that to ’s power he would
Have made them mules, silenced their pleaders, and
Dispropertied their freedoms; holding them
In human action and capacity
Of no more soul nor fitness for the world
Than camels in their war, who have their provand
Only for bearing burdens, and sore blows
For sinking under them.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
This, as you say, suggested
At some time when his soaring insolence
Shall touch the people—which time shall not want
If he be put upon ’t, and that’s as easy
As to set dogs on sheep—will be his fire
To kindle their dry stubble, and their blaze
Shall darken him forever.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: What’s the matter?

speaker: MESSENGER
text:
You are sent for to the Capitol. ’Tis thought
That Martius shall be consul. I have seen
The dumb men throng to see him, and the blind
To hear him speak; matrons flung gloves,
Ladies and maids their scarves and handkerchiefs,
Upon him as he passed; the nobles bended
As to Jove’s statue, and the Commons made
A shower and thunder with their caps and shouts.
I never saw the like.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Let’s to the Capitol,
And carry with us ears and eyes for th’ time,
But hearts for the event.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Have with you.

speaker: FIRST OFFICER
text:
Come, come. They are almost here. How
many stand for consulships?

speaker: SECOND OFFICER
text:
Three, they say; but ’tis thought of
everyone Coriolanus will carry it.

speaker: FIRST OFFICER
text:
That’s a brave fellow, but he’s vengeance
proud and loves not the common people.

speaker: SECOND OFFICER
text:
’Faith, there hath been many great
men that have flattered the people who ne’er loved
them; and there be many that they have loved they
know not wherefore; so that, if they love they
know not why, they hate upon no better a ground.
Therefore, for Coriolanus neither to care whether
they love or hate him manifests the true knowledge
he has in their disposition and, out of his noble
carelessness, lets them plainly see ’t.

speaker: FIRST OFFICER
text:
If he did not care whether he had their
love or no, he waved indifferently ’twixt doing them
neither good nor harm; but he seeks their hate with
greater devotion than they can render it him and
leaves nothing undone that may fully discover him
their opposite. Now, to seem to affect the malice
and displeasure of the people is as bad as that
which he dislikes, to flatter them for their love.

speaker: SECOND OFFICER
text:
He hath deserved worthily of his
country, and his ascent is not by such easy degrees
as those who, having been supple and courteous to
the people, bonneted, without any further deed to
have them at all into their estimation and report;
but he hath so planted his honors in their eyes and
his actions in their hearts that for their tongues to
be silent and not confess so much were a kind of
ingrateful injury. To report otherwise were a malice
that, giving itself the lie, would pluck reproof
and rebuke from every ear that heard it.

speaker: FIRST OFFICER
text:
No more of him; he’s a worthy man.
Make way. They are coming.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Having determined of the Volsces and
To send for Titus Lartius, it remains,
As the main point of this our after-meeting,
To gratify his noble service that
Hath thus stood for his country. Therefore please you,
Most reverend and grave elders, to desire
The present consul and last general
In our well-found successes to report
A little of that worthy work performed
By Martius Caius Coriolanus, whom
We met here both to thank and to remember
With honors like himself.

speaker: FIRST SENATOR
text:
Speak, good Cominius.
Leave nothing out for length, and make us think
Rather our state’s defective for requital,
Than we to stretch it out.Masters o’ th’ people,
We do request your kindest ears and, after,
Your loving motion toward the common body
To yield what passes here.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
We are convented
Upon a pleasing treaty and have hearts
Inclinable to honor and advance
The theme of our assembly.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Which the rather
We shall be blest to do if he remember
A kinder value of the people than
He hath hereto prized them at.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
That’s off, that’s off!
I would you rather had been silent. Please you
To hear Cominius speak?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Most willingly,
But yet my caution was more pertinent
Than the rebuke you give it.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
He loves your people,
But tie him not to be their bedfellow.—
Worthy Cominius, speak.
Nay, keep your place.

speaker: FIRST SENATOR
text:
Sit, Coriolanus. Never shame to hear
What you have nobly done.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Your Honors, pardon.
I had rather have my wounds to heal again
Than hear say how I got them.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Sir, I hope
My words disbenched you not?

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
No, sir. Yet oft,
When blows have made me stay, I fled from words.
You soothed not, therefore hurt not; but your people,
I love them as they weigh.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Pray now, sit down.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
I had rather have one scratch my head i’ th’ sun
When the alarum were struck than idly sit
To hear my nothings monstered.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Masters of the people,
Your multiplying spawn how can he flatter—
That’s thousand to one good one—when you now see
He had rather venture all his limbs for honor
Than one on ’s ears to hear it.—Proceed, Cominius.

speaker: COMINIUS
text:
I shall lack voice. The deeds of Coriolanus
Should not be uttered feebly. It is held
That valor is the chiefest virtue and
Most dignifies the haver; if it be,
The man I speak of cannot in the world
Be singly counterpoised. At sixteen years,
When Tarquin made a head for Rome, he fought
Beyond the mark of others. Our then dictator,
Whom with all praise I point at, saw him fight
When with his Amazonian chin he drove
The bristled lips before him. He bestrid
An o’erpressed Roman and i’ th’ Consul’s view
Slew three opposers. Tarquin’s self he met
And struck him on his knee. In that day’s feats,
When he might act the woman in the scene,
He proved best man i’ th’ field and for his meed
Was brow-bound with the oak. His pupil age
Man-entered thus, he waxèd like a sea,
And in the brunt of seventeen battles since
He lurched all swords of the garland. For this last,
Before and in Corioles, let me say,
I cannot speak him home. He stopped the flyers
And by his rare example made the coward
Turn terror into sport. As weeds before
A vessel under sail, so men obeyed
And fell below his stem. His sword, Death’s stamp,
Where it did mark, it took; from face to foot
He was a thing of blood, whose every motion
Was timed with dying cries. Alone he entered
The mortal gate o’ th’ city, which he painted
With shunless destiny; aidless came off
And with a sudden reinforcement struck
Corioles like a planet. Now all’s his,
When by and by the din of war gan pierce
His ready sense; then straight his doubled spirit
Requickened what in flesh was fatigate,
And to the battle came he, where he did
Run reeking o’er the lives of men as if
’Twere a perpetual spoil; and till we called
Both field and city ours, he never stood
To ease his breast with panting.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Worthy man!

speaker: FIRST SENATOR
text:
He cannot but with measure fit the honors
Which we devise him.

speaker: COMINIUS
text:
Our spoils he kicked at
And looked upon things precious as they were
The common muck of the world. He covets less
Than misery itself would give, rewards
His deeds with doing them, and is content
To spend the time to end it.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
He’s right noble.
Let him be called for.

speaker: FIRST SENATOR
text: Call Coriolanus.

speaker: OFFICER
text: He doth appear.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
The Senate, Coriolanus, are well pleased
To make thee consul.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
I do owe them still
My life and services.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
It then remains
That you do speak to the people.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
I do beseech you,
Let me o’erleap that custom, for I cannot
Put on the gown, stand naked, and entreat them
For my wounds’ sake to give their suffrage. Please you
That I may pass this doing.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Sir, the people
Must have their voices; neither will they bate
One jot of ceremony.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Put them not to ’t.
Pray you, go fit you to the custom, and
Take to you, as your predecessors have,
Your honor with your form.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
It is a part
That I shall blush in acting, and might well
Be taken from the people.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Mark you that?

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
To brag unto them “Thus I did, and thus!”
Show them th’ unaching scars, which I should hide,
As if I had received them for the hire
Of their breath only!

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Do not stand upon ’t.—
We recommend to you, tribunes of the people,
Our purpose to them, and to our noble consul
Wish we all joy and honor.

speaker: SENATORS
text: To Coriolanus come all joy and honor!

speaker: BRUTUS
text: You see how he intends to use the people.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
May they perceive ’s intent! He will require them
As if he did contemn what he requested
Should be in them to give.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Come, we’ll inform them
Of our proceedings here. On th’ marketplace
I know they do attend us.

speaker: FIRST CITIZEN
text:
Once, if he do require our voices, we
ought not to deny him.

speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
text: We may, sir, if we will.

speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
text:
We have power in ourselves to do it, but
it is a power that we have no power to do; for, if
he show us his wounds and tell us his deeds, we
are to put our tongues into those wounds and
speak for them. So, if he tell us his noble deeds, we
must also tell him our noble acceptance of them.
Ingratitude is monstrous, and for the multitude to
be ingrateful were to make a monster of the multitude,
of the which, we being members, should
bring ourselves to be monstrous members.

speaker: FIRST CITIZEN
text:
And to make us no better thought of, a
little help will serve; for once we stood up about
the corn, he himself stuck not to call us the many-headed
multitude.

speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
text:
We have been called so of many; not that
our heads are some brown, some black, some
abram, some bald, but that our wits are so diversely
colored; and truly I think if all our wits were to
issue out of one skull, they would fly east, west,
north, south, and their consent of one direct way
should be at once to all the points o’ th’ compass.

speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
text:
Think you so? Which way do you
judge my wit would fly?

speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
text:
Nay, your wit will not so soon out as another
man’s will; ’tis strongly wedged up in a blockhead.
But if it were at liberty, ’twould sure
southward.

speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
text: Why that way?

speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
text:
To lose itself in a fog, where, being three
parts melted away with rotten dews, the fourth
would return for conscience’ sake, to help to get
thee a wife.

speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
text:
You are never without your tricks. You
may, you may.

speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
text:
Are you all resolved to give your voices?
But that’s no matter; the greater part carries it. I
say, if he would incline to the people, there was
never a worthier man.
Here he comes, and in the gown of humility. Mark
his behavior. We are not to stay all together, but to
come by him where he stands, by ones, by twos,
and by threes. He’s to make his requests by particulars,
wherein every one of us has a single honor
in giving him our own voices with our own tongues.
Therefore follow me, and I’ll direct you how you
shall go by him.

speaker: ALL
text: Content, content.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
O sir, you are not right. Have you not known
The worthiest men have done ’t?

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
What must I say?
“I pray, sir?”—plague upon ’t! I cannot bring
My tongue to such a pace. “Look, sir, my wounds!
I got them in my country’s service when
Some certain of your brethren roared and ran
From th’ noise of our own drums.”

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
O me, the gods!
You must not speak of that. You must desire them
To think upon you.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Think upon me? Hang ’em!
I would they would forget me, like the virtues
Which our divines lose by ’em.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
You’ll mar all.
I’ll leave you. Pray you, speak to ’em, I pray you,
In wholesome manner.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Bid them wash their faces
And keep their teeth clean.
So, here comes a brace.—
You know the cause, sir, of my standing here.

speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
text: We do, sir. Tell us what hath brought you to ’t.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Mine own desert.

speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
text: Your own desert?

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Ay, but not mine own desire.

speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
text: How, not your own desire?

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
No, sir, ’twas never my desire yet to trouble
the poor with begging.

speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
text:
You must think if we give you anything,
we hope to gain by you.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Well then, I pray, your price o’ th’
consulship?

speaker: FIRST CITIZEN
text: The price is to ask it kindly.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Kindly, sir, I pray, let me ha ’t. I have
wounds to show you, which shall be yours in
private.—Your good voice, sir. What say you?

speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
text: You shall ha ’t, worthy sir.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
A match, sir. There’s in all two worthy
voices begged. I have your alms. Adieu.

speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
text:
But this is something
odd.

speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
text:
An ’twere to give again—but ’tis no
matter.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Pray you now, if it may stand with the
tune of your voices that I may be consul, I have
here the customary gown.

speaker: FOURTH CITIZEN
text:
You have deserved nobly of your
country, and you have not deserved nobly.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Your enigma?

speaker: FOURTH CITIZEN
CORIOLANUS
text:
You should account me the more virtuous
that I have not been common in my love. I will, sir,
flatter my sworn brother, the people, to earn a
dearer estimation of them; ’tis a condition they account
gentle. And since the wisdom of their choice
is rather to have my hat than my heart, I will practice
the insinuating nod and be off to them most
counterfeitly. That is, sir, I will counterfeit the bewitchment
of some popular man and give it bountiful
to the desirers. Therefore, beseech you, I may
be consul.

speaker: FIFTH CITIZEN
text:
We hope to find you our friend, and
therefore give you our voices heartily.

speaker: FOURTH CITIZEN
text:
You have received many wounds for
your country.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
I will not seal your knowledge with showing
them. I will make much of your voices and so
trouble you no farther.

speaker: BOTH
text: The gods give you joy, sir, heartily.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Most sweet voices!
Better it is to die, better to starve,
Than crave the hire which first we do deserve.
Why in this woolvish toge should I stand here
To beg of Hob and Dick that does appear
Their needless vouches? Custom calls me to ’t.
What custom wills, in all things should we do ’t?
The dust on antique time would lie unswept
And mountainous error be too highly heaped
For truth to o’erpeer. Rather than fool it so,
Let the high office and the honor go
To one that would do thus. I am half through;
The one part suffered, the other will I do.
Here come more voices.—
Your voices! For your voices I have fought;
Watched for your voices; for your voices bear
Of wounds two dozen odd. Battles thrice six
I have seen and heard of; for your voices have
Done many things, some less, some more. Your voices!
Indeed, I would be consul.

speaker: SIXTH CITIZEN
text:
He has done nobly, and cannot go
without any honest man’s voice.

speaker: SEVENTH CITIZEN
text:
Therefore let him be consul. The
gods give him joy, and make him good friend to
the people!

speaker: ALL
text: Amen, amen. God save thee, noble consul.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Worthy voices!

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
You have stood your limitation, and the Tribunes
Endue you with the people’s voice. Remains
That in th’ official marks invested, you
Anon do meet the Senate.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Is this done?

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
The custom of request you have discharged.
The people do admit you, and are summoned
To meet anon upon your approbation.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Where? At the Senate House?

speaker: SICINIUS
text: There, Coriolanus.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: May I change these garments?

speaker: SICINIUS
text: You may, sir.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
That I’ll straight do and, knowing myself again,
Repair to th’ Senate House.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: I’ll keep you company.—Will you along?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: We stay here for the people.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Fare you well.
He has it now; and by his looks, methinks,
’Tis warm at ’s heart.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
With a proud heart he wore
His humble weeds. Will you dismiss the people?

speaker: SICINIUS
text: How now, my masters, have you chose this man?

speaker: FIRST CITIZEN
text: He has our voices, sir.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: We pray the gods he may deserve your loves.

speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
text:
Amen, sir. To my poor unworthy notice,
He mocked us when he begged our voices.

speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
text: Certainly, he flouted us downright.

speaker: FIRST CITIZEN
text: No, ’tis his kind of speech. He did not mock us.

speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
text:
Not one amongst us, save yourself, but says
He used us scornfully. He should have showed us
His marks of merit, wounds received for ’s country.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Why, so he did, I am sure.

speaker: ALL
text: No, no. No man saw ’em.

speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
text:
He said he had wounds, which he could show in private,
And with his hat, thus waving it in scorn,
“I would be consul,” says he. “Agèd custom,
But by your voices, will not so permit me;
Your voices therefore.” When we granted that,
Here was “I thank you for your voices. Thank you.
Your most sweet voices! Now you have left your voices,
I have no further with you.” Was not this mockery?

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Why either were you ignorant to see ’t
Or, seeing it, of such childish friendliness
To yield your voices?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Could you not have told him
As you were lessoned? When he had no power,
But was a petty servant to the state,
He was your enemy, ever spake against
Your liberties and the charters that you bear
I’ th’ body of the weal; and, now arriving
A place of potency and sway o’ th’ state,
If he should still malignantly remain
Fast foe to th’ plebeii, your voices might
Be curses to yourselves. You should have said
That as his worthy deeds did claim no less
Than what he stood for, so his gracious nature
Would think upon you for your voices, and
Translate his malice towards you into love,
Standing your friendly lord.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Thus to have said,
As you were fore-advised, had touched his spirit
And tried his inclination; from him plucked
Either his gracious promise, which you might,
As cause had called you up, have held him to;
Or else it would have galled his surly nature,
Which easily endures not article
Tying him to aught. So putting him to rage,
You should have ta’en th’ advantage of his choler
And passed him unelected.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Did you perceive
He did solicit you in free contempt
When he did need your loves, and do you think
That his contempt shall not be bruising to you
When he hath power to crush? Why, had your bodies
No heart among you? Or had you tongues to cry
Against the rectorship of judgment?

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Have you ere now denied the asker? And now
Again, of him that did not ask but mock,
Bestow your sued-for tongues?

speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
text:
He’s not confirmed.
We may deny him yet.

speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
text:
And will deny him.
I’ll have five hundred voices of that sound.

speaker: FIRST CITIZEN
text: I twice five hundred, and their friends to piece ’em.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Get you hence instantly, and tell those friends
They have chose a consul that will from them take
Their liberties, make them of no more voice
Than dogs that are as often beat for barking
As therefor kept to do so.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Let them assemble
And, on a safer judgment, all revoke
Your ignorant election. Enforce his pride
And his old hate unto you. Besides, forget not
With what contempt he wore the humble weed,
How in his suit he scorned you; but your loves,
Thinking upon his services, took from you
Th’ apprehension of his present portance,
Which most gibingly, ungravely, he did fashion
After the inveterate hate he bears you.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Lay
A fault on us, your tribunes, that we labored,
No impediment between, but that you must
Cast your election on him.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Say you chose him
More after our commandment than as guided
By your own true affections, and that your minds,
Preoccupied with what you rather must do
Than what you should, made you against the grain
To voice him consul. Lay the fault on us.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Ay, spare us not. Say we read lectures to you,
How youngly he began to serve his country,
How long continued, and what stock he springs of,
The noble house o’ th’ Martians, from whence came
That Ancus Martius, Numa’s daughter’s son,
Who after great Hostilius here was king,
Of the same house Publius and Quintus were,
That our best water brought by conduits hither;
And Censorinus, that was so surnamed,
And nobly namèd so, twice being censor,
Was his great ancestor.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
One thus descended,
That hath besides well in his person wrought
To be set high in place, we did commend
To your remembrances; but you have found,
Scaling his present bearing with his past,
That he’s your fixèd enemy, and revoke
Your sudden approbation.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Say you ne’er had done ’t—
Harp on that still—but by our putting on.
And presently, when you have drawn your number,
Repair to th’ Capitol.

speaker: ALL
text:
We will so. Almost all
Repent in their election.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Let them go on.
This mutiny were better put in hazard
Than stay, past doubt, for greater.
If, as his nature is, he fall in rage
With their refusal, both observe and answer
The vantage of his anger.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
To th’ Capitol, come.
We will be there before the stream o’ th’ people,
And this shall seem, as partly ’tis, their own,
Which we have goaded onward.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Tullus Aufidius then had made new head?

speaker: LARTIUS
text:
He had, my lord, and that it was which caused
Our swifter composition.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
So then the Volsces stand but as at first,
Ready, when time shall prompt them, to make road
Upon ’s again.

speaker: COMINIUS
text:
They are worn, lord consul, so,
That we shall hardly in our ages see
Their banners wave again.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Saw you Aufidius?

speaker: LARTIUS
text:
On safeguard he came to me, and did curse
Against the Volsces, for they had so vilely
Yielded the town. He is retired to Antium.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Spoke he of me?

speaker: LARTIUS
text: He did, my lord.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: How? What?

speaker: LARTIUS
text:
How often he had met you sword to sword;
That of all things upon the earth he hated
Your person most; that he would pawn his fortunes
To hopeless restitution, so he might
Be called your vanquisher.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: At Antium lives he?

speaker: LARTIUS
text: At Antium.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
I wish I had a cause to seek him there,
To oppose his hatred fully. Welcome home.
Behold, these are the tribunes of the people,
The tongues o’ th’ common mouth. I do despise them,
For they do prank them in authority
Against all noble sufferance.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Pass no further.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Ha? What is that?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: It will be dangerous to go on. No further.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: What makes this change?

speaker: MENENIUS
text: The matter?

speaker: COMINIUS
text: Hath he not passed the noble and the common?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Cominius, no.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Have I had children’s voices?

speaker: FIRST SENATOR
text: Tribunes, give way. He shall to th’ marketplace.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: The people are incensed against him.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Stop,
Or all will fall in broil.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Are these your herd?
Must these have voices, that can yield them now
And straight disclaim their tongues? What are your offices?
You being their mouths, why rule you not their teeth?
Have you not set them on?

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Be calm, be calm.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
It is a purposed thing, and grows by plot,
To curb the will of the nobility.
Suffer ’t, and live with such as cannot rule
Nor ever will be ruled.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Call ’t not a plot.
The people cry you mocked them; and, of late,
When corn was given them gratis, you repined,
Scandaled the suppliants for the people, called them
Timepleasers, flatterers, foes to nobleness.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Why, this was known before.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Not to them all.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Have you informed them sithence?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: How? I inform them?

speaker: COMINIUS
text: You are like to do such business.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Not unlike, each way, to better yours.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Why then should I be consul? By yond clouds,
Let me deserve so ill as you, and make me
Your fellow tribune.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
You show too much of that
For which the people stir. If you will pass
To where you are bound, you must inquire your way,
Which you are out of, with a gentler spirit,
Or never be so noble as a consul,
Nor yoke with him for tribune.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Let’s be calm.

speaker: COMINIUS
text:
The people are abused, set on. This palt’ring
Becomes not Rome, nor has Coriolanus
Deserved this so dishonored rub, laid falsely
I’ th’ plain way of his merit.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Tell me of corn?
This was my speech, and I will speak ’t again.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Not now, not now.

speaker: FIRST SENATOR
text: Not in this heat, sir, now.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Now, as I live, I will.
My nobler friends, I crave their pardons. For
The mutable, rank-scented meiny, let them
Regard me, as I do not flatter, and
Therein behold themselves. I say again,
In soothing them, we nourish ’gainst our senate
The cockle of rebellion, insolence, sedition,
Which we ourselves have plowed for, sowed, and scattered
By mingling them with us, the honored number,
Who lack not virtue, no, nor power, but that
Which they have given to beggars.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Well, no more.

speaker: FIRST SENATOR
text: No more words, we beseech you.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
How? No more?
As for my country I have shed my blood,
Not fearing outward force, so shall my lungs
Coin words till their decay against those measles
Which we disdain should tetter us, yet sought
The very way to catch them.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
You speak o’ th’ people
As if you were a god to punish, not
A man of their infirmity.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
’Twere well
We let the people know ’t.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: What, what? His choler?

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Choler?
Were I as patient as the midnight sleep,
By Jove, ’twould be my mind.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
It is a mind
That shall remain a poison where it is,
Not poison any further.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
“Shall remain”?
Hear you this Triton of the minnows? Mark you
His absolute “shall”?

speaker: COMINIUS
text: ’Twas from the canon.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
“Shall”?
O good but most unwise patricians, why,
You grave but reckless senators, have you thus
Given Hydra here to choose an officer,
That with his peremptory “shall,” being but
The horn and noise o’ th’ monster’s, wants not spirit
To say he’ll turn your current in a ditch
And make your channel his? If he have power,
Then vail your ignorance; if none, awake
Your dangerous lenity. If you are learned,
Be not as common fools; if you are not,
Let them have cushions by you. You are plebeians,
If they be senators; and they are no less
When, both your voices blended, the great’st taste
Most palates theirs. They choose their magistrate,
And such a one as he, who puts his “shall,”
His popular “shall,” against a graver bench
Than ever frowned in Greece. By Jove himself,
It makes the consuls base! And my soul aches
To know, when two authorities are up,
Neither supreme, how soon confusion
May enter ’twixt the gap of both and take
The one by th’ other.

speaker: COMINIUS
text: Well, on to th’ marketplace.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Whoever gave that counsel to give forth
The corn o’ th’ storehouse gratis, as ’twas used
Sometime in Greece—

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Well, well, no more of that.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Though there the people had more absolute power,
I say they nourished disobedience, fed
The ruin of the state.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Why shall the people give
One that speaks thus their voice?

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
I’ll give my reasons,
More worthier than their voices. They know the corn
Was not our recompense, resting well assured
They ne’er did service for ’t. Being pressed to th’ war,
Even when the navel of the state was touched,
They would not thread the gates. This kind of service
Did not deserve corn gratis. Being i’ th’ war,
Their mutinies and revolts, wherein they showed
Most valor, spoke not for them. Th’ accusation
Which they have often made against the Senate,
All cause unborn, could never be the native
Of our so frank donation. Well, what then?
How shall this bosom multiplied digest
The Senate’s courtesy? Let deeds express
What’s like to be their words: “We did request it;
We are the greater poll, and in true fear
They gave us our demands.” Thus we debase
The nature of our seats and make the rabble
Call our cares fears, which will in time
Break ope the locks o’ th’ Senate and bring in
The crows to peck the eagles.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Come, enough.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Enough, with over-measure.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
No, take more!
What may be sworn by, both divine and human,
Seal what I end withal! This double worship—
Where one part does disdain with cause, the other
Insult without all reason, where gentry, title, wisdom
Cannot conclude but by the yea and no
Of general ignorance—it must omit
Real necessities and give way the while
To unstable slightness. Purpose so barred, it follows
Nothing is done to purpose. Therefore, beseech you—
You that will be less fearful than discreet,
That love the fundamental part of state
More than you doubt the change on ’t, that prefer
A noble life before a long, and wish
To jump a body with a dangerous physic
That’s sure of death without it—at once pluck out
The multitudinous tongue; let them not lick
The sweet which is their poison. Your dishonor
Mangles true judgment and bereaves the state
Of that integrity which should become ’t,
Not having the power to do the good it would
For th’ ill which doth control ’t.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: ’Has said enough.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
’Has spoken like a traitor and shall answer
As traitors do.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Thou wretch, despite o’erwhelm thee!
What should the people do with these bald tribunes,
On whom depending, their obedience fails
To th’ greater bench? In a rebellion,
When what’s not meet but what must be was law,
Then were they chosen. In a better hour,
Let what is meet be said it must be meet,
And throw their power i’ th’ dust.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Manifest treason.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: This a consul? No.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: The aediles, ho! Let him be apprehended.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Go, call the people; in whose name myself
Attach thee as a traitorous innovator,
A foe to th’ public weal. Obey, I charge thee,
And follow to thine answer.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Hence, old goat.

speaker: ALL PATRICIANS
text: We’ll surety him.

speaker: COMINIUS
text: Agèd sir, hands off.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Hence, rotten thing, or I shall shake thy bones
Out of thy garments.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Help, you citizens!

speaker: MENENIUS
text: On both sides more respect!

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Here’s he that would take from you all your power.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Seize him, aediles.

speaker: ALL PLEBEIANS
text: Down with him, down with him!

speaker: SECOND SENATOR
text:
Weapons, weapons, weapons!
Tribunes, patricians, citizens, what ho!
Sicinius, Brutus, Coriolanus, citizens!

speaker: ALL
text: Peace, peace, peace! Stay, hold, peace!

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
What is about to be? I am out of breath.
Confusion’s near. I cannot speak. You, tribunes
To th’ people!—Coriolanus, patience!—
Speak, good Sicinius.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Hear me, people! Peace!

speaker: ALL PLEBEIANS
text: Let’s hear our tribune. Peace! Speak, speak, speak.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
You are at point to lose your liberties.
Martius would have all from you, Martius,
Whom late you have named for consul.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Fie, fie, fie!
This is the way to kindle, not to quench.

speaker: FIRST SENATOR
text: To unbuild the city and to lay all flat.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: What is the city but the people?

speaker: ALL PLEBEIANS
text:
True,
The people are the city.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
By the consent of all, we were established
The people’s magistrates.

speaker: ALL PLEBEIANS
text: You so remain.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: And so are like to do.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
That is the way to lay the city flat,
To bring the roof to the foundation
And bury all which yet distinctly ranges
In heaps and piles of ruin.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: This deserves death.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Or let us stand to our authority
Or let us lose it. We do here pronounce,
Upon the part o’ th’ people, in whose power
We were elected theirs, Martius is worthy
Of present death.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Therefore lay hold of him,
Bear him to th’ rock Tarpeian, and from thence
Into destruction cast him.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Aediles, seize him!

speaker: ALL PLEBEIANS
text: Yield, Martius, yield!

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Hear me one word.
Beseech you, tribunes, hear me but a word.

speaker: AEDILES
text: Peace, peace!

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Be that you seem, truly your country’s friend,
And temp’rately proceed to what you would
Thus violently redress.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Sir, those cold ways,
That seem like prudent helps, are very poisonous
Where the disease is violent.—Lay hands upon him,
And bear him to the rock.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
No, I’ll die here.
There’s some among you have beheld me fighting.
Come, try upon yourselves what you have seen me.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Down with that sword!—Tribunes, withdraw awhile.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Lay hands upon him!

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Help Martius, help!
You that be noble, help him, young and old!

speaker: ALL PLEBEIANS
text: Down with him, down with him!

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Go, get you to your house. Begone, away.
All will be naught else.

speaker: SECOND SENATOR
text: Get you gone.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Stand fast!
We have as many friends as enemies.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Shall it be put to that?

speaker: FIRST SENATOR
MENENIUS
text:
For ’tis a sore upon us
You cannot tent yourself. Begone, beseech you.

speaker: COMINIUS
text: Come, sir, along with us.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
I would they were barbarians, as they are,
Though in Rome littered; not Romans, as they are not,
Though calved i’ th’ porch o’ th’ Capitol.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Begone!
Put not your worthy rage into your tongue.
One time will owe another.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
On fair ground
I could beat forty of them.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
I could myself
Take up a brace o’ th’ best of them, yea, the two tribunes.

speaker: COMINIUS
text:
But now ’tis odds beyond arithmetic,
And manhood is called foolery when it stands
Against a falling fabric. Will you hence,
Before the tag return, whose rage doth rend
Like interrupted waters and o’erbear
What they are used to bear?

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Pray you, begone.
I’ll try whether my old wit be in request
With those that have but little. This must be patched
With cloth of any color.

speaker: COMINIUS
text: Nay, come away.

speaker: PATRICIAN
text: This man has marred his fortune.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
His nature is too noble for the world.
He would not flatter Neptune for his trident
Or Jove for ’s power to thunder. His heart’s his mouth;
What his breast forges, that his tongue must vent,
And, being angry, does forget that ever
He heard the name of death.
Here’s goodly work.

speaker: PATRICIAN
text: I would they were abed!

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
I would they were in Tiber. What the vengeance,
Could he not speak ’em fair?

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Where is this viper
That would depopulate the city and
Be every man himself?

speaker: MENENIUS
text: You worthy tribunes—

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
He shall be thrown down the Tarpeian rock
With rigorous hands. He hath resisted law,
And therefore law shall scorn him further trial
Than the severity of the public power
Which he so sets at naught.

speaker: FIRST CITIZEN
text:
He shall well know
The noble tribunes are the people’s mouths
And we their hands.

speaker: ALL PLEBEIANS
text: He shall, sure on ’t.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Sir, sir—

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Peace!

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Do not cry havoc where you should but hunt
With modest warrant.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Sir, how comes 't that you
Have holp to make this rescue?

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Hear me speak.
As I do know the Consul’s worthiness,
So can I name his faults.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Consul? What consul?

speaker: MENENIUS
text: The consul Coriolanus.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: He consul?

speaker: ALL PLEBEIANS
text: No, no, no, no, no!

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
If, by the Tribunes’ leave, and yours, good people,
I may be heard, I would crave a word or two,
The which shall turn you to no further harm
Than so much loss of time.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Speak briefly then,
For we are peremptory to dispatch
This viperous traitor. To eject him hence
Were but one danger, and to keep him here
Our certain death. Therefore it is decreed
He dies tonight.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Now the good gods forbid
That our renownèd Rome, whose gratitude
Towards her deservèd children is enrolled
In Jove’s own book, like an unnatural dam
Should now eat up her own.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: He’s a disease that must be cut away.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
O, he’s a limb that has but a disease—
Mortal to cut it off; to cure it easy.
What has he done to Rome that’s worthy death?
Killing our enemies, the blood he hath lost—
Which I dare vouch is more than that he hath
By many an ounce—he dropped it for his country;
And what is left, to lose it by his country
Were to us all that do ’t and suffer it
A brand to th’ end o’ th’ world.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: This is clean cam.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Merely awry. When he did love his country,
It honored him.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
The service of the foot,
Being once gangrened, is not then respected
For what before it was.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
We’ll hear no more.
Pursue him to his house, and pluck him thence,
Lest his infection, being of catching nature,
Spread further.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
One word more, one word!
This tiger-footed rage, when it shall find
The harm of unscanned swiftness, will too late
Tie leaden pounds to ’s heels. Proceed by process,
Lest parties—as he is beloved—break out
And sack great Rome with Romans.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: If it were so—

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
What do you talk?
Have we not had a taste of his obedience?
Our aediles smote! Ourselves resisted! Come.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Consider this: he has been bred i’ th’ wars
Since he could draw a sword, and is ill schooled
In bolted language; meal and bran together
He throws without distinction. Give me leave,
I’ll go to him and undertake to bring him
Where he shall answer by a lawful form,
In peace, to his utmost peril.

speaker: FIRST SENATOR
text:
Noble tribunes,
It is the humane way: the other course
Will prove too bloody, and the end of it
Unknown to the beginning.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Noble Menenius,
Be you then as the people’s officer.—
Masters, lay down your weapons.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Go not home.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Meet on the marketplace. We’ll attend you there,
Where if you bring not Martius, we’ll proceed
In our first way.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
I’ll bring him to you.
Let me desire your company. He must come,
Or what is worst will follow.

speaker: FIRST SENATOR
text: Pray you, let’s to him.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Let them pull all about mine ears, present me
Death on the wheel or at wild horses’ heels,
Or pile ten hills on the Tarpeian rock,
That the precipitation might down stretch
Below the beam of sight, yet will I still
Be thus to them.

speaker: NOBLE
text: You do the nobler.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
I muse my mother
Does not approve me further, who was wont
To call them woolen vassals, things created
To buy and sell with groats, to show bare heads
In congregations, to yawn, be still, and wonder
When one but of my ordinance stood up
To speak of peace or war.
I talk of you.
Why did you wish me milder? Would you have me
False to my nature? Rather say I play
The man I am.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
O sir, sir, sir,
I would have had you put your power well on
Before you had worn it out.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Let go.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
You might have been enough the man you are
With striving less to be so. Lesser had been
The thwartings of your dispositions if
You had not showed them how you were disposed
Ere they lacked power to cross you.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Let them hang!

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text: Ay, and burn too.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Come, come, you have been too rough, something too rough.
You must return and mend it.

speaker: FIRST SENATOR
text:
There’s no remedy,
Unless, by not so doing, our good city
Cleave in the midst and perish.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
Pray be counseled.
I have a heart as little apt as yours,
But yet a brain that leads my use of anger
To better vantage.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Well said, noble woman.
Before he should thus stoop to th’ herd—but that
The violent fit o’ th’ time craves it as physic
For the whole state—I would put mine armor on,
Which I can scarcely bear.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: What must I do?

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Return to th’ Tribunes.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Well, what then? What then?

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Repent what you have spoke.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
For them? I cannot do it to the gods.
Must I then do ’t to them?

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
You are too absolute,
Though therein you can never be too noble
But when extremities speak. I have heard you say
Honor and policy, like unsevered friends,
I’ th’ war do grow together. Grant that, and tell me
In peace what each of them by th’ other lose
That they combine not there?

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Tush, tush!

speaker: MENENIUS
text: A good demand.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
If it be honor in your wars to seem
The same you are not, which for your best ends
You adopt your policy, how is it less or worse
That it shall hold companionship in peace
With honor as in war, since that to both
It stands in like request?

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Why force you this?

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
Because that now it lies you on to speak
To th’ people, not by your own instruction,
Nor by th’ matter which your heart prompts you,
But with such words that are but roted in
Your tongue, though but bastards and syllables
Of no allowance to your bosom’s truth.
Now, this no more dishonors you at all
Than to take in a town with gentle words,
Which else would put you to your fortune and
The hazard of much blood.
I would dissemble with my nature where
My fortunes and my friends at stake required
I should do so in honor. I am in this
Your wife, your son, these senators, the nobles;
And you will rather show our general louts
How you can frown than spend a fawn upon ’em
For the inheritance of their loves and safeguard
Of what that want might ruin.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Noble lady!—
Come, go with us; speak fair. You may salve so,
Not what is dangerous present, but the loss
Of what is past.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
I prithee now, my son,
Go to them with this bonnet in thy hand,
And thus far having stretched it—here be with them—
Thy knee bussing the stones—for in such business
Action is eloquence, and the eyes of th’ ignorant
More learnèd than the ears—waving thy head,
Which often thus correcting thy stout heart,
Now humble as the ripest mulberry
That will not hold the handling. Or say to them
Thou art their soldier and, being bred in broils,
Hast not the soft way, which thou dost confess
Were fit for thee to use as they to claim,
In asking their good loves; but thou wilt frame
Thyself, forsooth, hereafter theirs, so far
As thou hast power and person.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
This but done
Even as she speaks, why, their hearts were yours;
For they have pardons, being asked, as free
As words to little purpose.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
Prithee now,
Go, and be ruled; although I know thou hadst rather
Follow thine enemy in a fiery gulf
Than flatter him in a bower.
Here is Cominius.

speaker: COMINIUS
text:
I have been i’ th’ marketplace; and, sir, ’tis fit
You make strong party or defend yourself
By calmness or by absence. All’s in anger.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Only fair speech.

speaker: COMINIUS
text:
I think ’twill serve, if he
Can thereto frame his spirit.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
He must, and will.—
Prithee, now, say you will, and go about it.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Must I go show them my unbarbèd sconce? Must I
With my base tongue give to my noble heart
A lie that it must bear? Well, I will do ’t.
Yet, were there but this single plot to lose,
This mold of Martius, they to dust should grind it
And throw ’t against the wind. To th’ marketplace!
You have put me now to such a part which never
I shall discharge to th’ life.

speaker: COMINIUS
text: Come, come, we’ll prompt you.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
I prithee now, sweet son, as thou hast said
My praises made thee first a soldier, so,
To have my praise for this, perform a part
Thou hast not done before.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Well, I must do ’t.
Away, my disposition, and possess me
Some harlot’s spirit! My throat of war be turned,
Which choirèd with my drum, into a pipe
Small as an eunuch or the virgin voice
That babies lull asleep! The smiles of knaves
Tent in my cheeks, and schoolboys’ tears take up
The glasses of my sight! A beggar’s tongue
Make motion through my lips, and my armed knees,
Who bowed but in my stirrup, bend like his
That hath received an alms. I will not do ’t,
Lest I surcease to honor mine own truth
And, by my body’s action, teach my mind
A most inherent baseness.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
At thy choice, then.
To beg of thee, it is my more dishonor
Than thou of them. Come all to ruin. Let
Thy mother rather feel thy pride than fear
Thy dangerous stoutness, for I mock at death
With as big heart as thou. Do as thou list.
Thy valiantness was mine; thou suck’st it from me,
But owe thy pride thyself.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Pray be content.
Mother, I am going to the marketplace.
Chide me no more. I’ll mountebank their loves,
Cog their hearts from them, and come home beloved
Of all the trades in Rome. Look, I am going.
Commend me to my wife. I’ll return consul,
Or never trust to what my tongue can do
I’ th’ way of flattery further.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text: Do your will.

speaker: COMINIUS
text:
Away! The Tribunes do attend you. Arm yourself
To answer mildly, for they are prepared
With accusations, as I hear, more strong
Than are upon you yet.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
The word is “mildly.” Pray you, let us go.
Let them accuse me by invention, I
Will answer in mine honor.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Ay, but mildly.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Well, mildly be it, then. Mildly.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
In this point charge him home, that he affects
Tyrannical power. If he evade us there,
Enforce him with his envy to the people,
And that the spoil got on the Antiates
Was ne’er distributed.
What, will he come?

speaker: AEDILE
text: He’s coming.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: How accompanied?

speaker: AEDILE
text:
With old Menenius, and those senators
That always favored him.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Have you a catalogue
Of all the voices that we have procured,
Set down by th’ poll?

speaker: AEDILE
text: I have. ’Tis ready.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Have you collected them by tribes?

speaker: AEDILE
text: I have.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Assemble presently the people hither;
And when they hear me say “It shall be so
I’ th’ right and strength o’ th’ commons,” be it either
For death, for fine, or banishment, then let them
If I say “Fine,” cry “Fine,” if “Death,” cry “Death,”
Insisting on the old prerogative
And power i’ th’ truth o’ th’ cause.

speaker: AEDILE
text: I shall inform them.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
And when such time they have begun to cry,
Let them not cease, but with a din confused
Enforce the present execution
Of what we chance to sentence.

speaker: AEDILE
text: Very well.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Make them be strong and ready for this hint
When we shall hap to give ’t them.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Go about it.
Put him to choler straight. He hath been used
Ever to conquer and to have his worth
Of contradiction. Being once chafed, he cannot
Be reined again to temperance; then he speaks
What’s in his heart, and that is there which looks
With us to break his neck.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Well, here he comes.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Calmly, I do beseech you.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Ay, as an hostler that for th’ poorest piece
Will bear the knave by th’ volume.—Th’ honored gods
Keep Rome in safety and the chairs of justice
Supplied with worthy men! Plant love among ’s!
Throng our large temples with the shows of peace
And not our streets with war!

speaker: FIRST SENATOR
text: Amen, amen.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: A noble wish.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Draw near, you people.

speaker: AEDILE
text: List to your tribunes. Audience! Peace, I say!

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: First, hear me speak.

speaker: BOTH TRIBUNES
text: Well, say.—Peace, ho!

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Shall I be charged no further than this present?
Must all determine here?

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
I do demand
If you submit you to the people’s voices,
Allow their officers, and are content
To suffer lawful censure for such faults
As shall be proved upon you.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: I am content.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Lo, citizens, he says he is content.
The warlike service he has done, consider. Think
Upon the wounds his body bears, which show
Like graves i’ th’ holy churchyard.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Scratches with briars,
Scars to move laughter only.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
Consider further,
That when he speaks not like a citizen,
You find him like a soldier. Do not take
His rougher accents for malicious sounds,
But, as I say, such as become a soldier
Rather than envy you.

speaker: COMINIUS
text: Well, well, no more.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
What is the matter,
That, being passed for consul with full voice,
I am so dishonored that the very hour
You take it off again?

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Answer to us.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Say then. ’Tis true, I ought so.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
We charge you that you have contrived to take
From Rome all seasoned office and to wind
Yourself into a power tyrannical,
For which you are a traitor to the people.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: How? Traitor?

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Nay, temperately! Your promise.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
The fires i’ th’ lowest hell fold in the people!
Call me their traitor? Thou injurious tribune!
Within thine eyes sat twenty thousand deaths,
In thy hands clutched as many millions, in
Thy lying tongue both numbers, I would say
“Thou liest” unto thee with a voice as free
As I do pray the gods.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Mark you this, people?

speaker: ALL PLEBEIANS
text: To th’ rock, to th’ rock with him!

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Peace!
We need not put new matter to his charge.
What you have seen him do and heard him speak,
Beating your officers, cursing yourselves,
Opposing laws with strokes, and here defying
Those whose great power must try him—even this,
So criminal and in such capital kind,
Deserves th’ extremest death.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
But since he hath
Served well for Rome—

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: What do you prate of service?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: I talk of that that know it.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: You?

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Is this the promise that you made your mother?

speaker: COMINIUS
text: Know, I pray you—

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
I’ll know no further.
Let them pronounce the steep Tarpeian death,
Vagabond exile, flaying, pent to linger
But with a grain a day, I would not buy
Their mercy at the price of one fair word,
Nor check my courage for what they can give,
To have ’t with saying “Good morrow.”

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
For that he has,
As much as in him lies, from time to time
Envied against the people, seeking means
To pluck away their power, as now at last
Given hostile strokes, and that not in the presence
Of dreaded justice, but on the ministers
That doth distribute it, in the name o’ th’ people
And in the power of us the Tribunes, we,
Even from this instant, banish him our city
In peril of precipitation
From off the rock Tarpeian, never more
To enter our Rome gates. I’ th’ people’s name,
I say it shall be so.

speaker: ALL PLEBEIANS
text:
It shall be so, it shall be so! Let him away!
He’s banished, and it shall be so.

speaker: COMINIUS
text: Hear me, my masters and my common friends—

speaker: SICINIUS
text: He’s sentenced. No more hearing.

speaker: COMINIUS
text:
Let me speak.
I have been consul and can show for Rome
Her enemies’ marks upon me. I do love
My country’s good with a respect more tender,
More holy and profound, than mine own life,
My dear wife’s estimate, her womb’s increase,
And treasure of my loins. Then if I would
Speak that—

speaker: SICINIUS
text: We know your drift. Speak what?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
There’s no more to be said, but he is banished
As enemy to the people and his country.
It shall be so.

speaker: ALL PLEBEIANS
text: It shall be so, it shall be so!

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
You common cry of curs, whose breath I hate
As reek o’ th’ rotten fens, whose loves I prize
As the dead carcasses of unburied men
That do corrupt my air, I banish you!
And here remain with your uncertainty;
Let every feeble rumor shake your hearts;
Your enemies, with nodding of their plumes,
Fan you into despair! Have the power still
To banish your defenders, till at length
Your ignorance—which finds not till it feels,
Making but reservation of yourselves,
Still your own foes—deliver you
As most abated captives to some nation
That won you without blows! Despising
For you the city, thus I turn my back.
There is a world elsewhere.

speaker: AEDILE
text: The people’s enemy is gone, is gone.

speaker: ALL PLEBEIANS
text: Our enemy is banished; he is gone. Hoo, hoo!

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Go see him out at gates, and follow him,
As he hath followed you, with all despite.
Give him deserved vexation. Let a guard
Attend us through the city.

speaker: ALL PLEBEIANS
text:
Come, come, let’s see him out at gates! Come!
The gods preserve our noble tribunes! Come!

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Come, leave your tears. A brief farewell. The beast
With many heads butts me away. Nay, mother,
Where is your ancient courage? You were used
To say extremities was the trier of spirits;
That common chances common men could bear;
That when the sea was calm, all boats alike
Showed mastership in floating; fortune’s blows
When most struck home, being gentle wounded craves
A noble cunning. You were used to load me
With precepts that would make invincible
The heart that conned them.

speaker: VIRGILIA
text: O heavens! O heavens!

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Nay, I prithee, woman—

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
Now the red pestilence strike all trades in Rome,
And occupations perish!

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
What, what, what!
I shall be loved when I am lacked. Nay, mother,
Resume that spirit when you were wont to say
If you had been the wife of Hercules,
Six of his labors you’d have done and saved
Your husband so much sweat.—Cominius,
Droop not. Adieu.—Farewell, my wife, my mother.
I’ll do well yet.—Thou old and true Menenius,
Thy tears are salter than a younger man’s
And venomous to thine eyes.—My sometime general,
I have seen thee stern, and thou hast oft beheld
Heart-hard’ning spectacles. Tell these sad women
’Tis fond to wail inevitable strokes
As ’tis to laugh at ’em.—My mother, you wot well
My hazards still have been your solace, and—
Believe ’t not lightly—though I go alone,
Like to a lonely dragon that his fen
Makes feared and talked of more than seen, your son
Will or exceed the common or be caught
With cautelous baits and practice.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
My first son,
Whither wilt thou go? Take good Cominius
With thee awhile. Determine on some course
More than a wild exposure to each chance
That starts i’ th’ way before thee.

speaker: VIRGILIA
text: O the gods!

speaker: COMINIUS
text:
I’ll follow thee a month, devise with thee
Where thou shalt rest, that thou mayst hear of us
And we of thee; so if the time thrust forth
A cause for thy repeal, we shall not send
O’er the vast world to seek a single man
And lose advantage, which doth ever cool
I’ th’ absence of the needer.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Fare you well.
Thou hast years upon thee, and thou art too full
Of the wars’ surfeits to go rove with one
That’s yet unbruised. Bring me but out at gate.—
Come, my sweet wife, my dearest mother, and
My friends of noble touch. When I am forth,
Bid me farewell, and smile. I pray you, come.
While I remain above the ground, you shall
Hear from me still, and never of me aught
But what is like me formerly.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
That’s worthily
As any ear can hear. Come, let’s not weep.
If I could shake off but one seven years
From these old arms and legs, by the good gods,
I’d with thee every foot.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Give me thy hand.
Come.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Bid them all home. He’s gone, and we’ll no further.
The nobility are vexed, whom we see have sided
In his behalf.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Now we have shown our power,
Let us seem humbler after it is done
Than when it was a-doing.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Bid them home.
Say their great enemy is gone, and they
Stand in their ancient strength.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Dismiss them home.
Here comes his mother.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Let’s not meet her.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Why?

speaker: SICINIUS
text: They say she’s mad.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: They have ta’en note of us. Keep on your way.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
O, you’re well met. The hoarded plague o’ th’ gods
Requite your love!

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Peace, peace! Be not so loud.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
If that I could for weeping, you should hear—
Nay, and you shall hear some. Will you be gone?

speaker: VIRGILIA
text:
You shall stay too. I would I had the power
To say so to my husband.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: Are you mankind?

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
Ay, fool, is that a shame? Note but this, fool.
Was not a man my father? Hadst thou foxship
To banish him that struck more blows for Rome
Than thou hast spoken words?

speaker: SICINIUS
text: O blessèd heavens!

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
More noble blows than ever thou wise words,
And for Rome’s good. I’ll tell thee what—yet go.
Nay, but thou shalt stay too. I would my son
Were in Arabia and thy tribe before him,
His good sword in his hand.

speaker: SICINIUS
text: What then?

speaker: VIRGILIA
text:
What then?
He’d make an end of thy posterity.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
Bastards and all.
Good man, the wounds that he does bear for Rome!

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Come, come, peace.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
I would he had continued to his country
As he began, and not unknit himself
The noble knot he made.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: I would he had.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
“I would he had”? ’Twas you incensed the rabble.
Cats, that can judge as fitly of his worth
As I can of those mysteries which heaven
Will not have Earth to know.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Pray, let’s go.

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
Now, pray, sir, get you gone.
You have done a brave deed. Ere you go, hear this:
As far as doth the Capitol exceed
The meanest house in Rome, so far my son—
This lady’s husband here, this, do you see?—
Whom you have banished, does exceed you all.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Well, well, we’ll leave you.

speaker: SICINIUS
text:
Why stay we to be baited
With one that wants her wits?

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
Take my prayers with you.
I would the gods had nothing else to do
But to confirm my curses. Could I meet ’em
But once a day, it would unclog my heart
Of what lies heavy to ’t.

speaker: MENENIUS
text:
You have told them home,
And, by my troth, you have cause. You’ll sup with me?

speaker: VOLUMNIA
text:
Anger’s my meat. I sup upon myself
And so shall starve with feeding.
Come, let’s go.
Leave this faint puling, and lament as I do,
In anger, Juno-like. Come, come, come.

speaker: MENENIUS
text: Fie, fie, fie!

speaker: ROMAN
text:
I know you well, sir, and you know me. Your
name I think is Adrian.

speaker: VOLSCE
text: It is so, sir. Truly, I have forgot you.

speaker: ROMAN
text:
I am a Roman, and my services are, as you are,
against ’em. Know you me yet?

speaker: VOLSCE
text: Nicanor, no?

speaker: ROMAN
text: The same, sir.

speaker: VOLSCE
text:
You had more beard when I last saw you, but
your favor is well approved by your tongue.
What’s the news in Rome? I have a note from the
Volscian state to find you out there. You have well
saved me a day’s journey.

speaker: ROMAN
text:
There hath been in Rome strange insurrections,
the people against the senators, patricians,
and nobles.

speaker: VOLSCE
text:
Hath been? Is it ended, then? Our state thinks
not so. They are in a most warlike preparation and
hope to come upon them in the heat of their
division.

speaker: ROMAN
text:
The main blaze of it is past, but a small thing
would make it flame again; for the nobles receive
so to heart the banishment of that worthy Coriolanus
that they are in a ripe aptness to take all power
from the people and to pluck from them their tribunes
forever. This lies glowing, I can tell you, and
is almost mature for the violent breaking out.

speaker: VOLSCE
text: Coriolanus banished?

speaker: ROMAN
text: Banished, sir.

speaker: VOLSCE
text:
You will be welcome with this intelligence,
Nicanor.

speaker: ROMAN
text:
The day serves well for them now. I have heard
it said the fittest time to corrupt a man’s wife is
when she’s fall’n out with her husband. Your noble
Tullus Aufidius will appear well in these wars, his
great opposer Coriolanus being now in no request
of his country.

speaker: VOLSCE
text:
He cannot choose. I am most fortunate thus
accidentally to encounter you. You have ended my
business, and I will merrily accompany you home.

speaker: ROMAN
text:
I shall between this and supper tell you most
strange things from Rome, all tending to the good
of their adversaries. Have you an army ready, say
you?

speaker: VOLSCE
text:
A most royal one. The centurions and their
charges, distinctly billeted, already in th’ entertainment,
and to be on foot at an hour’s warning.

speaker: ROMAN
text:
I am joyful to hear of their readiness and am
the man, I think, that shall set them in present action.
So, sir, heartily well met, and most glad of
your company.

speaker: VOLSCE
text:
You take my part from me, sir. I have the most
cause to be glad of yours.

speaker: ROMAN
text: Well, let us go together.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
A goodly city is this Antium. City,
’Tis I that made thy widows. Many an heir
Of these fair edifices ’fore my wars
Have I heard groan and drop. Then, know me not,
Lest that thy wives with spits and boys with stones
In puny battle slay me.
Save you, sir.

speaker: CITIZEN
text: And you.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Direct me, if it be your will,
Where great Aufidius lies. Is he in Antium?

speaker: CITIZEN
text:
He is, and feasts the nobles of the state
At his house this night.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Which is his house, beseech you?

speaker: CITIZEN
text: This here before you.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Thank you, sir. Farewell.
O world, thy slippery turns! Friends now fast sworn,
Whose double bosoms seems to wear one heart,
Whose hours, whose bed, whose meal and exercise
Are still together, who twin, as ’twere, in love
Unseparable, shall within this hour,
On a dissension of a doit, break out
To bitterest enmity; so fellest foes,
Whose passions and whose plots have broke their sleep
To take the one the other, by some chance,
Some trick not worth an egg, shall grow dear friends
And interjoin their issues. So with me:
My birthplace hate I, and my love’s upon
This enemy town. I’ll enter. If he slay me,
He does fair justice; if he give me way,
I’ll do his country service.

speaker: FIRST SERVINGMAN
text:
Wine, wine, wine! What service is
here? I think our fellows are asleep.

speaker: SECOND SERVINGMAN
text:
Where’s Cotus? My master calls
for him. Cotus!

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
A goodly house. The feast smells well, but I
Appear not like a guest.

speaker: FIRST SERVINGMAN
text:
What would you have, friend?
Whence are you? Here’s no place for you. Pray, go
to the door.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
I have deserved no better entertainment
In being Coriolanus.

speaker: SECOND SERVINGMAN
text:
Whence are you, sir?—Has the
porter his eyes in his head, that he gives entrance
to such companions?—Pray, get you out.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Away!

speaker: SECOND SERVINGMAN
text: Away? Get you away.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Now th’ art troublesome.

speaker: SECOND SERVINGMAN
text:
Are you so brave? I’ll have you
talked with anon.

speaker: THIRD SERVINGMAN
text: What fellow’s this?

speaker: FIRST SERVINGMAN
text:
A strange one as ever I looked on. I
cannot get him out o’ th’ house. Prithee, call my
master to him.

speaker: THIRD SERVINGMAN
text:
What have you to do here, fellow?
Pray you, avoid the house.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Let me but stand. I will not hurt your
hearth.

speaker: THIRD SERVINGMAN
text: What are you?

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: A gentleman.

speaker: THIRD SERVINGMAN
text: A marv’llous poor one.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: True, so I am.

speaker: THIRD SERVINGMAN
text:
Pray you, poor gentleman, take up
some other station. Here’s no place for you. Pray
you, avoid. Come.

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Follow your function, go, and batten on
cold bits.

speaker: THIRD SERVINGMAN
text:
What, you will not?—Prithee, tell
my master what a strange guest he has here.

speaker: SECOND SERVINGMAN
text: And I shall.

speaker: THIRD SERVINGMAN
text: Where dwell’st thou?

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Under the canopy.

speaker: THIRD SERVINGMAN
text: Under the canopy?

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: Ay.

speaker: THIRD SERVINGMAN
text: Where’s that?

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: I’ th’ city of kites and crows.

speaker: THIRD SERVINGMAN
text:
I’ th’ city of kites and crows? What
an ass it is! Then thou dwell’st with daws too?

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text: No, I serve not thy master.

speaker: THIRD SERVINGMAN
text:
How, sir? Do you meddle with my
master?

speaker: CORIOLANUS
text:
Ay, ’tis an honester service than to meddle
with thy mistress. Thou prat’st and prat’st. Serve
with thy trencher. Hence!

speaker: AUFIDIUS
text: Where is this fellow?

speaker: SECOND SERVINGMAN
