But life, being weary of these worldly bars,
Never lacks power to dismiss itself.
If I know this, know all the world besides,
That part of tyranny that I do bear
I can shake off at pleasure.

speaker: CASCA
text:
So can I.
So every bondman in his own hand bears
The power to cancel his captivity.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
And why should Caesar be a tyrant, then?
Poor man, I know he would not be a wolf
But that he sees the Romans are but sheep;
He were no lion, were not Romans hinds.
Those that with haste will make a mighty fire
Begin it with weak straws. What trash is Rome,
What rubbish, and what offal when it serves
For the base matter to illuminate
So vile a thing as Caesar! But, O grief,
Where hast thou led me? I perhaps speak this
Before a willing bondman; then, I know
My answer must be made. But I am armed,
And dangers are to me indifferent.

speaker: CASCA
text:
You speak to Casca, and to such a man
That is no fleering telltale. Hold. My hand.
Be factious for redress of all these griefs,
And I will set this foot of mine as far
As who goes farthest.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
There’s a bargain made.
Now know you, Casca, I have moved already
Some certain of the noblest-minded Romans
To undergo with me an enterprise
Of honorable-dangerous consequence.
And I do know by this they stay for me
In Pompey’s Porch. For now, this fearful night,
There is no stir or walking in the streets;
And the complexion of the element
In favor ’s like the work we have in hand,
Most bloody, fiery, and most terrible.

speaker: CASCA
text: Stand close awhile, for here comes one in haste.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
’Tis Cinna; I do know him by his gait.
He is a friend.—Cinna, where haste you so?

speaker: CINNA
text: To find out you. Who’s that? Metellus Cimber?

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
No, it is Casca, one incorporate
To our attempts. Am I not stayed for, Cinna?

speaker: CINNA
text:
I am glad on ’t. What a fearful night is this!
There’s two or three of us have seen strange sights.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Am I not stayed for? Tell me.

speaker: CINNA
text:
Yes, you are. O Cassius, if you could
But win the noble Brutus to our party—

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Be you content. Good Cinna, take this paper,
And look you lay it in the Praetor’s chair,
Where Brutus may but find it; and throw this
In at his window; set this up with wax
Upon old Brutus’ statue. All this done,
Repair to Pompey’s Porch, where you shall find us.
Is Decius Brutus and Trebonius there?

speaker: CINNA
text:
All but Metellus Cimber, and he’s gone
To seek you at your house. Well, I will hie
And so bestow these papers as you bade me.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
That done, repair to Pompey’s Theater.
Come, Casca, you and I will yet ere day
See Brutus at his house. Three parts of him
Is ours already, and the man entire
Upon the next encounter yields him ours.

speaker: CASCA
text:
O, he sits high in all the people’s hearts,
And that which would appear offense in us
His countenance, like richest alchemy,
Will change to virtue and to worthiness.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Him and his worth and our great need of him
You have right well conceited. Let us go,
For it is after midnight, and ere day
We will awake him and be sure of him.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
What, Lucius, ho!—
I cannot by the progress of the stars
Give guess how near to day.—Lucius, I say!—
I would it were my fault to sleep so soundly.—
When, Lucius, when? Awake, I say! What, Lucius!

speaker: LUCIUS
text: Called you, my lord?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Get me a taper in my study, Lucius.
When it is lighted, come and call me here.

speaker: LUCIUS
text: I will, my lord.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
It must be by his death. And for my part
I know no personal cause to spurn at him,
But for the general. He would be crowned:
How that might change his nature, there’s the question.
It is the bright day that brings forth the adder,
And that craves wary walking. Crown him that,
And then I grant we put a sting in him
That at his will he may do danger with.
Th’ abuse of greatness is when it disjoins
Remorse from power. And, to speak truth of Caesar,
I have not known when his affections swayed
More than his reason. But ’tis a common proof
That lowliness is young ambition’s ladder,
Whereto the climber-upward turns his face;
But, when he once attains the upmost round,
He then unto the ladder turns his back,
Looks in the clouds, scorning the base degrees
By which he did ascend. So Caesar may.
Then, lest he may, prevent. And since the quarrel
Will bear no color for the thing he is,
Fashion it thus: that what he is, augmented,
Would run to these and these extremities.
And therefore think him as a serpent’s egg,
Which, hatched, would, as his kind, grow mischievous,
And kill him in the shell.

speaker: LUCIUS
text:
The taper burneth in your closet, sir.
Searching the window for a flint, I found
This paper, thus sealed up, and I am sure
It did not lie there when I went to bed.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Get you to bed again. It is not day.
Is not tomorrow, boy, the ides of March?

speaker: LUCIUS
text: I know not, sir.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Look in the calendar, and bring me word.

speaker: LUCIUS
text: I will, sir.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
The exhalations, whizzing in the air,
Give so much light that I may read by them.
Brutus, thou sleep’st. Awake, and see thyself!
Shall Rome, etc. Speak, strike, redress!
“Brutus, thou sleep’st. Awake.”
Such instigations have been often dropped
Where I have took them up.
“Shall Rome, etc.” Thus must I piece it out:
Shall Rome stand under one man’s awe? What, Rome?
My ancestors did from the streets of Rome
The Tarquin drive when he was called a king.
“Speak, strike, redress!” Am I entreated
To speak and strike? O Rome, I make thee promise,
If the redress will follow, thou receivest
Thy full petition at the hand of Brutus.

speaker: LUCIUS
text: Sir, March is wasted fifteen days.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
’Tis good. Go to the gate; somebody knocks.
Since Cassius first did whet me against Caesar,
I have not slept.
Between the acting of a dreadful thing
And the first motion, all the interim is
Like a phantasma or a hideous dream.
The genius and the mortal instruments
Are then in council, and the state of man,
Like to a little kingdom, suffers then
The nature of an insurrection.

speaker: LUCIUS
text:
Sir, ’tis your brother Cassius at the door,
Who doth desire to see you.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Is he alone?

speaker: LUCIUS
text: No, sir. There are more with him.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Do you know them?

speaker: LUCIUS
text:
No, sir. Their hats are plucked about their ears,
And half their faces buried in their cloaks,
That by no means I may discover them
By any mark of favor.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Let ’em enter.
They are the faction. O conspiracy,
Sham’st thou to show thy dang’rous brow by night,
When evils are most free? O, then, by day
Where wilt thou find a cavern dark enough
To mask thy monstrous visage? Seek none, conspiracy.
Hide it in smiles and affability;
For if thou path, thy native semblance on,
Not Erebus itself were dim enough
To hide thee from prevention.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
I think we are too bold upon your rest.
Good morrow, Brutus. Do we trouble you?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
I have been up this hour, awake all night.
Know I these men that come along with you?

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Yes, every man of them; and no man here
But honors you, and every one doth wish
You had but that opinion of yourself
Which every noble Roman bears of you.
This is Trebonius.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: He is welcome hither.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: This, Decius Brutus.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: He is welcome too.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: This, Casca; this, Cinna; and this, Metellus Cimber.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
They are all welcome.
What watchful cares do interpose themselves
Betwixt your eyes and night?

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Shall I entreat a word?

speaker: DECIUS
text: Here lies the east; doth not the day break here?

speaker: CASCA
text: No.

speaker: CINNA
text:
O pardon, sir, it doth; and yon gray lines
That fret the clouds are messengers of day.

speaker: CASCA
text:
You shall confess that you are both deceived.
Here, as I point my sword, the sun arises,
Which is a great way growing on the south,
Weighing the youthful season of the year.
Some two months hence, up higher toward the north
He first presents his fire, and the high east
Stands, as the Capitol, directly here.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Give me your hands all over, one by one.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: And let us swear our resolution.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
No, not an oath. If not the face of men,
The sufferance of our souls, the time’s abuse—
If these be motives weak, break off betimes,
And every man hence to his idle bed.
So let high-sighted tyranny range on
Till each man drop by lottery. But if these—
As I am sure they do—bear fire enough
To kindle cowards and to steel with valor
The melting spirits of women, then, countrymen,
What need we any spur but our own cause
To prick us to redress? What other bond
Than secret Romans that have spoke the word
And will not palter? And what other oath
Than honesty to honesty engaged
That this shall be or we will fall for it?
Swear priests and cowards and men cautelous,
Old feeble carrions, and such suffering souls
That welcome wrongs; unto bad causes swear
Such creatures as men doubt; but do not stain
The even virtue of our enterprise,
Nor th’ insuppressive mettle of our spirits,
To think that or our cause or our performance
Did need an oath, when every drop of blood
That every Roman bears, and nobly bears,
Is guilty of a several bastardy
If he do break the smallest particle
Of any promise that hath passed from him.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
But what of Cicero? Shall we sound him?
I think he will stand very strong with us.

speaker: CASCA
text: Let us not leave him out.

speaker: CINNA
text: No, by no means.

speaker: METELLUS
text:
O, let us have him, for his silver hairs
Will purchase us a good opinion
And buy men’s voices to commend our deeds.
It shall be said his judgment ruled our hands.
Our youths and wildness shall no whit appear,
But all be buried in his gravity.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
O, name him not! Let us not break with him,
For he will never follow anything
That other men begin.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Then leave him out.

speaker: CASCA
text: Indeed, he is not fit.

speaker: DECIUS
text: Shall no man else be touched, but only Caesar?

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Decius, well urged. I think it is not meet
Mark Antony, so well beloved of Caesar,
Should outlive Caesar. We shall find of him
A shrewd contriver; and, you know, his means,
If he improve them, may well stretch so far
As to annoy us all; which to prevent,
Let Antony and Caesar fall together.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Our course will seem too bloody, Caius Cassius,
To cut the head off and then hack the limbs,
Like wrath in death and envy afterwards;
For Antony is but a limb of Caesar.
Let’s be sacrificers, but not butchers, Caius.
We all stand up against the spirit of Caesar,
And in the spirit of men there is no blood.
O, that we then could come by Caesar’s spirit
And not dismember Caesar! But, alas,
Caesar must bleed for it. And, gentle friends,
Let’s kill him boldly, but not wrathfully.
Let’s carve him as a dish fit for the gods,
Not hew him as a carcass fit for hounds.
And let our hearts, as subtle masters do,
Stir up their servants to an act of rage
And after seem to chide ’em. This shall make
Our purpose necessary and not envious;
Which so appearing to the common eyes,
We shall be called purgers, not murderers.
And for Mark Antony, think not of him,
For he can do no more than Caesar’s arm
When Caesar’s head is off.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Yet I fear him,
For in the engrafted love he bears to Caesar—

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Alas, good Cassius, do not think of him.
If he love Caesar, all that he can do
Is to himself: take thought and die for Caesar.
And that were much he should, for he is given
To sports, to wildness, and much company.

speaker: TREBONIUS
text:
There is no fear in him. Let him not die,
For he will live and laugh at this hereafter.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Peace, count the clock.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: The clock hath stricken three.

speaker: TREBONIUS
text: ’Tis time to part.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
But it is doubtful yet
Whether Caesar will come forth today or no,
For he is superstitious grown of late,
Quite from the main opinion he held once
Of fantasy, of dreams, and ceremonies.
It may be these apparent prodigies,
The unaccustomed terror of this night,
And the persuasion of his augurers
May hold him from the Capitol today.

speaker: DECIUS
text:
Never fear that. If he be so resolved,
I can o’ersway him, for he loves to hear
That unicorns may be betrayed with trees,
And bears with glasses, elephants with holes,
Lions with toils, and men with flatterers.
But when I tell him he hates flatterers,
He says he does, being then most flatterèd.
Let me work,
For I can give his humor the true bent,
And I will bring him to the Capitol.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Nay, we will all of us be there to fetch him.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: By the eighth hour, is that the uttermost?

speaker: CINNA
text: Be that the uttermost, and fail not then.

speaker: METELLUS
text:
Caius Ligarius doth bear Caesar hard,
Who rated him for speaking well of Pompey.
I wonder none of you have thought of him.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Now, good Metellus, go along by him.
He loves me well, and I have given him reasons.
Send him but hither, and I’ll fashion him.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
The morning comes upon ’s. We’ll leave you, Brutus.
And, friends, disperse yourselves, but all remember
What you have said, and show yourselves true Romans.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Good gentlemen, look fresh and merrily.
Let not our looks put on our purposes,
But bear it, as our Roman actors do,
With untired spirits and formal constancy.
And so good morrow to you every one.
Boy! Lucius!—Fast asleep? It is no matter.
Enjoy the honey-heavy dew of slumber.
Thou hast no figures nor no fantasies
Which busy care draws in the brains of men.
Therefore thou sleep’st so sound.

speaker: PORTIA
text: Brutus, my lord.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Portia! What mean you? Wherefore rise you now?
It is not for your health thus to commit
Your weak condition to the raw cold morning.

speaker: PORTIA
text:
Nor for yours neither. You’ve ungently, Brutus,
Stole from my bed. And yesternight at supper
You suddenly arose and walked about,
Musing and sighing, with your arms across,
And when I asked you what the matter was,
You stared upon me with ungentle looks.
I urged you further; then you scratched your head
And too impatiently stamped with your foot.
Yet I insisted; yet you answered not,
But with an angry wafture of your hand
Gave sign for me to leave you. So I did,
Fearing to strengthen that impatience
Which seemed too much enkindled, and withal
Hoping it was but an effect of humor,
Which sometime hath his hour with every man.
It will not let you eat nor talk nor sleep,
And could it work so much upon your shape
As it hath much prevailed on your condition,
I should not know you Brutus. Dear my lord,
Make me acquainted with your cause of grief.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: I am not well in health, and that is all.

speaker: PORTIA
text:
Brutus is wise and, were he not in health,
He would embrace the means to come by it.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Why so I do. Good Portia, go to bed.

speaker: PORTIA
text:
Is Brutus sick? And is it physical
To walk unbracèd and suck up the humors
Of the dank morning? What, is Brutus sick,
And will he steal out of his wholesome bed
To dare the vile contagion of the night
And tempt the rheumy and unpurgèd air
To add unto his sickness? No, my Brutus,
You have some sick offense within your mind,
Which by the right and virtue of my place
I ought to know of. And upon my knees
I charm you, by my once commended beauty,
By all your vows of love, and that great vow
Which did incorporate and make us one,
That you unfold to me, your self, your half,
Why you are heavy, and what men tonight
Have had resort to you; for here have been
Some six or seven who did hide their faces
Even from darkness.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Kneel not, gentle Portia.

speaker: PORTIA
text:
I should not need, if you were gentle Brutus.
Within the bond of marriage, tell me, Brutus,
Is it excepted I should know no secrets
That appertain to you? Am I your self
But, as it were, in sort or limitation,
To keep with you at meals, comfort your bed,
And talk to you sometimes? Dwell I but in the suburbs
Of your good pleasure? If it be no more,
Portia is Brutus’ harlot, not his wife.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
You are my true and honorable wife,
As dear to me as are the ruddy drops
That visit my sad heart.

speaker: PORTIA
text:
If this were true, then should I know this secret.
I grant I am a woman, but withal
A woman that Lord Brutus took to wife.
I grant I am a woman, but withal
A woman well-reputed, Cato’s daughter.
Think you I am no stronger than my sex,
Being so fathered and so husbanded?
Tell me your counsels; I will not disclose ’em.
I have made strong proof of my constancy,
Giving myself a voluntary wound
Here, in the thigh. Can I bear that with patience,
And not my husband’s secrets?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
O you gods,
Render me worthy of this noble wife!
Hark, hark, one knocks. Portia, go in awhile,
And by and by thy bosom shall partake
The secrets of my heart.
All my engagements I will construe to thee,
All the charactery of my sad brows.
Leave me with haste.
Lucius, who ’s that knocks?

speaker: LUCIUS
text: Here is a sick man that would speak with you.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Caius Ligarius, that Metellus spoke of.—
Boy, stand aside.
Caius Ligarius, how?

speaker: LIGARIUS
text: Vouchsafe good morrow from a feeble tongue.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
O, what a time have you chose out, brave Caius,
To wear a kerchief! Would you were not sick!

speaker: LIGARIUS
text:
I am not sick, if Brutus have in hand
Any exploit worthy the name of honor.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Such an exploit have I in hand, Ligarius,
Had you a healthful ear to hear of it.

speaker: LIGARIUS
text:
By all the gods that Romans bow before,
I here discard my sickness.
Soul of Rome,
Brave son derived from honorable loins,
Thou like an exorcist hast conjured up
My mortifièd spirit. Now bid me run,
And I will strive with things impossible,
Yea, get the better of them. What’s to do?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: A piece of work that will make sick men whole.

speaker: LIGARIUS
text: But are not some whole that we must make sick?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
That must we also. What it is, my Caius,
I shall unfold to thee as we are going
To whom it must be done.

speaker: LIGARIUS
text:
Set on your foot,
And with a heart new-fired I follow you
To do I know not what; but it sufficeth
That Brutus leads me on.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Follow me then.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
Nor heaven nor Earth have been at peace tonight.
Thrice hath Calphurnia in her sleep cried out
“Help ho, they murder Caesar!”—Who’s within?

speaker: SERVANT
text: My lord.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
Go bid the priests do present sacrifice,
And bring me their opinions of success.

speaker: SERVANT
text: I will, my lord.

speaker: CALPHURNIA
text:
What mean you, Caesar? Think you to walk forth?
You shall not stir out of your house today.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
Caesar shall forth. The things that threatened me
Ne’er looked but on my back. When they shall see
The face of Caesar, they are vanishèd.

speaker: CALPHURNIA
text:
Caesar, I never stood on ceremonies,
Yet now they fright me. There is one within,
Besides the things that we have heard and seen,
Recounts most horrid sights seen by the watch.
A lioness hath whelpèd in the streets,
And graves have yawned and yielded up their dead.
Fierce fiery warriors fought upon the clouds
In ranks and squadrons and right form of war,
Which drizzled blood upon the Capitol.
The noise of battle hurtled in the air,
Horses did neigh, and dying men did groan,
And ghosts did shriek and squeal about the streets.
O Caesar, these things are beyond all use,
And I do fear them.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
What can be avoided
Whose end is purposed by the mighty gods?
Yet Caesar shall go forth, for these predictions
Are to the world in general as to Caesar.

speaker: CALPHURNIA
text:
When beggars die there are no comets seen;
The heavens themselves blaze forth the death of princes.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
Cowards die many times before their deaths;
The valiant never taste of death but once.
Of all the wonders that I yet have heard,
It seems to me most strange that men should fear,
Seeing that death, a necessary end,
Will come when it will come.
What say the augurers?

speaker: SERVANT
text:
They would not have you to stir forth today.
Plucking the entrails of an offering forth,
They could not find a heart within the beast.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
The gods do this in shame of cowardice.
Caesar should be a beast without a heart
If he should stay at home today for fear.
No, Caesar shall not. Danger knows full well
That Caesar is more dangerous than he.
We are two lions littered in one day,
And I the elder and more terrible.
And Caesar shall go forth.

speaker: CALPHURNIA
text:
Alas, my lord,
Your wisdom is consumed in confidence.
Do not go forth today. Call it my fear
That keeps you in the house, and not your own.
We’ll send Mark Antony to the Senate House,
And he shall say you are not well today.
Let me, upon my knee, prevail in this.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
Mark Antony shall say I am not well,
And for thy humor I will stay at home.
Here’s Decius Brutus; he shall tell them so.

speaker: DECIUS
text:
Caesar, all hail! Good morrow, worthy Caesar.
I come to fetch you to the Senate House.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
And you are come in very happy time
To bear my greeting to the Senators
And tell them that I will not come today.
Cannot is false, and that I dare not, falser.
I will not come today. Tell them so, Decius.

speaker: CALPHURNIA
text: Say he is sick.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
Shall Caesar send a lie?
Have I in conquest stretched mine arm so far,
To be afeard to tell graybeards the truth?
Decius, go tell them Caesar will not come.

speaker: DECIUS
text:
Most mighty Caesar, let me know some cause,
Lest I be laughed at when I tell them so.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
The cause is in my will. I will not come.
That is enough to satisfy the Senate.
But for your private satisfaction,
Because I love you, I will let you know.
Calphurnia here, my wife, stays me at home.
She dreamt tonight she saw my statue,
Which, like a fountain with an hundred spouts,
Did run pure blood; and many lusty Romans
Came smiling and did bathe their hands in it.
And these does she apply for warnings and portents
And evils imminent, and on her knee
Hath begged that I will stay at home today.

speaker: DECIUS
text:
This dream is all amiss interpreted.
It was a vision fair and fortunate.
Your statue spouting blood in many pipes,
In which so many smiling Romans bathed,
Signifies that from you great Rome shall suck
Reviving blood, and that great men shall press
For tinctures, stains, relics, and cognizance.
This by Calphurnia’s dream is signified.

speaker: CAESAR
text: And this way have you well expounded it.

speaker: DECIUS
text:
I have, when you have heard what I can say.
And know it now: the Senate have concluded
To give this day a crown to mighty Caesar.
If you shall send them word you will not come,
Their minds may change. Besides, it were a mock
Apt to be rendered, for someone to say
“Break up the Senate till another time,
When Caesar’s wife shall meet with better dreams.”
If Caesar hide himself, shall they not whisper
“Lo, Caesar is afraid”?
Pardon me, Caesar, for my dear dear love
To your proceeding bids me tell you this,
And reason to my love is liable.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
How foolish do your fears seem now, Calphurnia!
I am ashamèd I did yield to them.
Give me my robe, for I will go.
And look where Publius is come to fetch me.

speaker: PUBLIUS
text: Good morrow, Caesar.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
Welcome, Publius.—
What, Brutus, are you stirred so early too?—
Good morrow, Casca.—Caius Ligarius,
Caesar was ne’er so much your enemy
As that same ague which hath made you lean.—
What is ’t o’clock?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Caesar, ’tis strucken eight.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
I thank you for your pains and courtesy.
See, Antony that revels long a-nights
Is notwithstanding up.—Good morrow, Antony.

speaker: ANTONY
text: So to most noble Caesar.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
Bid them prepare within.—
I am to blame to be thus waited for.
Now, Cinna.—Now, Metellus.—What, Trebonius,
I have an hour’s talk in store for you.
Remember that you call on me today;
Be near me that I may remember you.

speaker: TREBONIUS
text:
Caesar, I will. And so near will I be
That your best friends shall wish I had been further.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
Good friends, go in and taste some wine with me,
And we, like friends, will straightway go together.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
That every like is not the same, O Caesar,
The heart of Brutus earns to think upon.

speaker: ARTEMIDORUS
text:
Here will I stand till Caesar pass along,
And as a suitor will I give him this.
My heart laments that virtue cannot live
Out of the teeth of emulation.
If thou read this, O Caesar, thou mayest live;
If not, the Fates with traitors do contrive.

speaker: PORTIA
text:
I prithee, boy, run to the Senate House.
Stay not to answer me, but get thee gone.
Why dost thou stay?

speaker: LUCIUS
text: To know my errand, madam.

speaker: PORTIA
text:
I would have had thee there and here again
Ere I can tell thee what thou shouldst do there.
O constancy, be strong upon my side;
Set a huge mountain ’tween my heart and tongue.
I have a man’s mind but a woman’s might.
How hard it is for women to keep counsel!—
Art thou here yet?

speaker: LUCIUS
text:
Madam, what should I do?
Run to the Capitol, and nothing else?
And so return to you, and nothing else?

speaker: PORTIA
text:
Yes, bring me word, boy, if thy lord look well,
For he went sickly forth. And take good note
What Caesar doth, what suitors press to him.
Hark, boy, what noise is that?

speaker: LUCIUS
text: I hear none, madam.

speaker: PORTIA
text:
Prithee, listen well.
I heard a bustling rumor like a fray,
And the wind brings it from the Capitol.

speaker: LUCIUS
text: Sooth, madam, I hear nothing.

speaker: PORTIA
text: Come hither, fellow. Which way hast thou been?

speaker: SOOTHSAYER
text: At mine own house, good lady.

speaker: PORTIA
text: What is ’t o’clock?

speaker: SOOTHSAYER
text: About the ninth hour, lady.

speaker: PORTIA
text: Is Caesar yet gone to the Capitol?

speaker: SOOTHSAYER
text:
Madam, not yet. I go to take my stand
To see him pass on to the Capitol.

speaker: PORTIA
text: Thou hast some suit to Caesar, hast thou not?

speaker: SOOTHSAYER
text:
That I have, lady. If it will please Caesar
To be so good to Caesar as to hear me,
I shall beseech him to befriend himself.

speaker: PORTIA
text: Why, know’st thou any harm's intended towards him?

speaker: SOOTHSAYER
text:
None that I know will be, much that I fear may chance.
Good morrow to you.—Here the street is narrow.
The throng that follows Caesar at the heels,
Of senators, of praetors, common suitors,
Will crowd a feeble man almost to death.
I’ll get me to a place more void, and there
Speak to great Caesar as he comes along.

speaker: PORTIA
text:
I must go in. Ay me, how weak a thing
The heart of woman is! O Brutus,
The heavens speed thee in thine enterprise!
Sure the boy heard me. Brutus hath a suit
That Caesar will not grant. O, I grow faint.—
Run, Lucius, and commend me to my lord.
Say I am merry. Come to me again
And bring me word what he doth say to thee.

speaker: CAESAR
text: The ides of March are come.

speaker: SOOTHSAYER
text: Ay, Caesar, but not gone.

speaker: ARTEMIDORUS
text: Hail, Caesar. Read this schedule.

speaker: DECIUS
text:
Trebonius doth desire you to o’erread,
At your best leisure, this his humble suit.

speaker: ARTEMIDORUS
text:
O Caesar, read mine first, for mine’s a suit
That touches Caesar nearer. Read it, great Caesar.

speaker: CAESAR
text: What touches us ourself shall be last served.

speaker: ARTEMIDORUS
text: Delay not, Caesar; read it instantly.

speaker: CAESAR
text: What, is the fellow mad?

speaker: PUBLIUS
text: Sirrah, give place.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
What, urge you your petitions in the street?
Come to the Capitol.

speaker: POPILIUS
text: I wish your enterprise today may thrive.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: What enterprise, Popilius?

speaker: POPILIUS
text: Fare you well.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: What said Popilius Lena?

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
He wished today our enterprise might thrive.
I fear our purpose is discoverèd.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Look how he makes to Caesar. Mark him.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Casca, be sudden, for we fear prevention.—
Brutus, what shall be done? If this be known,
Cassius or Caesar never shall turn back,
For I will slay myself.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Cassius, be constant.
Popilius Lena speaks not of our purposes,
For look, he smiles, and Caesar doth not change.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Trebonius knows his time, for look you, Brutus,
He draws Mark Antony out of the way.

speaker: DECIUS
text:
Where is Metellus Cimber? Let him go
And presently prefer his suit to Caesar.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: He is addressed. Press near and second him.

speaker: CINNA
text: Casca, you are the first that rears your hand.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
Are we all ready? What is now amiss
That Caesar and his Senate must redress?

speaker: METELLUS
text:
Most high, most mighty, and most puissant Caesar,
Metellus Cimber throws before thy seat
An humble heart.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
I must prevent thee, Cimber.
These couchings and these lowly courtesies
Might fire the blood of ordinary men
And turn preordinance and first decree
Into the law of children. Be not fond
To think that Caesar bears such rebel blood
That will be thawed from the true quality
With that which melteth fools—I mean sweet words,
Low-crookèd curtsies, and base spaniel fawning.
Thy brother by decree is banishèd.
If thou dost bend and pray and fawn for him,
I spurn thee like a cur out of my way.
Know: Caesar doth not wrong, nor without cause
Will he be satisfied.

speaker: METELLUS
text:
Is there no voice more worthy than my own
To sound more sweetly in great Caesar’s ear
For the repealing of my banished brother?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
I kiss thy hand, but not in flattery, Caesar,
Desiring thee that Publius Cimber may
Have an immediate freedom of repeal.

speaker: CAESAR
text: What, Brutus?

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Pardon, Caesar; Caesar, pardon!
As low as to thy foot doth Cassius fall
To beg enfranchisement for Publius Cimber.

speaker: CAESAR
text:
I could be well moved, if I were as you.
If I could pray to move, prayers would move me.
But I am constant as the Northern Star,
Of whose true fixed and resting quality
There is no fellow in the firmament.
The skies are painted with unnumbered sparks;
They are all fire, and every one doth shine.
But there’s but one in all doth hold his place.
So in the world: ’tis furnished well with men,
And men are flesh and blood, and apprehensive.
Yet in the number I do know but one
That unassailable holds on his rank,
Unshaked of motion; and that I am he
Let me a little show it, even in this:
That I was constant Cimber should be banished
And constant do remain to keep him so.

speaker: CINNA
text: O Caesar—

speaker: CAESAR
text: Hence. Wilt thou lift up Olympus?

speaker: DECIUS
text: Great Caesar—

speaker: CAESAR
text: Doth not Brutus bootless kneel?

speaker: CASCA
text: Speak, hands, for me!

speaker: CAESAR
text: Et tu, Brutè?—Then fall, Caesar.

speaker: CINNA
text:
Liberty! Freedom! Tyranny is dead!
Run hence, proclaim, cry it about the streets.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Some to the common pulpits and cry out
“Liberty, freedom, and enfranchisement.”

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
People and Senators, be not affrighted.
Fly not; stand still. Ambition’s debt is paid.

speaker: CASCA
text: Go to the pulpit, Brutus.

speaker: DECIUS
text: And Cassius too.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Where’s Publius?

speaker: CINNA
text: Here, quite confounded with this mutiny.

speaker: METELLUS
text:
Stand fast together, lest some friend of Caesar’s
Should chance—

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Talk not of standing.—Publius, good cheer.
There is no harm intended to your person,
Nor to no Roman else. So tell them, Publius.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
And leave us, Publius, lest that the people,
Rushing on us, should do your age some mischief.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Do so, and let no man abide this deed
But we the doers.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Where is Antony?

speaker: TREBONIUS
text:
Fled to his house amazed.
Men, wives, and children stare, cry out, and run
As it were doomsday.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Fates, we will know your pleasures.
That we shall die we know; ’tis but the time,
And drawing days out, that men stand upon.

speaker: CASCA
text:
Why, he that cuts off twenty years of life
Cuts off so many years of fearing death.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Grant that, and then is death a benefit.
So are we Caesar’s friends, that have abridged
His time of fearing death. Stoop, Romans, stoop,
And let us bathe our hands in Caesar’s blood
Up to the elbows and besmear our swords.
Then walk we forth, even to the marketplace,
And, waving our red weapons o’er our heads,
Let’s all cry “Peace, freedom, and liberty!”

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Stoop then, and wash.
How many ages hence
Shall this our lofty scene be acted over
In states unborn and accents yet unknown!

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
How many times shall Caesar bleed in sport,
That now on Pompey’s basis lies along
No worthier than the dust!

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
So oft as that shall be,
So often shall the knot of us be called
The men that gave their country liberty.

speaker: DECIUS
text: What, shall we forth?

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Ay, every man away.
Brutus shall lead, and we will grace his heels
With the most boldest and best hearts of Rome.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Soft, who comes here? A friend of Antony’s.

speaker: SERVANT
text:
Thus, Brutus, did my master bid me kneel.
Thus did Mark Antony bid me fall down,
And, being prostrate, thus he bade me say:
Brutus is noble, wise, valiant, and honest;
Caesar was mighty, bold, royal, and loving.
Say, I love Brutus, and I honor him;
Say, I feared Caesar, honored him, and loved him.
If Brutus will vouchsafe that Antony
May safely come to him and be resolved
How Caesar hath deserved to lie in death,
Mark Antony shall not love Caesar dead
So well as Brutus living, but will follow
The fortunes and affairs of noble Brutus
Thorough the hazards of this untrod state
With all true faith. So says my master Antony.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Thy master is a wise and valiant Roman.
I never thought him worse.
Tell him, so please him come unto this place,
He shall be satisfied and, by my honor,
Depart untouched.

speaker: SERVANT
text: I’ll fetch him presently.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: I know that we shall have him well to friend.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
I wish we may; but yet have I a mind
That fears him much, and my misgiving still
Falls shrewdly to the purpose.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: But here comes Antony.—Welcome, Mark Antony!

speaker: ANTONY
text:
O mighty Caesar, dost thou lie so low?
Are all thy conquests, glories, triumphs, spoils
Shrunk to this little measure? Fare thee well.—
I know not, gentlemen, what you intend,
Who else must be let blood, who else is rank.
If I myself, there is no hour so fit
As Caesar’s death’s hour, nor no instrument
Of half that worth as those your swords made rich
With the most noble blood of all this world.
I do beseech you, if you bear me hard,
Now, whilst your purpled hands do reek and smoke,
Fulfill your pleasure. Live a thousand years,
I shall not find myself so apt to die;
No place will please me so, no mean of death,
As here by Caesar, and by you cut off,
The choice and master spirits of this age.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
O Antony, beg not your death of us!
Though now we must appear bloody and cruel,
As by our hands and this our present act
You see we do, yet see you but our hands
And this the bleeding business they have done.
Our hearts you see not; they are pitiful;
And pity to the general wrong of Rome
(As fire drives out fire, so pity pity)
Hath done this deed on Caesar. For your part,
To you our swords have leaden points, Mark Antony.
Our arms in strength of malice, and our hearts
Of brothers’ temper, do receive you in
With all kind love, good thoughts, and reverence.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Your voice shall be as strong as any man’s
In the disposing of new dignities.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Only be patient till we have appeased
The multitude, beside themselves with fear;
And then we will deliver you the cause
Why I, that did love Caesar when I struck him,
Have thus proceeded.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
I doubt not of your wisdom.
Let each man render me his bloody hand.
First, Marcus Brutus, will I shake with you.—
Next, Caius Cassius, do I take your hand.—
Now, Decius Brutus, yours;—now yours, Metellus;—
Yours, Cinna;—and, my valiant Casca, yours;—
Though last, not least in love, yours, good Trebonius.—
Gentlemen all—alas, what shall I say?
My credit now stands on such slippery ground
That one of two bad ways you must conceit me,
Either a coward or a flatterer.—
That I did love thee, Caesar, O, ’tis true!
If then thy spirit look upon us now,
Shall it not grieve thee dearer than thy death
To see thy Antony making his peace,
Shaking the bloody fingers of thy foes—
Most noble!—in the presence of thy corpse?
Had I as many eyes as thou hast wounds,
Weeping as fast as they stream forth thy blood,
It would become me better than to close
In terms of friendship with thine enemies.
Pardon me, Julius! Here wast thou bayed, brave hart,
Here didst thou fall, and here thy hunters stand
Signed in thy spoil and crimsoned in thy Lethe.
O world, thou wast the forest to this hart,
And this indeed, O world, the heart of thee.
How like a deer strucken by many princes
Dost thou here lie!

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Mark Antony—

speaker: ANTONY
CASSIUS
text:
I blame you not for praising Caesar so.
But what compact mean you to have with us?
Will you be pricked in number of our friends,
Or shall we on and not depend on you?

speaker: ANTONY
text:
Therefore I took your hands, but was indeed
Swayed from the point by looking down on Caesar.
Friends am I with you all and love you all,
Upon this hope, that you shall give me reasons
Why and wherein Caesar was dangerous.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Or else were this a savage spectacle.
Our reasons are so full of good regard
That were you, Antony, the son of Caesar,
You should be satisfied.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
That’s all I seek;
And am, moreover, suitor that I may
Produce his body to the marketplace,
And in the pulpit, as becomes a friend,
Speak in the order of his funeral.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: You shall, Mark Antony.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Brutus, a word with you.
You know not what you do. Do not consent
That Antony speak in his funeral.
Know you how much the people may be moved
By that which he will utter?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
By your pardon,
I will myself into the pulpit first
And show the reason of our Caesar’s death.
What Antony shall speak I will protest
He speaks by leave and by permission,
And that we are contented Caesar shall
Have all true rites and lawful ceremonies.
It shall advantage more than do us wrong.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: I know not what may fall. I like it not.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Mark Antony, here, take you Caesar’s body.
You shall not in your funeral speech blame us
But speak all good you can devise of Caesar
And say you do ’t by our permission,
Else shall you not have any hand at all
About his funeral. And you shall speak
In the same pulpit whereto I am going,
After my speech is ended.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
Be it so.
I do desire no more.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Prepare the body, then, and follow us.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
O pardon me, thou bleeding piece of earth,
That I am meek and gentle with these butchers.
Thou art the ruins of the noblest man
That ever livèd in the tide of times.
Woe to the hand that shed this costly blood!
Over thy wounds now do I prophesy
(Which like dumb mouths do ope their ruby lips
To beg the voice and utterance of my tongue)
A curse shall light upon the limbs of men;
Domestic fury and fierce civil strife
Shall cumber all the parts of Italy;
Blood and destruction shall be so in use
And dreadful objects so familiar
That mothers shall but smile when they behold
Their infants quartered with the hands of war,
All pity choked with custom of fell deeds;
And Caesar’s spirit, ranging for revenge,
With Ate by his side come hot from hell,
Shall in these confines with a monarch’s voice
Cry “Havoc!” and let slip the dogs of war,
That this foul deed shall smell above the earth
With carrion men groaning for burial.
You serve Octavius Caesar, do you not?

speaker: SERVANT
text: I do, Mark Antony.

speaker: ANTONY
text: Caesar did write for him to come to Rome.

speaker: SERVANT
text:
He did receive his letters and is coming,
And bid me say to you by word of mouth—
O Caesar!

speaker: ANTONY
text:
Thy heart is big. Get thee apart and weep.
Passion, I see, is catching, for mine eyes,
Seeing those beads of sorrow stand in thine,
Began to water. Is thy master coming?

speaker: SERVANT
text: He lies tonight within seven leagues of Rome.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
Post back with speed and tell him what hath chanced.
Here is a mourning Rome, a dangerous Rome,
No Rome of safety for Octavius yet.
Hie hence and tell him so.—Yet stay awhile;
Thou shalt not back till I have borne this corpse
Into the marketplace. There shall I try,
In my oration, how the people take
The cruel issue of these bloody men,
According to the which thou shalt discourse
To young Octavius of the state of things.
Lend me your hand.

speaker: PLEBEIANS
text: We will be satisfied! Let us be satisfied!

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Then follow me and give me audience, friends.—
Cassius, go you into the other street
And part the numbers.—
Those that will hear me speak, let ’em stay here;
Those that will follow Cassius, go with him;
And public reasons shall be renderèd
Of Caesar’s death.

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: I will hear Brutus speak.

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text:
I will hear Cassius, and compare their reasons
When severally we hear them renderèd.

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text: The noble Brutus is ascended. Silence.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Be patient till the last.
Romans, countrymen, and lovers, hear me for my
cause, and be silent that you may hear. Believe me
for mine honor, and have respect to mine honor
that you may believe. Censure me in your wisdom,
and awake your senses that you may the better
judge. If there be any in this assembly, any dear
friend of Caesar’s, to him I say that Brutus’ love
to Caesar was no less than his. If then that friend
demand why Brutus rose against Caesar, this is my
answer: not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved
Rome more. Had you rather Caesar were living, and
die all slaves, than that Caesar were dead, to live all
freemen? As Caesar loved me, I weep for him. As he
was fortunate, I rejoice at it. As he was valiant, I
honor him. But, as he was ambitious, I slew him.
There is tears for his love, joy for his fortune, honor
for his valor, and death for his ambition. Who is
here so base that would be a bondman? If any,
speak, for him have I offended. Who is here so rude
that would not be a Roman? If any, speak, for him
have I offended. Who is here so vile that will not
love his country? If any, speak, for him have I
offended. I pause for a reply.

speaker: PLEBEIANS
text: None, Brutus, none.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Then none have I offended. I have done no
more to Caesar than you shall do to Brutus. The
question of his death is enrolled in the Capitol, his
glory not extenuated wherein he was worthy, nor
his offenses enforced for which he suffered death.
Here comes his body, mourned by Mark Antony,
who, though he had no hand in his death, shall
receive the benefit of his dying—a place in the
commonwealth—as which of you shall not? With
this I depart: that, as I slew my best lover for the
good of Rome, I have the same dagger for myself
when it shall please my country to need my death.

speaker: PLEBEIANS
text: Live, Brutus, live, live!

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: Bring him with triumph home unto his house.

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text: Give him a statue with his ancestors.

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text: Let him be Caesar.

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text:
Caesar’s better parts
Shall be crowned in Brutus.

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: We’ll bring him to his house with shouts and clamors.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: My countrymen—

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text: Peace, silence! Brutus speaks.

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: Peace, ho!

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Good countrymen, let me depart alone,
And, for my sake, stay here with Antony.
Do grace to Caesar’s corpse, and grace his speech
Tending to Caesar’s glories, which Mark Antony
(By our permission) is allowed to make.
I do entreat you, not a man depart,
Save I alone, till Antony have spoke.

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: Stay, ho, and let us hear Mark Antony!

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text: Let him go up into the public chair.

speaker: PLEBEIANS
text: We’ll hear him.—Noble Antony, go up.

speaker: ANTONY
text: For Brutus’ sake, I am beholding to you.

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text: What does he say of Brutus?

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text:
He says for Brutus’ sake
He finds himself beholding to us all.

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text: ’Twere best he speak no harm of Brutus here.

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: This Caesar was a tyrant.

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text:
Nay, that’s certain.
We are blest that Rome is rid of him.

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text: Peace, let us hear what Antony can say.

speaker: ANTONY
text: You gentle Romans—

speaker: PLEBEIANS
text: Peace, ho! Let us hear him.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears.
I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him.
The evil that men do lives after them;
The good is oft interrèd with their bones.
So let it be with Caesar. The noble Brutus
Hath told you Caesar was ambitious.
If it were so, it was a grievous fault,
And grievously hath Caesar answered it.
Here, under leave of Brutus and the rest
(For Brutus is an honorable man;
So are they all, all honorable men),
Come I to speak in Caesar’s funeral.
He was my friend, faithful and just to me,
But Brutus says he was ambitious,
And Brutus is an honorable man.
He hath brought many captives home to Rome,
Whose ransoms did the general coffers fill.
Did this in Caesar seem ambitious?
When that the poor have cried, Caesar hath wept;
Ambition should be made of sterner stuff.
Yet Brutus says he was ambitious,
And Brutus is an honorable man.
You all did see that on the Lupercal
I thrice presented him a kingly crown,
Which he did thrice refuse. Was this ambition?
Yet Brutus says he was ambitious,
And sure he is an honorable man.
I speak not to disprove what Brutus spoke,
But here I am to speak what I do know.
You all did love him once, not without cause.
What cause withholds you, then, to mourn for him?—
O judgment, thou art fled to brutish beasts,
And men have lost their reason!—Bear with me;
My heart is in the coffin there with Caesar,
And I must pause till it come back to me.

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: Methinks there is much reason in his sayings.

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text:
If thou consider rightly of the matter,
Caesar has had great wrong.

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text:
Has he, masters?
I fear there will a worse come in his place.

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text:
Marked you his words? He would not take the crown;
Therefore ’tis certain he was not ambitious.

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: If it be found so, some will dear abide it.

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text: Poor soul, his eyes are red as fire with weeping.

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text: There’s not a nobler man in Rome than Antony.

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text: Now mark him. He begins again to speak.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
But yesterday the word of Caesar might
Have stood against the world. Now lies he there,
And none so poor to do him reverence.
O masters, if I were disposed to stir
Your hearts and minds to mutiny and rage,
I should do Brutus wrong and Cassius wrong,
Who, you all know, are honorable men.
I will not do them wrong. I rather choose
To wrong the dead, to wrong myself and you,
Than I will wrong such honorable men.
But here’s a parchment with the seal of Caesar.
I found it in his closet. ’Tis his will.
Let but the commons hear this testament,
Which, pardon me, I do not mean to read,
And they would go and kiss dead Caesar’s wounds
And dip their napkins in his sacred blood—
Yea, beg a hair of him for memory
And, dying, mention it within their wills,
Bequeathing it as a rich legacy
Unto their issue.

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text: We’ll hear the will. Read it, Mark Antony.

speaker: PLEBEIANS
text: The will, the will! We will hear Caesar’s will.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
Have patience, gentle friends. I must not read it.
It is not meet you know how Caesar loved you.
You are not wood, you are not stones, but men.
And, being men, hearing the will of Caesar,
It will inflame you; it will make you mad.
’Tis good you know not that you are his heirs,
For if you should, O, what would come of it?

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text: Read the will! We’ll hear it, Antony.

speaker: PLEBEIANS
text: You shall read us the will, Caesar’s will.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
Will you be patient? Will you stay awhile?
I have o’ershot myself to tell you of it.
I fear I wrong the honorable men
Whose daggers have stabbed Caesar. I do fear it.

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text: They were traitors. Honorable men?

speaker: PLEBEIANS
text: The will! The testament!

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text:
They were villains, murderers. The
will! Read the will.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
You will compel me, then, to read the will?
Then make a ring about the corpse of Caesar,
And let me show you him that made the will.
Shall I descend? And will you give me leave?

speaker: PLEBEIANS
text: Come down.

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text: Descend.

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text: You shall have leave.

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text: A ring; stand round.

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: Stand from the hearse. Stand from the body.

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text: Room for Antony, most noble Antony.

speaker: ANTONY
text: Nay, press not so upon me. Stand far off.

speaker: PLEBEIANS
text: Stand back! Room! Bear back!

speaker: ANTONY
text:
If you have tears, prepare to shed them now.
You all do know this mantle. I remember
The first time ever Caesar put it on.
’Twas on a summer’s evening in his tent,
That day he overcame the Nervii.
Look, in this place ran Cassius’ dagger through.
See what a rent the envious Casca made.
Through this the well-belovèd Brutus stabbed,
And, as he plucked his cursèd steel away,
Mark how the blood of Caesar followed it,
As rushing out of doors to be resolved
If Brutus so unkindly knocked or no;
For Brutus, as you know, was Caesar’s angel.
Judge, O you gods, how dearly Caesar loved him!
This was the most unkindest cut of all.
For when the noble Caesar saw him stab,
Ingratitude, more strong than traitors’ arms,
Quite vanquished him. Then burst his mighty heart,
And, in his mantle muffling up his face,
Even at the base of Pompey’s statue
(Which all the while ran blood) great Caesar fell.
O, what a fall was there, my countrymen!
Then I and you and all of us fell down,
Whilst bloody treason flourished over us.
O, now you weep, and I perceive you feel
The dint of pity. These are gracious drops.
Kind souls, what, weep you when you but behold
Our Caesar’s vesture wounded? Look you here,
Here is himself, marred as you see with traitors.

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: O piteous spectacle!

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text: O noble Caesar!

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text: O woeful day!

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text: O traitors, villains!

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: O most bloody sight!

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text: We will be revenged.

speaker: PLEBEIANS
text:
Revenge! About! Seek! Burn! Fire! Kill!
Slay! Let not a traitor live!

speaker: ANTONY
text: Stay, countrymen.

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: Peace there! Hear the noble Antony.

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text:
We’ll hear him, we’ll follow him,
we’ll die with him.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
Good friends, sweet friends, let me not stir you up
To such a sudden flood of mutiny.
They that have done this deed are honorable.
What private griefs they have, alas, I know not,
That made them do it. They are wise and honorable
And will no doubt with reasons answer you.
I come not, friends, to steal away your hearts.
I am no orator, as Brutus is,
But, as you know me all, a plain blunt man
That love my friend, and that they know full well
That gave me public leave to speak of him.
For I have neither wit, nor words, nor worth,
Action, nor utterance, nor the power of speech
To stir men’s blood. I only speak right on.
I tell you that which you yourselves do know,
Show you sweet Caesar’s wounds, poor poor dumb mouths,
And bid them speak for me. But were I Brutus,
And Brutus Antony, there were an Antony
Would ruffle up your spirits and put a tongue
In every wound of Caesar that should move
The stones of Rome to rise and mutiny.

speaker: PLEBEIANS
text: We’ll mutiny.

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: We’ll burn the house of Brutus.

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text: Away then. Come, seek the conspirators.

speaker: ANTONY
text: Yet hear me, countrymen; yet hear me speak.

speaker: PLEBEIANS
text: Peace, ho! Hear Antony, most noble Antony!

speaker: ANTONY
text:
Why, friends, you go to do you know not what.
Wherein hath Caesar thus deserved your loves?
Alas, you know not. I must tell you then.
You have forgot the will I told you of.

speaker: PLEBEIANS
text: Most true. The will! Let’s stay and hear the will.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
Here is the will, and under Caesar’s seal:
To every Roman citizen he gives,
To every several man, seventy-five drachmas.

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text: Most noble Caesar! We’ll revenge his death.

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text: O royal Caesar!

speaker: ANTONY
text: Hear me with patience.

speaker: PLEBEIANS
text: Peace, ho!

speaker: ANTONY
text:
Moreover, he hath left you all his walks,
His private arbors, and new-planted orchards,
On this side Tiber. He hath left them you,
And to your heirs forever—common pleasures
To walk abroad and recreate yourselves.
Here was a Caesar! When comes such another?

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text:
Never, never!—Come, away, away!
We’ll burn his body in the holy place
And with the brands fire the traitors’ houses.
Take up the body.

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text: Go fetch fire.

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text: Pluck down benches.

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text:
Pluck down forms, windows,
anything.

speaker: ANTONY
SERVANT
text: Sir, Octavius is already come to Rome.

speaker: ANTONY
text: Where is he?

speaker: SERVANT
text: He and Lepidus are at Caesar’s house.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
And thither will I straight to visit him.
He comes upon a wish. Fortune is merry
And in this mood will give us anything.

speaker: SERVANT
text:
I heard him say Brutus and Cassius
Are rid like madmen through the gates of Rome.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
Belike they had some notice of the people
How I had moved them. Bring me to Octavius.

speaker: CINNA
text:
I dreamt tonight that I did feast with Caesar,
And things unluckily charge my fantasy.
I have no will to wander forth of doors,
Yet something leads me forth.

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: What is your name?

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text: Whither are you going?

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text: Where do you dwell?

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text:
Are you a married man or a
bachelor?

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text: Answer every man directly.

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: Ay, and briefly.

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text: Ay, and wisely.

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text: Ay, and truly, you were best.

speaker: CINNA
text:
What is my name? Whither am I going? Where
do I dwell? Am I a married man or a bachelor?
Then to answer every man directly and briefly,
wisely and truly: wisely I say, I am a bachelor.

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text:
That’s as much as to say they are
fools that marry. You’ll bear me a bang for that, I
fear. Proceed directly.

speaker: CINNA
text: Directly, I am going to Caesar’s funeral.

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: As a friend or an enemy?

speaker: CINNA
text: As a friend.

speaker: SECOND PLEBEIAN
text: That matter is answered directly.

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text: For your dwelling—briefly.

speaker: CINNA
text: Briefly, I dwell by the Capitol.

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text: Your name, sir, truly.

speaker: CINNA
text: Truly, my name is Cinna.

speaker: FIRST PLEBEIAN
text: Tear him to pieces! He’s a conspirator.

speaker: CINNA
text: I am Cinna the poet, I am Cinna the poet!

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text:
Tear him for his bad verses, tear him
for his bad verses!

speaker: CINNA
text: I am not Cinna the conspirator.

speaker: FOURTH PLEBEIAN
text:
It is no matter. His name’s Cinna.
Pluck but his name out of his heart, and turn him
going.

speaker: THIRD PLEBEIAN
text:
Tear him, tear him! Come, brands, ho,
firebrands! To Brutus’, to Cassius’, burn all! Some
to Decius’ house, and some to Casca’s, some to
Ligarius’. Away, go!

speaker: ANTONY
text: These many, then, shall die; their names are pricked.

speaker: OCTAVIUS
text: Your brother too must die. Consent you, Lepidus?

speaker: LEPIDUS
text: I do consent.

speaker: OCTAVIUS
text: Prick him down, Antony.

speaker: LEPIDUS
text:
Upon condition Publius shall not live,
Who is your sister’s son, Mark Antony.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
He shall not live; look, with a spot I damn him.
But, Lepidus, go you to Caesar’s house;
Fetch the will hither, and we shall determine
How to cut off some charge in legacies.

speaker: LEPIDUS
text: What, shall I find you here?

speaker: OCTAVIUS
text: Or here, or at the Capitol.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
This is a slight, unmeritable man,
Meet to be sent on errands. Is it fit,
The threefold world divided, he should stand
One of the three to share it?

speaker: OCTAVIUS
text:
So you thought him
And took his voice who should be pricked to die
In our black sentence and proscription.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
Octavius, I have seen more days than you,
And, though we lay these honors on this man
To ease ourselves of diverse sland’rous loads,
He shall but bear them as the ass bears gold,
To groan and sweat under the business,
Either led or driven, as we point the way;
And having brought our treasure where we will,
Then take we down his load and turn him off
(Like to the empty ass) to shake his ears
And graze in commons.

speaker: OCTAVIUS
text:
You may do your will,
But he’s a tried and valiant soldier.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
So is my horse, Octavius, and for that
I do appoint him store of provender.
It is a creature that I teach to fight,
To wind, to stop, to run directly on,
His corporal motion governed by my spirit;
And, in some taste, is Lepidus but so.
He must be taught and trained and bid go forth—
A barren-spirited fellow, one that feeds
On objects, arts, and imitations
Which, out of use and staled by other men,
Begin his fashion. Do not talk of him
But as a property. And now, Octavius,
Listen great things. Brutus and Cassius
Are levying powers. We must straight make head.
Therefore let our alliance be combined,
Our best friends made, our means stretched;
And let us presently go sit in council
How covert matters may be best disclosed
And open perils surest answerèd.

speaker: OCTAVIUS
text:
Let us do so, for we are at the stake
And bayed about with many enemies,
And some that smile have in their hearts, I fear,
Millions of mischiefs.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Stand ho!

speaker: LUCILIUS
text: Give the word, ho, and stand!

speaker: BRUTUS
text: What now, Lucilius, is Cassius near?

speaker: LUCILIUS
text:
He is at hand, and Pindarus is come
To do you salutation from his master.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
He greets me well.—Your master, Pindarus,
In his own change or by ill officers,
Hath given me some worthy cause to wish
Things done undone, but if he be at hand
I shall be satisfied.

speaker: PINDARUS
text:
I do not doubt
But that my noble master will appear
Such as he is, full of regard and honor.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
He is not doubted.
A word, Lucilius,
How he received you. Let me be resolved.

speaker: LUCILIUS
text:
With courtesy and with respect enough,
But not with such familiar instances
Nor with such free and friendly conference
As he hath used of old.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Thou hast described
A hot friend cooling. Ever note, Lucilius,
When love begins to sicken and decay
It useth an enforcèd ceremony.
There are no tricks in plain and simple faith;
But hollow men, like horses hot at hand,
Make gallant show and promise of their mettle,
But when they should endure the bloody spur,
They fall their crests and, like deceitful jades,
Sink in the trial. Comes his army on?

speaker: LUCILIUS
text:
They mean this night in Sardis to be quartered.
The greater part, the horse in general,
Are come with Cassius.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Hark, he is arrived.
March gently on to meet him.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Stand ho!

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Stand ho! Speak the word along.

speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
text: Stand!

speaker: SECOND SOLDIER
text: Stand!

speaker: THIRD SOLDIER
text: Stand!

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Most noble brother, you have done me wrong.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Judge me, you gods! Wrong I mine enemies?
And if not so, how should I wrong a brother?

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Brutus, this sober form of yours hides wrongs,
And when you do them—

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Cassius, be content.
Speak your griefs softly. I do know you well.
Before the eyes of both our armies here
(Which should perceive nothing but love from us),
Let us not wrangle. Bid them move away.
Then in my tent, Cassius, enlarge your griefs,
And I will give you audience.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Pindarus,
Bid our commanders lead their charges off
A little from this ground.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Lucius, do you the like, and let no man
Come to our tent till we have done our conference.
Let Lucilius and Titinius guard our door.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
That you have wronged me doth appear in this:
You have condemned and noted Lucius Pella
For taking bribes here of the Sardians,
Wherein my letters, praying on his side
Because I knew the man, was slighted off.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: You wronged yourself to write in such a case.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
In such a time as this it is not meet
That every nice offense should bear his comment.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Let me tell you, Cassius, you yourself
Are much condemned to have an itching palm,
To sell and mart your offices for gold
To undeservers.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
I an itching palm?
You know that you are Brutus that speaks this,
Or, by the gods, this speech were else your last.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
The name of Cassius honors this corruption,
And chastisement doth therefore hide his head.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Chastisement?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Remember March; the ides of March remember.
Did not great Julius bleed for justice’ sake?
What villain touched his body that did stab
And not for justice? What, shall one of us
That struck the foremost man of all this world
But for supporting robbers, shall we now
Contaminate our fingers with base bribes
And sell the mighty space of our large honors
For so much trash as may be graspèd thus?
I had rather be a dog and bay the moon
Than such a Roman.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Brutus, bait not me.
I’ll not endure it. You forget yourself
To hedge me in. I am a soldier, I,
Older in practice, abler than yourself
To make conditions.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Go to! You are not, Cassius.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: I am.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: I say you are not.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Urge me no more. I shall forget myself.
Have mind upon your health. Tempt me no farther.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Away, slight man!

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Is ’t possible?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Hear me, for I will speak.
Must I give way and room to your rash choler?
Shall I be frighted when a madman stares?

speaker: CASSIUS
text: O you gods, you gods, must I endure all this?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
All this? Ay, more. Fret till your proud heart break.
Go show your slaves how choleric you are
And make your bondmen tremble. Must I budge?
Must I observe you? Must I stand and crouch
Under your testy humor? By the gods,
You shall digest the venom of your spleen
Though it do split you. For, from this day forth,
I’ll use you for my mirth, yea, for my laughter,
When you are waspish.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Is it come to this?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
You say you are a better soldier.
Let it appear so, make your vaunting true,
And it shall please me well. For mine own part,
I shall be glad to learn of noble men.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
You wrong me every way, you wrong me, Brutus.
I said an elder soldier, not a better.
Did I say “better”?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: If you did, I care not.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: When Caesar lived he durst not thus have moved me.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Peace, peace! You durst not so have tempted him.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: I durst not?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: No.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: What? Durst not tempt him?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: For your life you durst not.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Do not presume too much upon my love.
I may do that I shall be sorry for.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
You have done that you should be sorry for.
There is no terror, Cassius, in your threats,
For I am armed so strong in honesty
That they pass by me as the idle wind,
Which I respect not. I did send to you
For certain sums of gold, which you denied me,
For I can raise no money by vile means.
By heaven, I had rather coin my heart
And drop my blood for drachmas than to wring
From the hard hands of peasants their vile trash
By any indirection. I did send
To you for gold to pay my legions,
Which you denied me. Was that done like Cassius?
Should I have answered Caius Cassius so?
When Marcus Brutus grows so covetous
To lock such rascal counters from his friends,
Be ready, gods, with all your thunderbolts;
Dash him to pieces!

speaker: CASSIUS
text: I denied you not.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: You did.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
I did not. He was but a fool that brought
My answer back. Brutus hath rived my heart.
A friend should bear his friend’s infirmities,
But Brutus makes mine greater than they are.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: I do not, till you practice them on me.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: You love me not.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: I do not like your faults.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: A friendly eye could never see such faults.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
A flatterer’s would not, though they do appear
As huge as high Olympus.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Come, Antony, and young Octavius, come!
Revenge yourselves alone on Cassius,
For Cassius is aweary of the world—
Hated by one he loves, braved by his brother,
Checked like a bondman, all his faults observed,
Set in a notebook, learned and conned by rote
To cast into my teeth. O, I could weep
My spirit from mine eyes! There is my dagger,
And here my naked breast; within, a heart
Dearer than Pluto’s mine, richer than gold.
If that thou be’st a Roman, take it forth.
I that denied thee gold will give my heart.
Strike as thou didst at Caesar, for I know
When thou didst hate him worst, thou lovedst him better
Than ever thou lovedst Cassius.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Sheathe your dagger.
Be angry when you will, it shall have scope.
Do what you will, dishonor shall be humor.
O Cassius, you are yokèd with a lamb
That carries anger as the flint bears fire,
Who, much enforcèd, shows a hasty spark
And straight is cold again.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Hath Cassius lived
To be but mirth and laughter to his Brutus
When grief and blood ill-tempered vexeth him?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: When I spoke that, I was ill-tempered too.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Do you confess so much? Give me your hand.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: And my heart too.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: O Brutus!

speaker: BRUTUS
text: What’s the matter?

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Have not you love enough to bear with me
When that rash humor which my mother gave me
Makes me forgetful?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Yes, Cassius, and from henceforth
When you are over-earnest with your Brutus,
He’ll think your mother chides, and leave you so.

speaker: POET
text:
Let me go in to see the Generals.
There is some grudge between ’em; ’tis not meet
They be alone.

speaker: LUCILIUS
text: You shall not come to them.

speaker: POET
text: Nothing but death shall stay me.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: How now, what’s the matter?

speaker: POET
text:
For shame, you generals, what do you mean?
Love and be friends as two such men should be,
For I have seen more years, I’m sure, than ye.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Ha, ha, how vilely doth this cynic rhyme!

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Get you hence, sirrah! Saucy fellow, hence!

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Bear with him, Brutus. ’Tis his fashion.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
I’ll know his humor when he knows his time.
What should the wars do with these jigging fools?—
Companion, hence!

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Away, away, be gone!

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Lucilius and Titinius, bid the commanders
Prepare to lodge their companies tonight.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
And come yourselves, and bring Messala with you
Immediately to us.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Lucius, a bowl of wine.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: I did not think you could have been so angry.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: O Cassius, I am sick of many griefs.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Of your philosophy you make no use
If you give place to accidental evils.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: No man bears sorrow better. Portia is dead.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Ha? Portia?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: She is dead.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
How ’scaped I killing when I crossed you so?
O insupportable and touching loss!
Upon what sickness?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Impatient of my absence,
And grief that young Octavius with Mark Antony
Have made themselves so strong—for with her death
That tidings came—with this she fell distract
And, her attendants absent, swallowed fire.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: And died so?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Even so.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: O you immortal gods!

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Speak no more of her.—Give me a bowl of wine.—
In this I bury all unkindness, Cassius.

speaker: CASSIUS
BRUTUS
text:
Come in, Titinius. Welcome, good Messala.
Now sit we close about this taper here,
And call in question our necessities.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Portia, art thou gone?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
No more, I pray you.—
Messala, I have here receivèd letters
That young Octavius and Mark Antony
Come down upon us with a mighty power,
Bending their expedition toward Philippi.

speaker: MESSALA
text: Myself have letters of the selfsame tenor.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: With what addition?

speaker: MESSALA
text:
That by proscription and bills of outlawry,
Octavius, Antony, and Lepidus
Have put to death an hundred senators.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Therein our letters do not well agree.
Mine speak of seventy senators that died
By their proscriptions, Cicero being one.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Cicero one?

speaker: MESSALA
text:
Cicero is dead,
And by that order of proscription.
Had you your letters from your wife, my lord?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: No, Messala.

speaker: MESSALA
text: Nor nothing in your letters writ of her?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Nothing, Messala.

speaker: MESSALA
text: That methinks is strange.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Why ask you? Hear you aught of her in yours?

speaker: MESSALA
text: No, my lord.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Now, as you are a Roman, tell me true.

speaker: MESSALA
text:
Then like a Roman bear the truth I tell,
For certain she is dead, and by strange manner.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Why, farewell, Portia. We must die, Messala.
With meditating that she must die once,
I have the patience to endure it now.

speaker: MESSALA
text: Even so great men great losses should endure.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
I have as much of this in art as you,
But yet my nature could not bear it so.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Well, to our work alive. What do you think
Of marching to Philippi presently?

speaker: CASSIUS
text: I do not think it good.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Your reason?

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
This it is:
’Tis better that the enemy seek us;
So shall he waste his means, weary his soldiers,
Doing himself offense, whilst we, lying still,
Are full of rest, defense, and nimbleness.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Good reasons must of force give place to better.
The people ’twixt Philippi and this ground
Do stand but in a forced affection,
For they have grudged us contribution.
The enemy, marching along by them,
By them shall make a fuller number up,
Come on refreshed, new-added, and encouraged,
From which advantage shall we cut him off
If at Philippi we do face him there,
These people at our back.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Hear me, good brother—

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Under your pardon. You must note besides
That we have tried the utmost of our friends,
Our legions are brim full, our cause is ripe.
The enemy increaseth every day;
We, at the height, are ready to decline.
There is a tide in the affairs of men
Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune;
Omitted, all the voyage of their life
Is bound in shallows and in miseries.
On such a full sea are we now afloat,
And we must take the current when it serves
Or lose our ventures.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
Then, with your will, go on;
We’ll along ourselves and meet them at Philippi.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
The deep of night is crept upon our talk,
And nature must obey necessity,
Which we will niggard with a little rest.
There is no more to say.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
No more. Good night.
Early tomorrow will we rise and hence.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Lucius.
My gown.
Farewell, good Messala.—
Good night, Titinius.—Noble, noble Cassius,
Good night and good repose.

speaker: CASSIUS
text:
O my dear brother,
This was an ill beginning of the night.
Never come such division ’tween our souls!
Let it not, Brutus.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Everything is well.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Good night, my lord.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Good night, good brother.

speaker: TITINIUS / MESSALA
text: Good night, Lord Brutus.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Farewell, everyone.
Give me the gown. Where is thy instrument?

speaker: LUCIUS
text: Here in the tent.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
What, thou speak’st drowsily?
Poor knave, I blame thee not; thou art o’erwatched.
Call Claudius and some other of my men;
I’ll have them sleep on cushions in my tent.

speaker: LUCIUS
text: Varro and Claudius.

speaker: VARRO
text: Calls my lord?

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
I pray you, sirs, lie in my tent and sleep.
It may be I shall raise you by and by
On business to my brother Cassius.

speaker: VARRO
text: So please you, we will stand and watch your pleasure.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
I will not have it so. Lie down, good sirs.
It may be I shall otherwise bethink me.
Look, Lucius, here’s the book I sought for so.
I put it in the pocket of my gown.

speaker: LUCIUS
text: I was sure your Lordship did not give it me.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Bear with me, good boy, I am much forgetful.
Canst thou hold up thy heavy eyes awhile
And touch thy instrument a strain or two?

speaker: LUCIUS
text: Ay, my lord, an ’t please you.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
It does, my boy.
I trouble thee too much, but thou art willing.

speaker: LUCIUS
text: It is my duty, sir.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
I should not urge thy duty past thy might.
I know young bloods look for a time of rest.

speaker: LUCIUS
text: I have slept, my lord, already.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
It was well done, and thou shalt sleep again.
I will not hold thee long. If I do live,
I will be good to thee.
This is a sleepy tune. O murd’rous slumber,
Layest thou thy leaden mace upon my boy,
That plays thee music?—Gentle knave, good night.
I will not do thee so much wrong to wake thee.
If thou dost nod, thou break’st thy instrument.
I’ll take it from thee and, good boy, good night.
Let me see, let me see; is not the leaf turned down
Where I left reading? Here it is, I think.
How ill this taper burns.
Ha, who comes here?—
I think it is the weakness of mine eyes
That shapes this monstrous apparition.
It comes upon me.—Art thou any thing?
Art thou some god, some angel, or some devil,
That mak’st my blood cold and my hair to stare?
Speak to me what thou art.

speaker: GHOST
text: Thy evil spirit, Brutus.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Why com’st thou?

speaker: GHOST
text: To tell thee thou shalt see me at Philippi.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Well, then I shall see thee again?

speaker: GHOST
text: Ay, at Philippi.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Why, I will see thee at Philippi, then.
Now I have taken heart, thou vanishest.
Ill spirit, I would hold more talk with thee.—
Boy, Lucius!—Varro, Claudius, sirs, awake!
Claudius!

speaker: LUCIUS
text: The strings, my lord, are false.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
He thinks he still is at his instrument.
Lucius, awake!

speaker: LUCIUS
text: My lord?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Didst thou dream, Lucius, that thou so criedst out?

speaker: LUCIUS
text: My lord, I do not know that I did cry.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Yes, that thou didst. Didst thou see anything?

speaker: LUCIUS
text: Nothing, my lord.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Sleep again, Lucius.—Sirrah Claudius!
Fellow thou, awake!

speaker: VARRO
text: My lord?

speaker: CLAUDIUS
text: My lord?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Why did you so cry out, sirs, in your sleep?

speaker: BOTH
text: Did we, my lord?

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Ay. Saw you anything?

speaker: VARRO
text: No, my lord, I saw nothing.

speaker: CLAUDIUS
text: Nor I, my lord.

speaker: BRUTUS
text:
Go and commend me to my brother Cassius.
Bid him set on his powers betimes before,
And we will follow.

speaker: BOTH
text: It shall be done, my lord.

speaker: OCTAVIUS
text:
Now, Antony, our hopes are answerèd.
You said the enemy would not come down
But keep the hills and upper regions.
It proves not so; their battles are at hand.
They mean to warn us at Philippi here,
Answering before we do demand of them.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
Tut, I am in their bosoms, and I know
Wherefore they do it. They could be content
To visit other places, and come down
With fearful bravery, thinking by this face
To fasten in our thoughts that they have courage.
But ’tis not so.

speaker: MESSENGER
text:
Prepare you, generals.
The enemy comes on in gallant show.
Their bloody sign of battle is hung out,
And something to be done immediately.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
Octavius, lead your battle softly on
Upon the left hand of the even field.

speaker: OCTAVIUS
text: Upon the right hand, I; keep thou the left.

speaker: ANTONY
text: Why do you cross me in this exigent?

speaker: OCTAVIUS
text: I do not cross you, but I will do so.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: They stand and would have parley.

speaker: CASSIUS
text: Stand fast, Titinius. We must out and talk.

speaker: OCTAVIUS
text: Mark Antony, shall we give sign of battle?

speaker: ANTONY
text:
No, Caesar, we will answer on their charge.
Make forth. The Generals would have some words.

speaker: OCTAVIUS
text: Stir not until the signal.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Words before blows; is it so, countrymen?

speaker: OCTAVIUS
text: Not that we love words better, as you do.

speaker: BRUTUS
text: Good words are better than bad strokes, Octavius.

speaker: ANTONY
text:
In your bad strokes, Brutus, you give good words.
