speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
I pray you do. I’ll attend her here—
And woo her with some spirit when she comes!
Say that she rail, why then I’ll tell her plain
She sings as sweetly as a nightingale.
Say that she frown, I’ll say she looks as clear
As morning roses newly washed with dew.
Say she be mute and will not speak a word,
Then I’ll commend her volubility
And say she uttereth piercing eloquence.
If she do bid me pack, I’ll give her thanks
As though she bid me stay by her a week.
If she deny to wed, I’ll crave the day
When I shall ask the banns, and when be marrièd.
But here she comes—and now, Petruchio, speak.
Good morrow, Kate, for that’s your name, I hear.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
Well have you heard, but something hard of hearing.
They call me Katherine that do talk of me.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
You lie, in faith, for you are called plain Kate,
And bonny Kate, and sometimes Kate the curst.
But Kate, the prettiest Kate in Christendom,
Kate of Kate Hall, my super-dainty Kate
(For dainties are all Kates)—and therefore, Kate,
Take this of me, Kate of my consolation:
Hearing thy mildness praised in every town,
Thy virtues spoke of, and thy beauty sounded
(Yet not so deeply as to thee belongs),
Myself am moved to woo thee for my wife.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
“Moved,” in good time! Let him that moved you hither
Remove you hence. I knew you at the first
You were a movable.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Why, what’s a movable?

speaker: KATHERINE
text: A joint stool.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Thou hast hit it. Come, sit on me.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Asses are made to bear, and so are you.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Women are made to bear, and so are you.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: No such jade as you, if me you mean.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Alas, good Kate, I will not burden thee,
For knowing thee to be but young and light—

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
Too light for such a swain as you to catch,
And yet as heavy as my weight should be.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: “Should be”—should buzz!

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Well ta’en, and like a buzzard.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: O slow-winged turtle, shall a buzzard take thee?

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Ay, for a turtle, as he takes a buzzard.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Come, come, you wasp! I’ faith, you are too angry.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: If I be waspish, best beware my sting.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: My remedy is then to pluck it out.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Ay, if the fool could find it where it lies.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Who knows not where a wasp does wear his sting?
In his tail.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: In his tongue.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Whose tongue?

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Yours, if you talk of tales, and so farewell.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
What, with my tongue in your tail?
Nay, come again, good Kate. I am a gentleman—

speaker: KATHERINE
text: That I’ll try.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: I swear I’ll cuff you if you strike again.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
So may you lose your arms.
If you strike me, you are no gentleman,
And if no gentleman, why then no arms.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: A herald, Kate? O, put me in thy books.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: What is your crest? A coxcomb?

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: A combless cock, so Kate will be my hen.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: No cock of mine. You crow too like a craven.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Nay, come, Kate, come. You must not look so sour.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: It is my fashion when I see a crab.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Why, here’s no crab, and therefore look not sour.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: There is, there is.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Then show it me.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Had I a glass, I would.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: What, you mean my face?

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Well aimed of such a young one.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Now, by Saint George, I am too young for you.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Yet you are withered.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: ’Tis with cares.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: I care not.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Nay, hear you, Kate—in sooth, you ’scape not so.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: I chafe you if I tarry. Let me go.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
No, not a whit. I find you passing gentle.
’Twas told me you were rough, and coy, and sullen,
And now I find report a very liar.
For thou art pleasant, gamesome, passing courteous,
But slow in speech, yet sweet as springtime flowers.
Thou canst not frown, thou canst not look askance,
Nor bite the lip as angry wenches will,
Nor hast thou pleasure to be cross in talk.
But thou with mildness entertain’st thy wooers,
With gentle conference, soft, and affable.
Why does the world report that Kate doth limp?
O sland’rous world! Kate like the hazel twig
Is straight, and slender, and as brown in hue
As hazelnuts, and sweeter than the kernels.
O, let me see thee walk! Thou dost not halt.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Go, fool, and whom thou keep’st command.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Did ever Dian so become a grove
As Kate this chamber with her princely gait?
O, be thou Dian and let her be Kate,
And then let Kate be chaste and Dian sportful.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Where did you study all this goodly speech?

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: It is extempore, from my mother wit.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: A witty mother, witless else her son.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Am I not wise?

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Yes, keep you warm.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Marry, so I mean, sweet Katherine, in thy bed.
And therefore, setting all this chat aside,
Thus in plain terms: your father hath consented
That you shall be my wife, your dowry ’greed on,
And, will you, nill you, I will marry you.
Now, Kate, I am a husband for your turn,
For by this light, whereby I see thy beauty,
Thy beauty that doth make me like thee well,
Thou must be married to no man but me.
For I am he am born to tame you, Kate,
And bring you from a wild Kate to a Kate
Conformable as other household Kates.
Here comes your father. Never make denial.
I must and will have Katherine to my wife.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: Now, Signior Petruchio, how speed you with my daughter?

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
How but well, sir? How but well?
It were impossible I should speed amiss.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: Why, how now, daughter Katherine? In your dumps?

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
Call you me daughter? Now I promise you
You have showed a tender fatherly regard,
To wish me wed to one half lunatic,
A madcap ruffian and a swearing Jack,
That thinks with oaths to face the matter out.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Father, ’tis thus: yourself and all the world
That talked of her have talked amiss of her.
If she be curst, it is for policy,
For she’s not froward, but modest as the dove;
She is not hot, but temperate as the morn.
For patience she will prove a second Grissel,
And Roman Lucrece for her chastity.
And to conclude, we have ’greed so well together
That upon Sunday is the wedding day.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: I’ll see thee hanged on Sunday first.

speaker: GREMIO
text:
Hark, Petruchio, she says she’ll see thee
hanged first.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Is this your speeding? Nay,
then, goodnight our part.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Be patient, gentlemen. I choose her for myself.
If she and I be pleased, what’s that to you?
’Tis bargained ’twixt us twain, being alone,
That she shall still be curst in company.
I tell you, ’tis incredible to believe
How much she loves me. O, the kindest Kate!
She hung about my neck, and kiss on kiss
She vied so fast, protesting oath on oath,
That in a twink she won me to her love.
O, you are novices! ’Tis a world to see
How tame, when men and women are alone,
A meacock wretch can make the curstest shrew.—
Give me thy hand, Kate. I will unto Venice
To buy apparel ’gainst the wedding day.—
Provide the feast, father, and bid the guests.
I will be sure my Katherine shall be fine.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
I know not what to say, but give me your hands.
God send you joy, Petruchio. ’Tis a match.

speaker: GREMIO and TRANIO
text: Amen, say we. We will be witnesses.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Father, and wife, and gentlemen, adieu.
I will to Venice. Sunday comes apace.
We will have rings, and things, and fine array,
And kiss me, Kate. We will be married o’ Sunday.

speaker: GREMIO
text: Was ever match clapped up so suddenly?

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
Faith, gentlemen, now I play a merchant’s part
And venture madly on a desperate mart.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
’Twas a commodity lay fretting by you.
’Twill bring you gain, or perish on the seas.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: The gain I seek, is quiet in the match.

speaker: GREMIO
text:
No doubt but he hath got a quiet catch.
But now, Baptista, to your younger daughter.
Now is the day we long have lookèd for.
I am your neighbor and was suitor first.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
And I am one that love Bianca more
Than words can witness or your thoughts can guess.

speaker: GREMIO
text: Youngling, thou canst not love so dear as I.

speaker: TRANIO
text: Graybeard, thy love doth freeze.

speaker: GREMIO
text:
But thine doth fry!
Skipper, stand back. ’Tis age that nourisheth.

speaker: TRANIO
text: But youth in ladies’ eyes that flourisheth.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
Content you, gentlemen. I will compound this strife.
’Tis deeds must win the prize, and he of both
That can assure my daughter greatest dower
Shall have my Bianca’s love.
Say, Signior Gremio, what can you assure her?

speaker: GREMIO
text:
First, as you know, my house within the city
Is richly furnishèd with plate and gold,
Basins and ewers to lave her dainty hands;
My hangings all of Tyrian tapestry;
In ivory coffers I have stuffed my crowns,
In cypress chests my arras counterpoints,
Costly apparel, tents, and canopies,
Fine linen, Turkey cushions bossed with pearl,
Valance of Venice gold in needlework,
Pewter and brass, and all things that belongs
To house or housekeeping. Then, at my farm
I have a hundred milch-kine to the pail,
Six score fat oxen standing in my stalls,
And all things answerable to this portion.
Myself am struck in years, I must confess,
And if I die tomorrow this is hers,
If whilst I live she will be only mine.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
That “only” came well in. Sir, list to me:
I am my father’s heir and only son.
If I may have your daughter to my wife,
I’ll leave her houses three or four as good,
Within rich Pisa walls, as any one
Old Signior Gremio has in Padua,
Besides two thousand ducats by the year
Of fruitful land, all which shall be her jointure.—
What, have I pinched you, Signior Gremio?

speaker: GREMIO
text:
Two thousand ducats by the year of land?
My land amounts not to so much in all.—
That she shall have, besides an argosy
That now is lying in Marcellus’ road.
What, have I choked you with an argosy?

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Gremio, ’tis known my father hath no less
Than three great argosies, besides two galliasses
And twelve tight galleys. These I will assure her,
And twice as much whate’er thou off’rest next.

speaker: GREMIO
text:
Nay, I have offered all. I have no more,
And she can have no more than all I have.
If you like me, she shall have me and mine.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Why, then, the maid is mine from all the world,
By your firm promise. Gremio is outvied.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
I must confess your offer is the best,
And, let your father make her the assurance,
She is your own; else, you must pardon me.
If you should die before him, where’s her dower?

speaker: TRANIO
text: That’s but a cavil. He is old, I young.

speaker: GREMIO
text: And may not young men die as well as old?

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
Well, gentlemen, I am thus resolved:
On Sunday next, you know
My daughter Katherine is to be married.
Now, on the Sunday following, shall Bianca
Be bride to you, if you make this assurance.
If not, to Signior Gremio.
And so I take my leave, and thank you both.

speaker: GREMIO
text:
Adieu, good neighbor.
Now I fear thee not.
Sirrah young gamester, your father were a fool
To give thee all and in his waning age
Set foot under thy table. Tut, a toy!
An old Italian fox is not so kind, my boy.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
A vengeance on your crafty withered hide!—
Yet I have faced it with a card of ten.
’Tis in my head to do my master good.
I see no reason but supposed Lucentio
Must get a father, called “supposed Vincentio”—
And that’s a wonder. Fathers commonly
Do get their children. But in this case of wooing,
A child shall get a sire, if I fail not of my cunning.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
Fiddler, forbear. You grow too forward, sir.
Have you so soon forgot the entertainment
Her sister Katherine welcomed you withal?

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
But, wrangling pedant, this is
The patroness of heavenly harmony.
Then give me leave to have prerogative,
And when in music we have spent an hour,
Your lecture shall have leisure for as much.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
Preposterous ass, that never read so far
To know the cause why music was ordained.
Was it not to refresh the mind of man
After his studies or his usual pain?
Then give me leave to read philosophy,
And, while I pause, serve in your harmony.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: Sirrah, I will not bear these braves of thine.

speaker: BIANCA
text:
Why, gentlemen, you do me double wrong
To strive for that which resteth in my choice.
I am no breeching scholar in the schools.
I’ll not be tied to hours, nor ’pointed times,
But learn my lessons as I please myself.
And, to cut off all strife, here sit we down.
Take you your instrument, play you the whiles;
His lecture will be done ere you have tuned.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: You’ll leave his lecture when I am in tune?

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: That will be never. Tune your instrument.

speaker: BIANCA
text: Where left we last?

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
Here, madam:
Hic ibat Simois, hic est Sigeia tellus,
Hic steterat Priami regia celsa senis.

speaker: BIANCA
text: Conster them.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
Hic ibat, as I told you before, Simois, I am
Lucentio, hic est, son unto Vincentio of Pisa,
Sigeia tellus, disguised thus to get your love, Hic
steterat, and that “Lucentio” that comes a-wooing,
Priami, is my man Tranio, regia, bearing my port,
celsa senis, that we might beguile the old pantaloon.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
Madam, my instrument’s in
tune.

speaker: BIANCA
text: Let’s hear. Oh fie, the treble jars!

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
Spit in the hole, man, and tune
again.

speaker: BIANCA
text:
Now let me see if I can conster it. Hic ibat
Simois, I know you not; hic est Sigeia tellus, I trust
you not; Hic steterat Priami, take heed he hear us
not; regia, presume not; celsa senis, despair not.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: Madam, ’tis now in tune.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: All but the bass.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
The bass is right. ’Tis the base knave that jars.
How fiery and forward our pedant is.
Now for my life the knave doth court my love!
Pedascule, I’ll watch you better yet.

speaker: BIANCA
text: In time I may believe, yet I mistrust.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
Mistrust it not, for sure Aeacides
Was Ajax, called so from his grandfather.

speaker: BIANCA
text:
I must believe my master; else, I promise you,
I should be arguing still upon that doubt.
But let it rest.—Now, Litio, to you.
Good master, take it not unkindly, pray,
That I have been thus pleasant with you both.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
You may go walk, and give me leave awhile.
My lessons make no music in three parts.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
Are you so formal, sir? Well, I must wait
And watch withal, for, but I be deceived,
Our fine musician groweth amorous.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
Madam, before you touch the instrument,
To learn the order of my fingering
I must begin with rudiments of art,
To teach you gamut in a briefer sort,
More pleasant, pithy, and effectual
Than hath been taught by any of my trade.
And there it is in writing fairly drawn.

speaker: BIANCA
text: Why, I am past my gamut long ago.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: Yet read the gamut of Hortensio.

speaker: BIANCA
SERVANT
text:
Mistress, your father prays you leave your books
And help to dress your sister’s chamber up.
You know tomorrow is the wedding day.

speaker: BIANCA
text: Farewell, sweet masters both. I must be gone.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: Faith, mistress, then I have no cause to stay.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
But I have cause to pry into this pedant.
Methinks he looks as though he were in love.
Yet if thy thoughts, Bianca, be so humble
To cast thy wand’ring eyes on every stale,
Seize thee that list! If once I find thee ranging,
Hortensio will be quit with thee by changing.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
Signior Lucentio, this is the ’pointed day
That Katherine and Petruchio should be married,
And yet we hear not of our son-in-law.
What will be said? What mockery will it be,
To want the bridegroom when the priest attends
To speak the ceremonial rites of marriage?
What says Lucentio to this shame of ours?

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
No shame but mine. I must, forsooth, be forced
To give my hand, opposed against my heart,
Unto a mad-brain rudesby, full of spleen,
Who wooed in haste and means to wed at leisure.
I told you, I, he was a frantic fool,
Hiding his bitter jests in blunt behavior,
And, to be noted for a merry man,
He’ll woo a thousand, ’point the day of marriage,
Make friends, invite, and proclaim the banns,
Yet never means to wed where he hath wooed.
Now must the world point at poor Katherine
And say “Lo, there is mad Petruchio’s wife,
If it would please him come and marry her.”

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Patience, good Katherine, and Baptista too.
Upon my life, Petruchio means but well,
Whatever fortune stays him from his word.
Though he be blunt, I know him passing wise;
Though he be merry, yet withal he’s honest.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Would Katherine had never seen him, though!

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
Go, girl. I cannot blame thee now to weep,
For such an injury would vex a very saint,
Much more a shrew of thy impatient humor.

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
Master, master, news! And such old
news as you never heard of!

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: Is it new and old too? How may that be?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
Why, is it not news to hear of Petruchio’s
coming?

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: Is he come?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text: Why, no, sir.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: What then?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text: He is coming.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: When will he be here?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text: When he stands where I am, and sees you there.

speaker: TRANIO
text: But say, what to thine old news?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
Why, Petruchio is coming in a new hat and
an old jerkin, a pair of old breeches thrice turned,
a pair of boots that have been candle-cases, one
buckled, another laced; an old rusty sword ta’en
out of the town armory, with a broken hilt, and
chapeless; with two broken points; his horse
hipped, with an old mothy saddle and stirrups of no
kindred, besides possessed with the glanders and
like to mose in the chine, troubled with the lampass,
infected with the fashions, full of windgalls,
sped with spavins, rayed with the yellows, past cure
of the fives, stark spoiled with the staggers, begnawn
with the bots, swayed in the back and shoulder-shotten,
near-legged before, and with a half-checked
bit and a headstall of sheep’s leather,
which, being restrained to keep him from stumbling,
hath been often burst, and now repaired with
knots; one girth six times pieced, and a woman’s
crupper of velour, which hath two letters for her
name fairly set down in studs, and here and there
pieced with packthread.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: Who comes with him?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
Oh, sir, his lackey, for all the world caparisoned
like the horse: with a linen stock on one leg
and a kersey boot-hose on the other, gartered with
a red and blue list; an old hat, and the humor of
forty fancies pricked in ’t for a feather. A monster,
a very monster in apparel, and not like a Christian
footboy or a gentleman’s lackey.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
’Tis some odd humor pricks him to this fashion,
Yet oftentimes he goes but mean-appareled.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: I am glad he’s come, howsoe’er he comes.

speaker: BIONDELLO
text: Why, sir, he comes not.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: Didst thou not say he comes?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text: Who? That Petruchio came?

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: Ay, that Petruchio came!

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
No, sir, I say his horse comes with him on
his back.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: Why, that’s all one.

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
Nay, by Saint Jamy.
I hold you a penny,
A horse and a man
Is more than one,
And yet not many.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Come, where be these gallants? Who’s at home?

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: You are welcome, sir.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: And yet I come not well.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: And yet you halt not.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Not so well appareled as I wish
you were.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Were it better I should rush in thus—
But where is Kate? Where is my lovely bride?
How does my father? Gentles, methinks you frown.
And wherefore gaze this goodly company
As if they saw some wondrous monument,
Some comet or unusual prodigy?

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
Why, sir, you know this is your wedding day.
First were we sad, fearing you would not come,
Now sadder that you come so unprovided.
Fie, doff this habit, shame to your estate,
An eyesore to our solemn festival.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
And tell us what occasion of import
Hath all so long detained you from your wife
And sent you hither so unlike yourself.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Tedious it were to tell, and harsh to hear.
Sufficeth I am come to keep my word,
Though in some part enforcèd to digress,
Which at more leisure I will so excuse
As you shall well be satisfied with all.
But where is Kate? I stay too long from her.
The morning wears. ’Tis time we were at church.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
See not your bride in these unreverent robes.
Go to my chamber, put on clothes of mine.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Not I, believe me. Thus I’ll visit her.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: But thus, I trust, you will not marry her.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Good sooth, even thus. Therefore, ha’ done with words.
To me she’s married, not unto my clothes.
Could I repair what she will wear in me,
As I can change these poor accoutrements,
’Twere well for Kate and better for myself.
But what a fool am I to chat with you
When I should bid good morrow to my bride
And seal the title with a lovely kiss!

speaker: TRANIO
text:
He hath some meaning in his mad attire.
We will persuade him, be it possible,
To put on better ere he go to church.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: I’ll after him, and see the event of this.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
But, sir, to love concerneth us to add
Her father’s liking, which to bring to pass,
As I before imparted to your Worship,
I am to get a man (whate’er he be
It skills not much, we’ll fit him to our turn),
And he shall be “Vincentio of Pisa,”
And make assurance here in Padua
Of greater sums than I have promisèd.
So shall you quietly enjoy your hope
And marry sweet Bianca with consent.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
Were it not that my fellow schoolmaster
Doth watch Bianca’s steps so narrowly,
’Twere good, methinks, to steal our marriage,
Which, once performed, let all the world say no,
I’ll keep mine own despite of all the world.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
That by degrees we mean to look into,
And watch our vantage in this business.
We’ll overreach the graybeard, Gremio,
The narrow prying father, Minola,
The quaint musician, amorous Litio,
All for my master’s sake, Lucentio.

speaker: TRANIO
text: Signior Gremio, came you from the church?

speaker: GREMIO
text: As willingly as e’er I came from school.

speaker: TRANIO
text: And is the bride and bridegroom coming home?

speaker: GREMIO
text:
A bridegroom, say you? ’Tis a groom indeed,
A grumbling groom, and that the girl shall find.

speaker: TRANIO
text: Curster than she? Why, ’tis impossible.

speaker: GREMIO
text: Why, he’s a devil, a devil, a very fiend.

speaker: TRANIO
text: Why, she’s a devil, a devil, the devil’s dam.

speaker: GREMIO
text:
Tut, she’s a lamb, a dove, a fool to him.
I’ll tell you, Sir Lucentio: when the priest
Should ask if Katherine should be his wife,
“Ay, by gog’s wouns!” quoth he, and swore so loud
That, all amazed, the priest let fall the book,
And as he stooped again to take it up,
This mad-brained bridegroom took him such a cuff
That down fell priest and book, and book and priest.
“Now, take them up,” quoth he, “if any list.”

speaker: TRANIO
text: What said the wench when he rose again?

speaker: GREMIO
text:
Trembled and shook, for why he stamped and swore
As if the vicar meant to cozen him.
But after many ceremonies done,
He calls for wine. “A health!” quoth he, as if
He had been aboard, carousing to his mates
After a storm; quaffed off the muscatel
And threw the sops all in the sexton’s face,
Having no other reason
But that his beard grew thin and hungerly,
And seemed to ask him sops as he was drinking.
This done, he took the bride about the neck
And kissed her lips with such a clamorous smack
That at the parting all the church did echo.
And I, seeing this, came thence for very shame,
And after me I know the rout is coming.
Such a mad marriage never was before!
Hark, hark, I hear the minstrels play.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Gentlemen and friends, I thank you for your pains.
I know you think to dine with me today
And have prepared great store of wedding cheer,
But so it is, my haste doth call me hence,
And therefore here I mean to take my leave.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: Is ’t possible you will away tonight?

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
I must away today, before night come.
Make it no wonder. If you knew my business,
You would entreat me rather go than stay.
And, honest company, I thank you all,
That have beheld me give away myself
To this most patient, sweet, and virtuous wife.
Dine with my father, drink a health to me,
For I must hence, and farewell to you all.

speaker: TRANIO
text: Let us entreat you stay till after dinner.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: It may not be.

speaker: GREMIO
text: Let me entreat you.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: It cannot be.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Let me entreat you.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: I am content.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Are you content to stay?

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
I am content you shall entreat me stay,
But yet not stay, entreat me how you can.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Now, if you love me, stay.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Grumio, my horse.

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Ay, sir, they be ready; the oats have eaten the
horses.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
Nay, then,
Do what thou canst, I will not go today,
No, nor tomorrow, not till I please myself.
The door is open, sir. There lies your way.
You may be jogging whiles your boots are green.
For me, I’ll not be gone till I please myself.
’Tis like you’ll prove a jolly surly groom,
That take it on you at the first so roundly.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: O Kate, content thee. Prithee, be not angry.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
I will be angry. What hast thou to do?—
Father, be quiet. He shall stay my leisure.

speaker: GREMIO
text: Ay, marry, sir, now it begins to work.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
Gentlemen, forward to the bridal dinner.
I see a woman may be made a fool
If she had not a spirit to resist.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
They shall go forward, Kate, at thy command.—
Obey the bride, you that attend on her.
Go to the feast, revel and domineer,
Carouse full measure to her maidenhead,
Be mad and merry, or go hang yourselves.
But for my bonny Kate, she must with me.
Nay, look not big, nor stamp, nor stare, nor fret;
I will be master of what is mine own.
She is my goods, my chattels; she is my house,
My household stuff, my field, my barn,
My horse, my ox, my ass, my anything.
And here she stands, touch her whoever dare.
I’ll bring mine action on the proudest he
That stops my way in Padua.—Grumio,
Draw forth thy weapon. We are beset with thieves.
Rescue thy mistress if thou be a man!—
Fear not, sweet wench, they shall not touch thee, Kate.
I’ll buckler thee against a million.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: Nay, let them go. A couple of quiet ones!

speaker: GREMIO
text: Went they not quickly, I should die with laughing.

speaker: TRANIO
text: Of all mad matches never was the like.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: Mistress, what’s your opinion of your sister?

speaker: BIANCA
text: That being mad herself, she’s madly mated.

speaker: GREMIO
text: I warrant him, Petruchio is Kated.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
Neighbors and friends, though bride and bridegroom wants
For to supply the places at the table,
You know there wants no junkets at the feast.
Lucentio, you shall supply the bridegroom’s place,
And let Bianca take her sister’s room.

speaker: TRANIO
text: Shall sweet Bianca practice how to bride it?

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: She shall, Lucentio. Come, gentlemen, let’s go.

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Fie, fie on all tired jades, on all mad masters,
and all foul ways! Was ever man so beaten? Was
ever man so ’rayed? Was ever man so weary? I am
sent before to make a fire, and they are coming
after to warm them. Now were not I a little pot and
soon hot, my very lips might freeze to my teeth, my
tongue to the roof of my mouth, my heart in my
belly, ere I should come by a fire to thaw me. But I
with blowing the fire shall warm myself. For, considering
the weather, a taller man than I will take
cold.—Holla, ho, Curtis!

speaker: CURTIS
text: Who is that calls so coldly?

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
A piece of ice. If thou doubt it, thou mayst
slide from my shoulder to my heel with no greater
a run but my head and my neck. A fire, good Curtis!

speaker: CURTIS
text: Is my master and his wife coming, Grumio?

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Oh, ay, Curtis, ay, and therefore fire, fire! Cast
on no water.

speaker: CURTIS
text: Is she so hot a shrew as she’s reported?

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
She was, good Curtis, before this frost. But
thou know’st winter tames man, woman, and
beast, for it hath tamed my old master and my new
mistress and myself, fellow Curtis.

speaker: CURTIS
text: Away, you three-inch fool, I am no beast!

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Am I but three inches? Why, thy horn is a
foot, and so long am I, at the least. But wilt thou
make a fire? Or shall I complain on thee to our
mistress, whose hand (she being now at hand) thou
shalt soon feel, to thy cold comfort, for being slow in
thy hot office?

speaker: CURTIS
text:
I prithee, good Grumio, tell me, how goes the
world?

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
A cold world, Curtis, in every office but thine,
and therefore fire! Do thy duty, and have thy duty,
for my master and mistress are almost frozen to
death.

speaker: CURTIS
text:
There’s fire ready. And therefore, good Grumio,
the news!

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Why, “Jack boy, ho boy!” and as much news
as wilt thou.

speaker: CURTIS
text: Come, you are so full of cony-catching.

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Why, therefore fire, for I have caught extreme
cold. Where’s the cook? Is supper ready, the house
trimmed, rushes strewed, cobwebs swept, the servingmen
in their new fustian, their white stockings,
and every officer his wedding garment on? Be
the Jacks fair within, the Jills fair without, the
carpets laid, and everything in order?

speaker: CURTIS
text: All ready. And therefore, I pray thee, news.

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
First, know my horse is tired, my master and
mistress fallen out.

speaker: CURTIS
text: How?

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Out of their saddles into the dirt, and thereby
hangs a tale.

speaker: CURTIS
text: Let’s ha’ t, good Grumio.

speaker: GRUMIO
text: Lend thine ear.

speaker: CURTIS
text: Here.

speaker: GRUMIO
text: There!

speaker: CURTIS
text: This ’tis to feel a tale, not to hear a tale.

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
And therefore ’tis called a sensible tale. And
this cuff was but to knock at your ear and beseech
list’ning. Now I begin: Imprimis, we came down a
foul hill, my master riding behind my mistress—

speaker: CURTIS
text: Both of one horse?

speaker: GRUMIO
text: What’s that to thee?

speaker: CURTIS
text: Why, a horse.

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Tell thou the tale! But hadst thou not crossed
me, thou shouldst have heard how her horse fell,
and she under her horse; thou shouldst have heard
in how miry a place, how she was bemoiled, how he
left her with the horse upon her, how he beat me
because her horse stumbled, how she waded
through the dirt to pluck him off me, how he swore,
how she prayed that never prayed before, how I
cried, how the horses ran away, how her bridle was
burst, how I lost my crupper, with many things of
worthy memory which now shall die in oblivion,
and thou return unexperienced to thy grave.

speaker: CURTIS
text: By this reck’ning, he is more shrew than she.

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Ay, and that thou and the proudest of you all
shall find when he comes home. But what talk I of
this? Call forth Nathaniel, Joseph, Nicholas, Phillip,
Walter, Sugarsop, and the rest. Let their heads
be slickly combed, their blue coats brushed, and
their garters of an indifferent knit. Let them curtsy
with their left legs, and not presume to touch a hair
of my master’s horse-tail till they kiss their hands.
Are they all ready?

speaker: CURTIS
text: They are.

speaker: GRUMIO
text: Call them forth.

speaker: CURTIS
text:
Do you hear, ho? You must meet
my master to countenance my mistress.

speaker: GRUMIO
text: Why, she hath a face of her own.

speaker: CURTIS
text: Who knows not that?

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Thou, it seems, that calls for company to
countenance her.

speaker: CURTIS
text: I call them forth to credit her.

speaker: GRUMIO
text: Why, she comes to borrow nothing of them.

speaker: NATHANIEL
text: Welcome home, Grumio.

speaker: PHILLIP
text: How now, Grumio?

speaker: JOSEPH
text: What, Grumio!

speaker: NICHOLAS
text: Fellow Grumio!

speaker: NATHANIEL
text: How now, old lad?

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Welcome, you!—How now, you?—What,
you!—Fellow, you!—And thus much for greeting.
Now, my spruce companions, is all ready and all
things neat?

speaker: NATHANIEL
text:
All things is ready. How near is our
master?

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
E’en at hand, alighted by this. And therefore
be not—Cock’s passion, silence! I hear my master.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Where be these knaves? What, no man at door
To hold my stirrup nor to take my horse?
Where is Nathaniel, Gregory, Phillip?

speaker: ALL THE SERVANTS
text: Here! Here, sir, here, sir!

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
“Here, sir! Here, sir! Here, sir! Here, sir!”
You loggerheaded and unpolished grooms.
What? No attendance? No regard? No duty?
Where is the foolish knave I sent before?

speaker: GRUMIO
text: Here, sir, as foolish as I was before.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
You peasant swain, you whoreson malt-horse drudge!
Did I not bid thee meet me in the park
And bring along these rascal knaves with thee?

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Nathaniel’s coat, sir, was not fully made,
And Gabriel’s pumps were all unpinked i’ th’ heel.
There was no link to color Peter’s hat,
And Walter’s dagger was not come from sheathing.
There were none fine but Adam, Rafe, and Gregory.
The rest were ragged, old, and beggarly.
Yet, as they are, here are they come to meet you.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Go, rascals, go, and fetch my supper in!
Where is the life that late I led?
Where are those—
Sit down, Kate, and welcome.
Soud, soud, soud, soud!
Why, when, I say?—Nay, good sweet Kate, be merry.—
Off with my boots, you rogues, you villains! When?
It was the friar of orders gray,
As he forth walkèd on his way—
Out, you rogue! You pluck my foot awry.
Take that!
And mend the plucking of the other.—
Be merry, Kate.—Some water here! What ho!
Where’s my spaniel Troilus? Sirrah, get you hence
And bid my cousin Ferdinand come hither.
One, Kate, that you must kiss and be acquainted with.—
Where are my slippers? Shall I have some water?—
Come, Kate, and wash, and welcome heartily.—
You whoreson villain, will you let it fall?

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Patience, I pray you, ’twas a fault unwilling.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
A whoreson beetle-headed flap-eared knave!—
Come, Kate, sit down. I know you have a stomach.
Will you give thanks, sweet Kate, or else shall I?—
What’s this? Mutton?

speaker: FIRST SERVANT
text: Ay.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Who brought it?

speaker: PETER
text: I.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
’Tis burnt, and so is all the meat.
What dogs are these? Where is the rascal cook?
How durst you, villains, bring it from the dresser
And serve it thus to me that love it not?
There, take it to you, trenchers, cups, and all!
You heedless joltheads and unmannered slaves!
What, do you grumble? I’ll be with you straight.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
I pray you, husband, be not so disquiet.
The meat was well, if you were so contented.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
I tell thee, Kate, ’twas burnt and dried away,
And I expressly am forbid to touch it,
For it engenders choler, planteth anger,
And better ’twere that both of us did fast
(Since of ourselves, ourselves are choleric)
Than feed it with such over-roasted flesh.
Be patient. Tomorrow ’t shall be mended,
And for this night we’ll fast for company.
Come, I will bring thee to thy bridal chamber.

speaker: NATHANIEL
text: Peter, didst ever see the like?

speaker: PETER
text: He kills her in her own humor.

speaker: GRUMIO
text: Where is he?

speaker: CURTIS
text:
In her chamber,
Making a sermon of continency to her,
And rails and swears and rates, that she (poor soul)
Knows not which way to stand, to look, to speak,
And sits as one new-risen from a dream.
Away, away, for he is coming hither!

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Thus have I politicly begun my reign,
And ’tis my hope to end successfully.
My falcon now is sharp and passing empty,
And, till she stoop, she must not be full-gorged,
For then she never looks upon her lure.
Another way I have to man my haggard,
To make her come and know her keeper’s call.
That is, to watch her, as we watch these kites
That bate and beat and will not be obedient.
She ate no meat today, nor none shall eat.
Last night she slept not, nor tonight she shall not.
As with the meat, some undeservèd fault
I’ll find about the making of the bed,
And here I’ll fling the pillow, there the bolster,
This way the coverlet, another way the sheets.
Ay, and amid this hurly I intend
That all is done in reverend care of her.
And, in conclusion, she shall watch all night,
And, if she chance to nod, I’ll rail and brawl,
And with the clamor keep her still awake.
This is a way to kill a wife with kindness.
And thus I’ll curb her mad and headstrong humor.
He that knows better how to tame a shrew,
Now let him speak; ’tis charity to shew.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Is ’t possible, friend Litio, that mistress Bianca
Doth fancy any other but Lucentio?
I tell you, sir, she bears me fair in hand.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
Sir, to satisfy you in what I have said,
Stand by, and mark the manner of his teaching.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: Now mistress, profit you in what you read?

speaker: BIANCA
text: What, master, read you? First resolve me that.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: I read that I profess, The Art to Love.

speaker: BIANCA
text: And may you prove, sir, master of your art.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: While you, sweet dear, prove mistress of my heart.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
Quick proceeders, marry! Now tell me, I pray,
You that durst swear that your mistress Bianca
Loved none in the world so well as Lucentio.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
O despiteful love, unconstant womankind!
I tell thee, Litio, this is wonderful!

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
Mistake no more. I am not Litio,
Nor a musician as I seem to be,
But one that scorn to live in this disguise
For such a one as leaves a gentleman
And makes a god of such a cullion.
Know, sir, that I am called Hortensio.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Signior Hortensio, I have often heard
Of your entire affection to Bianca,
And since mine eyes are witness of her lightness,
I will with you, if you be so contented,
Forswear Bianca and her love forever.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
See how they kiss and court! Signior Lucentio,
Here is my hand, and here I firmly vow
Never to woo her more, but do forswear her
As one unworthy all the former favors
That I have fondly flattered her withal.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
And here I take the like unfeignèd oath,
Never to marry with her, though she would entreat.
Fie on her, see how beastly she doth court him!

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
Would all the world but he had quite forsworn!
For me, that I may surely keep mine oath,
I will be married to a wealthy widow
Ere three days pass, which hath as long loved me
As I have loved this proud disdainful haggard.
And so farewell, Signior Lucentio.
Kindness in women, not their beauteous looks,
Shall win my love, and so I take my leave,
In resolution as I swore before.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Mistress Bianca, bless you with such grace
As ’longeth to a lover’s blessèd case!
Nay, I have ta’en you napping, gentle love,
And have forsworn you with Hortensio.

speaker: BIANCA
text: Tranio, you jest. But have you both forsworn me?

speaker: TRANIO
text: Mistress, we have.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: Then we are rid of Litio.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
I’ faith, he’ll have a lusty widow now
That shall be wooed and wedded in a day.

speaker: BIANCA
text: God give him joy.

speaker: TRANIO
text: Ay, and he’ll tame her.

speaker: BIANCA
text: He says so, Tranio?

speaker: TRANIO
text: Faith, he is gone unto the taming school.

speaker: BIANCA
text: The taming school? What, is there such a place?

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Ay, mistress, and Petruchio is the master,
That teacheth tricks eleven and twenty long
To tame a shrew and charm her chattering tongue.

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
O master, master, I have watched so long
That I am dog-weary, but at last I spied
An ancient angel coming down the hill
Will serve the turn.

speaker: TRANIO
text: What is he, Biondello?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
Master, a marcantant, or a pedant,
I know not what, but formal in apparel,
In gait and countenance surely like a father.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: And what of him, Tranio?

speaker: TRANIO
text:
If he be credulous, and trust my tale,
I’ll make him glad to seem Vincentio
And give assurance to Baptista Minola
As if he were the right Vincentio.
Take in your love, and then let me alone.

speaker: MERCHANT
text: God save you, sir.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
And you, sir. You are welcome.
Travel you far on, or are you at the farthest?

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
Sir, at the farthest for a week or two,
But then up farther, and as far as Rome,
And so to Tripoli, if God lend me life.

speaker: TRANIO
text: What countryman, I pray?

speaker: MERCHANT
text: Of Mantua.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Of Mantua, sir? Marry, God forbid!
And come to Padua, careless of your life?

speaker: MERCHANT
text: My life, sir? How, I pray? For that goes hard.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
’Tis death for anyone in Mantua
To come to Padua. Know you not the cause?
Your ships are stayed at Venice, and the Duke,
For private quarrel ’twixt your duke and him,
Hath published and proclaimed it openly.
’Tis marvel, but that you are but newly come,
You might have heard it else proclaimed about.

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
Alas, sir, it is worse for me than so,
For I have bills for money by exchange
From Florence, and must here deliver them.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Well, sir, to do you courtesy,
This will I do, and this I will advise you.
First tell me, have you ever been at Pisa?

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
Ay, sir, in Pisa have I often been,
Pisa renownèd for grave citizens.

speaker: TRANIO
text: Among them know you one Vincentio?

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
I know him not, but I have heard of him:
A merchant of incomparable wealth.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
He is my father, sir, and sooth to say,
In count’nance somewhat doth resemble you.

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
As much as an apple doth an
oyster, and all one.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
To save your life in this extremity,
This favor will I do you for his sake
(And think it not the worst of all your fortunes
That you are like to Sir Vincentio):
His name and credit shall you undertake,
And in my house you shall be friendly lodged.
Look that you take upon you as you should.
You understand me, sir. So shall you stay
Till you have done your business in the city.
If this be court’sy, sir, accept of it.

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
O sir, I do, and will repute you ever
The patron of my life and liberty.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Then go with me, to make the matter good.
This, by the way, I let you understand:
My father is here looked for every day
To pass assurance of a dower in marriage
’Twixt me and one Baptista’s daughter here.
In all these circumstances I’ll instruct you.
Go with me to clothe you as becomes you.

speaker: GRUMIO
text: No, no, forsooth, I dare not for my life.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
The more my wrong, the more his spite appears.
What, did he marry me to famish me?
Beggars that come unto my father’s door
Upon entreaty have a present alms.
If not, elsewhere they meet with charity.
But I, who never knew how to entreat,
Nor never needed that I should entreat,
Am starved for meat, giddy for lack of sleep,
With oaths kept waking and with brawling fed.
And that which spites me more than all these wants,
He does it under name of perfect love,
As who should say, if I should sleep or eat
’Twere deadly sickness or else present death.
I prithee, go, and get me some repast,
I care not what, so it be wholesome food.

speaker: GRUMIO
text: What say you to a neat’s foot?

speaker: KATHERINE
text: ’Tis passing good. I prithee let me have it.

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
I fear it is too choleric a meat.
How say you to a fat tripe finely broiled?

speaker: KATHERINE
text: I like it well. Good Grumio, fetch it me.

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
I cannot tell. I fear ’tis choleric.
What say you to a piece of beef and mustard?

speaker: KATHERINE
text: A dish that I do love to feed upon.

speaker: GRUMIO
text: Ay, but the mustard is too hot a little.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Why then, the beef, and let the mustard rest.

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Nay then, I will not. You shall have the mustard
Or else you get no beef of Grumio.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Then both, or one, or any thing thou wilt.

speaker: GRUMIO
text: Why then, the mustard without the beef.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
Go, get thee gone, thou false deluding slave,
That feed’st me with the very name of meat.
Sorrow on thee, and all the pack of you
That triumph thus upon my misery.
Go, get thee gone, I say.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: How fares my Kate? What, sweeting, all amort?

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: Mistress, what cheer?

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Faith, as cold as can be.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Pluck up thy spirits. Look cheerfully upon me.
Here, love, thou seest how diligent I am,
To dress thy meat myself and bring it thee.
I am sure, sweet Kate, this kindness merits thanks.
What, not a word? Nay then, thou lov’st it not,
And all my pains is sorted to no proof.
Here, take away this dish.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: I pray you, let it stand.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
The poorest service is repaid with thanks,
And so shall mine before you touch the meat.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: I thank you, sir.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
Signior Petruchio, fie, you are to blame.
Come, Mistress Kate, I’ll bear you company.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Eat it up all, Hortensio, if thou lovest me.—
Much good do it unto thy gentle heart.
Kate, eat apace.
And now, my honey love,
Will we return unto thy father’s house
And revel it as bravely as the best,
With silken coats and caps and golden rings,
With ruffs and cuffs and farthingales and things,
With scarves and fans and double change of brav’ry,
With amber bracelets, beads, and all this knav’ry.
What, hast thou dined? The tailor stays thy leisure
To deck thy body with his ruffling treasure.
Come, tailor, let us see these ornaments.
Lay forth the gown.
What news with you, sir?

speaker: HABERDASHER
text: Here is the cap your Worship did bespeak.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Why, this was molded on a porringer!
A velvet dish! Fie, fie, ’tis lewd and filthy.
Why, ’tis a cockle or a walnut shell,
A knack, a toy, a trick, a baby’s cap.
Away with it! Come, let me have a bigger.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
I’ll have no bigger. This doth fit the time,
And gentlewomen wear such caps as these.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
When you are gentle, you shall have one too,
And not till then.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: That will not be in haste.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
Why, sir, I trust I may have leave to speak,
And speak I will. I am no child, no babe.
Your betters have endured me say my mind,
And if you cannot, best you stop your ears.
My tongue will tell the anger of my heart,
Or else my heart, concealing it, will break,
And, rather than it shall, I will be free
Even to the uttermost, as I please, in words.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Why, thou sayst true. It is a paltry cap,
A custard-coffin, a bauble, a silken pie.
I love thee well in that thou lik’st it not.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
Love me, or love me not, I like the cap,
And it I will have, or I will have none.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Thy gown? Why, ay. Come, tailor, let us see ’t.
O mercy God, what masking-stuff is here?
What’s this? A sleeve? ’Tis like a demi-cannon.
What, up and down carved like an apple tart?
Here’s snip and nip and cut and slish and slash,
Like to a censer in a barber’s shop.
Why, what a devil’s name, tailor, call’st thou this?

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: I see she’s like to have neither cap nor gown.

speaker: TAILOR
text:
You bid me make it orderly and well,
According to the fashion and the time.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Marry, and did. But if you be remembered,
I did not bid you mar it to the time.
Go, hop me over every kennel home,
For you shall hop without my custom, sir.
I’ll none of it. Hence, make your best of it.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
I never saw a better-fashioned gown,
More quaint, more pleasing, nor more commendable.
Belike you mean to make a puppet of me.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Why, true, he means to make a puppet of thee.

speaker: TAILOR
text: She says your Worship means to make a puppet of her.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
O monstrous arrogance! Thou liest, thou thread, thou thimble,
Thou yard, three-quarters, half-yard, quarter, nail!
Thou flea, thou nit, thou winter cricket, thou!
Braved in mine own house with a skein of thread?
Away, thou rag, thou quantity, thou remnant,
Or I shall so be-mete thee with thy yard
As thou shalt think on prating whilst thou liv’st.
I tell thee, I, that thou hast marred her gown.

speaker: TAILOR
text:
Your Worship is deceived. The gown is made
Just as my master had direction.
Grumio gave order how it should be done.

speaker: GRUMIO
text: I gave him no order. I gave him the stuff.

speaker: TAILOR
text: But how did you desire it should be made?

speaker: GRUMIO
text: Marry, sir, with needle and thread.

speaker: TAILOR
text: But did you not request to have it cut?

speaker: GRUMIO
text: Thou hast faced many things.

speaker: TAILOR
text: I have.

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Face not me. Thou hast braved many men;
brave not me. I will neither be faced nor braved. I
say unto thee, I bid thy master cut out the gown,
but I did not bid him cut it to pieces. Ergo, thou
liest.

speaker: TAILOR
text: Why, here is the note of the fashion to testify.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Read it.

speaker: GRUMIO
text: The note lies in ’s throat, if he say I said so.

speaker: TAILOR
text: “Imprimis, a loose-bodied gown—”

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Master, if ever I said “loose-bodied gown,”
sew me in the skirts of it and beat me to death with
a bottom of brown thread. I said “a gown.”

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Proceed.

speaker: TAILOR
text: “With a small-compassed cape—”

speaker: GRUMIO
text: I confess the cape.

speaker: TAILOR
text: “With a trunk sleeve—”

speaker: GRUMIO
text: I confess two sleeves.

speaker: TAILOR
text: “The sleeves curiously cut.”

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Ay, there’s the villainy.

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Error i’ th’ bill, sir, error i’ th’ bill! I commanded
the sleeves should be cut out and sewed
up again, and that I’ll prove upon thee, though thy
little finger be armed in a thimble.

speaker: TAILOR
text:
This is true that I say. An I had thee in place
where, thou shouldst know it.

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
I am for thee straight. Take thou the bill, give
me thy mete-yard, and spare not me.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
God-a-mercy, Grumio, then he shall have
no odds.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Well, sir, in brief, the gown is not for me.

speaker: GRUMIO
text: You are i’ th’ right, sir, ’tis for my mistress.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Go, take it up unto thy master’s use.

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
Villain, not for thy life! Take up my mistress’
gown for thy master’s use!

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Why, sir, what’s your conceit in that?

speaker: GRUMIO
text:
O, sir, the conceit is deeper than you think
for. Take up my mistress’ gown to his master’s use!
O, fie, fie, fie!

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Hortensio, say thou wilt see the tailor paid.
Go, take it hence. Begone, and say no more.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
Tailor, I’ll pay thee for thy gown tomorrow.
Take no unkindness of his hasty words.
Away, I say. Commend me to thy master.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Well, come, my Kate, we will unto your father’s,
Even in these honest mean habiliments.
Our purses shall be proud, our garments poor,
For ’tis the mind that makes the body rich,
And as the sun breaks through the darkest clouds,
So honor peereth in the meanest habit.
What, is the jay more precious than the lark
Because his feathers are more beautiful?
Or is the adder better than the eel
Because his painted skin contents the eye?
O no, good Kate. Neither art thou the worse
For this poor furniture and mean array.
If thou account’st it shame, lay it on me,
And therefore frolic! We will hence forthwith
To feast and sport us at thy father’s house.
Go, call my men, and let us straight to him,
And bring our horses unto Long-lane end.
There will we mount, and thither walk on foot.
Let’s see, I think ’tis now some seven o’clock,
And well we may come there by dinner time.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
I dare assure you, sir, ’tis almost two,
And ’twill be supper time ere you come there.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
It shall be seven ere I go to horse.
Look what I speak, or do, or think to do,
You are still crossing it.—Sirs, let ’t alone.
I will not go today, and, ere I do,
It shall be what o’clock I say it is.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: Why, so, this gallant will command the sun!

speaker: TRANIO
text: Sir, this is the house. Please it you that I call?

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
Ay, what else? And but I be deceived,
Signior Baptista may remember me,
Near twenty years ago, in Genoa,
Where we were lodgers at the Pegasus.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
’Tis well. And hold your own in any case
With such austerity as ’longeth to a father.

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
I warrant you.
But, sir, here comes your boy.
’Twere good he were schooled.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Fear you not him.—Sirrah Biondello,
Now do your duty throughly, I advise you.
Imagine ’twere the right Vincentio.

speaker: BIONDELLO
text: Tut, fear not me.

speaker: TRANIO
text: But hast thou done thy errand to Baptista?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
I told him that your father was at Venice,
And that you looked for him this day in Padua.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Thou ’rt a tall fellow. Hold thee that to drink.
Here comes Baptista. Set your countenance, sir.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Signior Baptista, you are happily met.—
Sir, this is the gentleman I told you of.
I pray you stand good father to me now.
Give me Bianca for my patrimony.

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
Soft, son.—
Sir, by your leave, having come to Padua
To gather in some debts, my son Lucentio
Made me acquainted with a weighty cause
Of love between your daughter and himself.
And, for the good report I hear of you,
And for the love he beareth to your daughter
And she to him, to stay him not too long,
I am content, in a good father’s care,
To have him matched. And if you please to like
No worse than I, upon some agreement
Me shall you find ready and willing
With one consent to have her so bestowed,
For curious I cannot be with you,
Signior Baptista, of whom I hear so well.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
Sir, pardon me in what I have to say.
Your plainness and your shortness please me well.
Right true it is your son Lucentio here
Doth love my daughter, and she loveth him,
Or both dissemble deeply their affections.
And therefore, if you say no more than this,
That like a father you will deal with him
And pass my daughter a sufficient dower,
The match is made, and all is done.
Your son shall have my daughter with consent.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
I thank you, sir. Where then do you know best
We be affied and such assurance ta’en
As shall with either part’s agreement stand?

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
Not in my house, Lucentio, for you know
Pitchers have ears, and I have many servants.
Besides, old Gremio is heark’ning still,
And happily we might be interrupted.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Then at my lodging, an it like you.
There doth my father lie, and there this night
We’ll pass the business privately and well.
Send for your daughter by your servant here.
My boy shall fetch the scrivener presently.
The worst is this: that at so slender warning
You are like to have a thin and slender pittance.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
It likes me well.—Cambio, hie you home,
And bid Bianca make her ready straight.
And, if you will, tell what hath happenèd:
Lucentio’s father is arrived in Padua,
And how she’s like to be Lucentio’s wife.

speaker: BIONDELLO
text: I pray the gods she may, with all my heart.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Dally not with the gods, but get thee gone.—
Signior Baptista, shall I lead the way?
Welcome! One mess is like to be your cheer.
Come, sir, we will better it in Pisa.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: I follow you.

speaker: BIONDELLO
text: Cambio.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: What sayst thou, Biondello?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
You saw my master wink and laugh upon
you?

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: Biondello, what of that?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
Faith, nothing; but ’has left me here behind
to expound the meaning or moral of his signs
and tokens.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: I pray thee, moralize them.

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
Then thus: Baptista is safe, talking with
the deceiving father of a deceitful son.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: And what of him?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
His daughter is to be brought by you to the
supper.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: And then?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
The old priest at Saint Luke’s Church is at
your command at all hours.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: And what of all this?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
I cannot tell, except they are busied
about a counterfeit assurance. Take you assurance
of her cum privilegio ad imprimendum solum. To th’
church take the priest, clerk, and some sufficient
honest witnesses.
If this be not that you look for, I have no more to say,
But bid Bianca farewell forever and a day.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: Hear’st thou, Biondello?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
I cannot tarry. I knew a wench married in
an afternoon as she went to the garden for parsley
to stuff a rabbit, and so may you, sir. And so adieu,
sir. My master hath appointed me to go to Saint
Luke’s to bid the priest be ready to come against
you come with your appendix.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
I may, and will, if she be so contented.
She will be pleased. Then wherefore should I doubt?
Hap what hap may, I’ll roundly go about her.
It shall go hard if “Cambio” go without her.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Come on, i’ God’s name, once more toward our father’s.
Good Lord, how bright and goodly shines the moon!

speaker: KATHERINE
text: The moon? The sun! It is not moonlight now.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: I say it is the moon that shines so bright.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: I know it is the sun that shines so bright.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Now, by my mother’s son, and that’s myself,
It shall be moon, or star, or what I list,
Or e’er I journey to your father’s house.
Go on, and fetch our horses back again.—
Evermore crossed and crossed, nothing but crossed!

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: Say as he says, or we shall never go.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
Forward, I pray, since we have come so far,
And be it moon, or sun, or what you please.
And if you please to call it a rush candle,
Henceforth I vow it shall be so for me.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: I say it is the moon.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: I know it is the moon.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Nay, then you lie. It is the blessèd sun.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
Then God be blest, it is the blessèd sun.
But sun it is not, when you say it is not,
And the moon changes even as your mind.
What you will have it named, even that it is,
And so it shall be so for Katherine.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: Petruchio, go thy ways, the field is won.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Well, forward, forward. Thus the bowl should run,
And not unluckily against the bias.
But soft! Company is coming here.
Good morrow, gentle mistress, where away?—
Tell me, sweet Kate, and tell me truly, too,
Hast thou beheld a fresher gentlewoman?
Such war of white and red within her cheeks!
What stars do spangle heaven with such beauty
As those two eyes become that heavenly face?—
Fair lovely maid, once more good day to thee.—
Sweet Kate, embrace her for her beauty’s sake.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: He will make the man mad, to make the woman of him.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
Young budding virgin, fair and fresh and sweet,
Whither away, or where is thy abode?
Happy the parents of so fair a child!
Happier the man whom favorable stars
Allots thee for his lovely bedfellow.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Why, how now, Kate? I hope thou art not mad!
This is a man—old, wrinkled, faded, withered—
And not a maiden, as thou sayst he is.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
Pardon, old father, my mistaking eyes
That have been so bedazzled with the sun
That everything I look on seemeth green.
Now I perceive thou art a reverend father.
Pardon, I pray thee, for my mad mistaking.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Do, good old grandsire, and withal make known
Which way thou travelest. If along with us,
We shall be joyful of thy company.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text:
Fair sir, and you, my merry mistress,
That with your strange encounter much amazed me,
My name is called Vincentio, my dwelling Pisa,
And bound I am to Padua, there to visit
A son of mine which long I have not seen.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: What is his name?

speaker: VINCENTIO
text: Lucentio, gentle sir.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Happily met, the happier for thy son.
And now by law as well as reverend age,
I may entitle thee my loving father.
The sister to my wife, this gentlewoman,
Thy son by this hath married. Wonder not,
Nor be not grieved. She is of good esteem,
Her dowry wealthy, and of worthy birth;
Beside, so qualified as may beseem
The spouse of any noble gentleman.
Let me embrace with old Vincentio,
And wander we to see thy honest son,
Who will of thy arrival be full joyous.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text:
But is this true, or is it else your pleasure,
Like pleasant travelers, to break a jest
Upon the company you overtake?

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: I do assure thee, father, so it is.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Come, go along and see the truth hereof,
For our first merriment hath made thee jealous.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
Well, Petruchio, this has put me in heart!
Have to my widow, and if she be froward,
Then hast thou taught Hortensio to be untoward.

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
Softly and swiftly, sir, for the priest is
ready.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
I fly, Biondello. But they may chance to
need thee at home. Therefore leave us.

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
Nay, faith, I’ll see the church a’ your back,
and then come back to my master’s as soon as I
can.

speaker: GREMIO
text: I marvel Cambio comes not all this while.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Sir, here’s the door. This is Lucentio’s house.
My father’s bears more toward the marketplace.
Thither must I, and here I leave you, sir.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text:
You shall not choose but drink before you go.
I think I shall command your welcome here,
And by all likelihood some cheer is toward.

speaker: GREMIO
text: They’re busy within. You were best knock louder.

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
What’s he that knocks as
he would beat down the gate?

speaker: VINCENTIO
text: Is Signior Lucentio within, sir?

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
He’s within, sir, but not to
be spoken withal.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text:
What if a man bring him a hundred pound
or two to make merry withal?

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
Keep your hundred
pounds to yourself. He shall need none so long as I
live.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Nay, I told you your son was
well beloved in Padua.—Do you hear, sir? To leave
frivolous circumstances, I pray you tell Signior
Lucentio that his father is come from Pisa and is
here at the door to speak with him.

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
Thou liest. His father is
come from Padua and here looking out at the
window.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text: Art thou his father?

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
Ay, sir, so his mother says,
if I may believe her.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Why, how now, gentleman!
Why, this is flat knavery, to take upon you another
man’s name.

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
Lay hands on the villain. I
believe he means to cosen somebody in this city
under my countenance.

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
I have seen them in the church
together. God send ’em good shipping! But who is
here? Mine old master Vincentio! Now we are
undone and brought to nothing.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text: Come hither, crack-hemp.

speaker: BIONDELLO
text: I hope I may choose, sir.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text:
Come hither, you rogue! What, have you
forgot me?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
Forgot you? No, sir. I could not forget you,
for I never saw you before in all my life.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text:
What, you notorious villain, didst thou
never see thy master’s father, Vincentio?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
What, my old worshipful old master? Yes,
marry, sir. See where he looks out of the window.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text: Is ’t so indeed?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
Help, help, help! Here’s a madman will
murder me.

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
Help, son! Help, Signior
Baptista!

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Prithee, Kate, let’s stand aside and see the
end of this controversy.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Sir, what are you that offer to
beat my servant?

speaker: VINCENTIO
text:
What am I, sir? Nay, what are you, sir! O
immortal gods! O fine villain! A silken doublet, a
velvet hose, a scarlet cloak, and a copatain hat! O, I
am undone, I am undone! While I play the good
husband at home, my son and my servant spend all
at the university.

speaker: TRANIO
text: How now, what’s the matter?

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: What, is the man lunatic?

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Sir, you seem a sober ancient
gentleman by your habit, but your words show you
a madman. Why, sir, what ’cerns it you if I wear
pearl and gold? I thank my good father, I am able
to maintain it.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text:
Thy father! O villain, he is a sailmaker in
Bergamo.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
You mistake, sir, you mistake, sir! Pray, what
do you think is his name?

speaker: VINCENTIO
text:
His name? As if I knew not his name! I have
brought him up ever since he was three years old,
and his name is Tranio.

speaker: MERCHANT
text:
Away, away, mad ass! His
name is Lucentio and he is mine only son, and heir
to the lands of me, Signior Vincentio.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text:
Lucentio? O, he hath murdered his master!
Lay hold on him, I charge you in the Duke’s name.
O, my son, my son! Tell me, thou villain, where is
my son Lucentio?

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Call forth an officer.
Carry this mad knave to the jail.—Father Baptista, I
charge you see that he be forthcoming.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text: Carry me to the jail?

speaker: GREMIO
text: Stay, officer. He shall not go to prison.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
Talk not, Signior Gremio. I say he shall go to
prison.

speaker: GREMIO
text:
Take heed, Signior Baptista, lest you be cony-catched
in this business. I dare swear this is the
right Vincentio.

speaker: MERCHANT
text: Swear, if thou dar’st.

speaker: GREMIO
text: Nay, I dare not swear it.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
Then thou wert best say that I
am not Lucentio.

speaker: GREMIO
text: Yes, I know thee to be Signior Lucentio.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: Away with the dotard, to the jail with him.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text:
Thus strangers may be haled and abused.—
O monstrous villain!

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
O, we are spoiled, and yonder he is! Deny
him, forswear him, or else we are all undone.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: Pardon, sweet father.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text: Lives my sweet son?

speaker: BIANCA
text: Pardon, dear father.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
How hast thou offended?
Where is Lucentio?

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
Here’s Lucentio,
Right son to the right Vincentio,
That have by marriage made thy daughter mine
While counterfeit supposes bleared thine eyne.

speaker: GREMIO
text: Here’s packing, with a witness, to deceive us all!

speaker: VINCENTIO
text:
Where is that damnèd villain, Tranio,
That faced and braved me in this matter so?

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: Why, tell me, is not this my Cambio?

speaker: BIANCA
text: Cambio is changed into Lucentio.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
Love wrought these miracles. Bianca’s love
Made me exchange my state with Tranio,
While he did bear my countenance in the town,
And happily I have arrivèd at the last
Unto the wishèd haven of my bliss.
What Tranio did, myself enforced him to.
Then pardon him, sweet father, for my sake.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text:
I’ll slit the villain’s nose that would have
sent me to the jail!

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
But do you hear, sir, have you married my
daughter without asking my goodwill?

speaker: VINCENTIO
text:
Fear not, Baptista, we will content you. Go
to! But I will in to be revenged for this villainy.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: And I to sound the depth of this knavery.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
Look not pale, Bianca. Thy father will not
frown.

speaker: GREMIO
text:
My cake is dough, but I’ll in among the rest,
Out of hope of all but my share of the feast.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
Husband, let’s follow to see the end of
this ado.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: First kiss me, Kate, and we will.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: What, in the midst of the street?

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: What, art thou ashamed of me?

speaker: KATHERINE
text: No, sir, God forbid, but ashamed to kiss.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Why, then, let’s home again. Come, sirrah, let’s away.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
Nay, I will give thee a kiss.
Now pray thee, love, stay.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Is not this well? Come, my sweet Kate.
Better once than never, for never too late.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
At last, though long, our jarring notes agree,
And time it is when raging war is done
To smile at ’scapes and perils overblown.
My fair Bianca, bid my father welcome,
While I with selfsame kindness welcome thine.
Brother Petruchio, sister Katherina,
And thou, Hortensio, with thy loving widow,
Feast with the best, and welcome to my house.
My banquet is to close our stomachs up
After our great good cheer. Pray you, sit down,
For now we sit to chat as well as eat.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Nothing but sit and sit, and eat and eat!

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: Padua affords this kindness, son Petruchio.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Padua affords nothing but what is kind.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: For both our sakes I would that word were true.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Now, for my life, Hortensio fears his widow!

speaker: WIDOW
text: Then never trust me if I be afeard.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
You are very sensible, and yet you miss my sense:
I mean Hortensio is afeard of you.

speaker: WIDOW
text: He that is giddy thinks the world turns round.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Roundly replied.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: Mistress, how mean you that?

speaker: WIDOW
text: Thus I conceive by him.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Conceives by me? How likes Hortensio that?

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: My widow says, thus she conceives her tale.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Very well mended. Kiss him for that, good widow.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
“He that is giddy thinks the world turns round”—
I pray you tell me what you meant by that.

speaker: WIDOW
text:
Your husband being troubled with a shrew
Measures my husband’s sorrow by his woe.
And now you know my meaning.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: A very mean meaning.

speaker: WIDOW
text: Right, I mean you.

speaker: KATHERINE
text: And I am mean indeed, respecting you.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: To her, Kate!

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: To her, widow!

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: A hundred marks, my Kate does put her down.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: That’s my office.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Spoke like an officer! Ha’ to thee, lad.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: How likes Gremio these quick-witted folks?

speaker: GREMIO
text: Believe me, sir, they butt together well.

speaker: BIANCA
text:
Head and butt! An hasty-witted body
Would say your head and butt were head and horn.

speaker: VINCENTIO
text: Ay, mistress bride, hath that awakened you?

speaker: BIANCA
text: Ay, but not frighted me. Therefore I’ll sleep again.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Nay, that you shall not. Since you have begun,
Have at you for a bitter jest or two.

speaker: BIANCA
text:
Am I your bird? I mean to shift my bush,
And then pursue me as you draw your bow.—
You are welcome all.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
She hath prevented me. Here, Signior Tranio,
This bird you aimed at, though you hit her not.—
Therefore a health to all that shot and missed.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
O, sir, Lucentio slipped me like his greyhound,
Which runs himself and catches for his master.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: A good swift simile, but something currish.

speaker: TRANIO
text:
’Tis well, sir, that you hunted for yourself.
’Tis thought your deer does hold you at a bay.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: O, O, Petruchio! Tranio hits you now.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: I thank thee for that gird, good Tranio.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: Confess, confess! Hath he not hit you here?

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
He has a little galled me, I confess.
And as the jest did glance away from me,
’Tis ten to one it maimed you two outright.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
Now, in good sadness, son Petruchio,
I think thou hast the veriest shrew of all.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Well, I say no. And therefore, for assurance,
Let’s each one send unto his wife,
And he whose wife is most obedient
To come at first when he doth send for her
Shall win the wager which we will propose.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: Content, what’s the wager?

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: Twenty crowns.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Twenty crowns?
I’ll venture so much of my hawk or hound,
But twenty times so much upon my wife.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: A hundred, then.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: Content.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: A match! ’Tis done.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: Who shall begin?

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
That will I.
Go, Biondello, bid your mistress come to me.

speaker: BIONDELLO
text: I go.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: Son, I’ll be your half Bianca comes.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
I’ll have no halves. I’ll bear it all myself.
How now, what news?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
Sir, my mistress sends you word
That she is busy, and she cannot come.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
How? “She’s busy, and she cannot come”?
Is that an answer?

speaker: GREMIO
text:
Ay, and a kind one, too.
Pray God, sir, your wife send you not a worse.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: I hope better.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
Sirrah Biondello, go and entreat my wife
To come to me forthwith.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
O ho, entreat her!
Nay, then, she must needs come.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text:
I am afraid, sir,
Do what you can, yours will not be entreated.
Now, where’s my wife?

speaker: BIONDELLO
text:
She says you have some goodly jest in hand.
She will not come. She bids you come to her.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Worse and worse. She will not come!
O vile, intolerable, not to be endured!—
Sirrah Grumio, go to your mistress,
Say I command her come to me.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: I know her answer.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: What?

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: She will not.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: The fouler fortune mine, and there an end.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text: Now by my holidam, here comes Katherina!

speaker: KATHERINE
text: What is your will, sir, that you send for me?

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Where is your sister, and Hortensio’s wife?

speaker: KATHERINE
text: They sit conferring by the parlor fire.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Go fetch them hither. If they deny to come,
Swinge me them soundly forth unto their husbands.
Away, I say, and bring them hither straight.

speaker: LUCENTIO
text: Here is a wonder, if you talk of a wonder.

speaker: HORTENSIO
text: And so it is. I wonder what it bodes.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Marry, peace it bodes, and love, and quiet life,
An awful rule, and right supremacy,
And, to be short, what not that’s sweet and happy.

speaker: BAPTISTA
text:
Now fair befall thee, good Petruchio!
The wager thou hast won, and I will add
Unto their losses twenty thousand crowns,
Another dowry to another daughter,
For she is changed as she had never been.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Nay, I will win my wager better yet,
And show more sign of her obedience,
Her new-built virtue and obedience.
See where she comes, and brings your froward wives
As prisoners to her womanly persuasion.—
Katherine, that cap of yours becomes you not.
Off with that bauble, throw it underfoot.

speaker: WIDOW
text:
Lord, let me never have a cause to sigh
Till I be brought to such a silly pass.

speaker: BIANCA
text: Fie, what a foolish duty call you this?

speaker: LUCENTIO
text:
I would your duty were as foolish too.
The wisdom of your duty, fair Bianca,
Hath cost me a hundred crowns since suppertime.

speaker: BIANCA
text: The more fool you for laying on my duty.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text:
Katherine, I charge thee tell these headstrong women
What duty they do owe their lords and husbands.

speaker: WIDOW
text: Come, come, you’re mocking. We will have no telling.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: Come on, I say, and first begin with her.

speaker: WIDOW
text: She shall not.

speaker: PETRUCHIO
text: I say she shall.—And first begin with her.

speaker: KATHERINE
text:
Fie, fie! Unknit that threat’ning unkind brow,
And dart not scornful glances from those eyes
To wound thy lord, thy king, thy governor.
It blots thy beauty as frosts do bite the meads,
Confounds thy fame as whirlwinds shake fair buds,
And in no sense is meet or amiable.
A woman moved is like a fountain troubled,
Muddy, ill-seeming, thick, bereft of beauty,
And while it is so, none so dry or thirsty
Will deign to sip or touch one drop of it.
Thy husband is thy lord, thy life, thy keeper,
Thy head, thy sovereign, one that cares for thee,
And for thy maintenance commits his body
To painful labor both by sea and land,
To watch the night in storms, the day in cold,
Whilst thou liest warm at home, secure and safe,
And craves no other tribute at thy hands
But love, fair looks, and true obedience—
Too little payment for so great a debt.
Such duty as the subject owes the prince,
Even such a woman oweth to her husband;
And when she is froward, peevish, sullen, sour,
And not obedient to his honest will,
What is she but a foul contending rebel
And graceless traitor to her loving lord?
I am ashamed that women are so simple
To offer war where they should kneel for peace,
Or seek for rule, supremacy, and sway
When they are bound to serve, love, and obey.
Why are our bodies soft and weak and smooth,
Unapt to toil and trouble in the world,
But that our soft conditions and our hearts
