Is led on in the conduct of my will—
My will enkindled by mine eyes and ears,
Two traded pilots ’twixt the dangerous shores
Of will and judgment. How may I avoid,
Although my will distaste what it elected,
The wife I choose? There can be no evasion
To blench from this and to stand firm by honor.
We turn not back the silks upon the merchant
When we have soiled them, nor the remainder viands
We do not throw in unrespective sieve
Because we now are full. It was thought meet
Paris should do some vengeance on the Greeks.
Your breath with full consent bellied his sails;
The seas and winds, old wranglers, took a truce
And did him service. He touched the ports desired,
And for an old aunt whom the Greeks held captive,
He brought a Grecian queen, whose youth and freshness
Wrinkles Apollo’s and makes pale the morning.
Why keep we her? The Grecians keep our aunt.
Is she worth keeping? Why, she is a pearl
Whose price hath launched above a thousand ships
And turned crowned kings to merchants.
If you’ll avouch ’twas wisdom Paris went—
As you must needs, for you all cried “Go, go”—
If you’ll confess he brought home worthy prize—
As you must needs, for you all clapped your hands
And cried “Inestimable”—why do you now
The issue of your proper wisdoms rate
And do a deed that never Fortune did,
Beggar the estimation which you prized
Richer than sea and land? O, theft most base,
That we have stol’n what we do fear to keep!
But thieves unworthy of a thing so stol’n,
That in their country did them that disgrace
We fear to warrant in our native place.

speaker: CASSANDRA
text: Cry, Trojans, cry!

speaker: PRIAM
text: What noise? What shriek is this?

speaker: TROILUS
text: ’Tis our mad sister. I do know her voice.

speaker: CASSANDRA
text: Cry, Trojans!

speaker: HECTOR
text: It is Cassandra.

speaker: CASSANDRA
text:
Cry, Trojans, cry! Lend me ten thousand eyes,
And I will fill them with prophetic tears.

speaker: HECTOR
text: Peace, sister, peace!

speaker: CASSANDRA
text:
Virgins and boys, mid-age and wrinkled elders,
Soft infancy, that nothing canst but cry,
Add to my clamors. Let us pay betimes
A moiety of that mass of moan to come.
Cry, Trojans, cry! Practice your eyes with tears.
Troy must not be, nor goodly Ilium stand.
Our firebrand brother Paris burns us all.
Cry, Trojans, cry! A Helen and a woe!
Cry, cry! Troy burns, or else let Helen go.

speaker: HECTOR
text:
Now, youthful Troilus, do not these high strains
Of divination in our sister work
Some touches of remorse? Or is your blood
So madly hot that no discourse of reason
Nor fear of bad success in a bad cause
Can qualify the same?

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Why, brother Hector,
We may not think the justness of each act
Such and no other than event doth form it,
Nor once deject the courage of our minds
Because Cassandra’s mad. Her brainsick raptures
Cannot distaste the goodness of a quarrel
Which hath our several honors all engaged
To make it gracious. For my private part,
I am no more touched than all Priam’s sons;
And Jove forbid there should be done amongst us
Such things as might offend the weakest spleen
To fight for and maintain!

speaker: PARIS
text:
Else might the world convince of levity
As well my undertakings as your counsels.
But I attest the gods, your full consent
Gave wings to my propension and cut off
All fears attending on so dire a project.
For what, alas, can these my single arms?
What propugnation is in one man’s valor
To stand the push and enmity of those
This quarrel would excite? Yet, I protest,
Were I alone to pass the difficulties
And had as ample power as I have will,
Paris should ne’er retract what he hath done
Nor faint in the pursuit.

speaker: PRIAM
text:
Paris, you speak
Like one besotted on your sweet delights.
You have the honey still, but these the gall.
So to be valiant is no praise at all.

speaker: PARIS
text:
Sir, I propose not merely to myself
The pleasures such a beauty brings with it,
But I would have the soil of her fair rape
Wiped off in honorable keeping her.
What treason were it to the ransacked queen,
Disgrace to your great worths, and shame to me,
Now to deliver her possession up
On terms of base compulsion? Can it be
That so degenerate a strain as this
Should once set footing in your generous bosoms?
There’s not the meanest spirit on our party
Without a heart to dare or sword to draw
When Helen is defended, nor none so noble
Whose life were ill bestowed or death unfamed
Where Helen is the subject. Then I say,
Well may we fight for her whom, we know well,
The world’s large spaces cannot parallel.

speaker: HECTOR
text:
Paris and Troilus, you have both said well,
And on the cause and question now in hand
Have glozed—but superficially, not much
Unlike young men, whom Aristotle thought
Unfit to hear moral philosophy.
The reasons you allege do more conduce
To the hot passion of distempered blood
Than to make up a free determination
’Twixt right and wrong, for pleasure and revenge
Have ears more deaf than adders to the voice
Of any true decision. Nature craves
All dues be rendered to their owners. Now,
What nearer debt in all humanity
Than wife is to the husband? If this law
Of nature be corrupted through affection,
And that great minds, of partial indulgence
To their benumbèd wills, resist the same,
There is a law in each well-ordered nation
To curb those raging appetites that are
Most disobedient and refractory.
If Helen, then, be wife to Sparta’s king,
As it is known she is, these moral laws
Of nature and of nations speak aloud
To have her back returned. Thus to persist
In doing wrong extenuates not wrong,
But makes it much more heavy. Hector’s opinion
Is this in way of truth; yet, ne’ertheless,
My sprightly brethren, I propend to you
In resolution to keep Helen still,
For ’tis a cause that hath no mean dependence
Upon our joint and several dignities.

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Why, there you touched the life of our design!
Were it not glory that we more affected
Than the performance of our heaving spleens,
I would not wish a drop of Trojan blood
Spent more in her defense. But, worthy Hector,
She is a theme of honor and renown,
A spur to valiant and magnanimous deeds,
Whose present courage may beat down our foes,
And fame in time to come canonize us;
For I presume brave Hector would not lose
So rich advantage of a promised glory
As smiles upon the forehead of this action
For the wide world’s revenue.

speaker: HECTOR
text:
I am yours,
You valiant offspring of great Priamus.
I have a roisting challenge sent amongst
The dull and factious nobles of the Greeks
Will strike amazement to their drowsy spirits.
I was advertised their great general slept,
Whilst emulation in the army crept.
This, I presume, will wake him.

speaker: THERSITES
text:
How now, Thersites? What, lost in the
labyrinth of thy fury? Shall the elephant Ajax carry
it thus? He beats me, and I rail at him. O, worthy
satisfaction! Would it were otherwise, that I could
beat him whilst he railed at me. ’Sfoot, I’ll learn to
conjure and raise devils but I’ll see some issue of
my spiteful execrations. Then there’s Achilles, a
rare enginer! If Troy be not taken till these two undermine
it, the walls will stand till they fall of
themselves. O thou great thunder-darter of Olympus,
forget that thou art Jove, the king of gods;
and, Mercury, lose all the serpentine craft of thy
caduceus, if you take not that little, little, less than
little wit from them that they have, which short-armed
ignorance itself knows is so abundant
scarce it will not in circumvention deliver a fly
from a spider without drawing their massy irons
and cutting the web. After this, the vengeance on
the whole camp! Or rather, the Neapolitan bone-ache!
For that, methinks, is the curse depending
on those that war for a placket. I have said my
prayers, and devil Envy say “Amen.”—What ho,
my lord Achilles!

speaker: PATROCLUS
text:
Who’s there? Thersites? Good
Thersites, come in and rail.

speaker: THERSITES
text:
If I could ’a remembered a gilt counterfeit,
thou couldst not have slipped out of my contemplation.
But it is no matter. Thyself upon thyself! The
common curse of mankind, folly and ignorance,
be thine in great revenue! Heaven bless thee from
a tutor, and discipline come not near thee! Let thy
blood be thy direction till thy death; then if she
that lays thee out says thou art a fair corse, I’ll be
sworn and sworn upon ’t she never shrouded any
but lazars. Amen.
Where’s Achilles?

speaker: PATROCLUS
text:
What, art thou devout? Wast thou in
prayer?

speaker: THERSITES
text: Ay. The heavens hear me!

speaker: PATROCLUS
text: Amen.

speaker: ACHILLES
text: Who’s there?

speaker: PATROCLUS
text: Thersites, my lord.

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
Where? Where? O, where?
Art thou come? Why, my cheese, my
digestion, why hast thou not served thyself in to my
table so many meals? Come, what’s Agamemnon?

speaker: THERSITES
text:
Thy commander, Achilles.—Then, tell me,
Patroclus, what’s Achilles?

speaker: PATROCLUS
text:
Thy lord, Thersites. Then, tell me, I pray
thee, what’s Thersites?

speaker: THERSITES
text:
Thy knower, Patroclus. Then, tell me, Patroclus,
what art thou?

speaker: PATROCLUS
text: Thou must tell that knowest.

speaker: ACHILLES
text: O tell, tell.

speaker: THERSITES
text:
I’ll decline the whole question. Agamemnon
commands Achilles, Achilles is my lord, I am
Patroclus’ knower, and Patroclus is a fool.

speaker: PATROCLUS
text: You rascal!

speaker: THERSITES
text: Peace, fool. I have not done.

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
He is a privileged man.—Proceed,
Thersites.

speaker: THERSITES
text:
Agamemnon is a fool, Achilles is a fool,
Thersites is a fool, and, as aforesaid, Patroclus is a
fool.

speaker: ACHILLES
text: Derive this. Come.

speaker: THERSITES
text:
Agamemnon is a fool to offer to command
Achilles, Achilles is a fool to be commanded of
Agamemnon, Thersites is a fool to serve such a fool,
and this Patroclus is a fool positive.

speaker: PATROCLUS
text: Why am I a fool?

speaker: THERSITES
text:
Make that demand of the creator. It suffices
me thou art.
Look you, who comes here?

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
Patroclus, I’ll speak with nobody.—Come in
with me, Thersites.

speaker: THERSITES
text:
Here is such patchery, such juggling, and
such knavery. All the argument is a whore and a
cuckold, a good quarrel to draw emulous factions
and bleed to death upon. Now the dry serpigo on
the subject, and war and lechery confound all!

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: Where is Achilles?

speaker: PATROCLUS
text: Within his tent, but ill-disposed, my lord.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text:
Let it be known to him that we are here.
He shent our messengers, and we lay by
Our appertainments, visiting of him.
Let him be told so, lest perchance he think
We dare not move the question of our place
Or know not what we are.

speaker: PATROCLUS
text: I shall say so to him.

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
We saw him at the opening of his tent.
He is not sick.

speaker: AJAX
text:
Yes, lion-sick, sick of proud heart. You may call
it melancholy if you will favor the man, but, by my
head, ’tis pride. But, why, why? Let him show us a
cause.—A word, my lord.

speaker: NESTOR
text: What moves Ajax thus to bay at him?

speaker: ULYSSES
text: Achilles hath inveigled his fool from him.

speaker: NESTOR
text: Who, Thersites?

speaker: ULYSSES
text: He.

speaker: NESTOR
text:
Then will Ajax lack matter, if he have lost his
argument.

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
No. You see, he is his argument that has his
argument: Achilles.

speaker: NESTOR
text:
All the better. Their fraction is more our wish
than their faction. But it was a strong composure a
fool could disunite.

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
The amity that wisdom knits not, folly may
easily untie.
Here comes Patroclus.

speaker: NESTOR
text: No Achilles with him.

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
The elephant hath joints, but none for courtesy;
his legs are legs for necessity, not for flexure.

speaker: PATROCLUS
text:
Achilles bids me say he is much sorry
If anything more than your sport and pleasure
Did move your greatness and this noble state
To call upon him. He hopes it is no other
But for your health and your digestion sake,
An after-dinner’s breath.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text:
Hear you, Patroclus:
We are too well acquainted with these answers,
But his evasion, winged thus swift with scorn,
Cannot outfly our apprehensions.
Much attribute he hath, and much the reason
Why we ascribe it to him. Yet all his virtues,
Not virtuously on his own part beheld,
Do in our eyes begin to lose their gloss,
Yea, and like fair fruit in an unwholesome dish,
Are like to rot untasted. Go and tell him
We come to speak with him; and you shall not sin
If you do say we think him overproud
And underhonest, in self-assumption greater
Than in the note of judgment; and worthier than himself
Here tend the savage strangeness he puts on,
Disguise the holy strength of their command,
And underwrite in an observing kind
His humorous predominance—yea, watch
His course and time, his ebbs and flows, as if
The passage and whole carriage of this action
Rode on his tide. Go tell him this, and add
That, if he overhold his price so much,
We’ll none of him. But let him, like an engine
Not portable, lie under this report:
“Bring action hither; this cannot go to war.”
A stirring dwarf we do allowance give
Before a sleeping giant. Tell him so.

speaker: PATROCLUS
text: I shall, and bring his answer presently.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text:
In second voice we’ll not be satisfied;
We come to speak with him.—Ulysses, enter you.

speaker: AJAX
text: What is he more than another?

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: No more than what he thinks he is.

speaker: AJAX
text:
Is he so much? Do you not think he thinks himself
a better man than I am?

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: No question.

speaker: AJAX
text: Will you subscribe his thought and say he is?

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text:
No, noble Ajax. You are as strong, as
valiant, as wise, no less noble, much more gentle,
and altogether more tractable.

speaker: AJAX
text:
Why should a man be proud? How doth pride
grow? I know not what pride is.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text:
Your mind is the clearer, Ajax, and your
virtues the fairer. He that is proud eats up himself.
Pride is his own glass, his own trumpet, his own
chronicle; and whatever praises itself but in the
deed devours the deed in the praise.

speaker: AJAX
text:
I do hate a proud man as I hate the engendering
of toads.

speaker: NESTOR
text: And yet he loves himself. Is ’t not strange?

speaker: ULYSSES
text: Achilles will not to the field tomorrow.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: What’s his excuse?

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
He doth rely on none,
But carries on the stream of his dispose,
Without observance or respect of any,
In will peculiar and in self-admission.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text:
Why, will he not, upon our fair request,
Untent his person and share th’ air with us?

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
Things small as nothing, for request’s sake only,
He makes important. Possessed he is with greatness
And speaks not to himself but with a pride
That quarrels at self-breath. Imagined worth
Holds in his blood such swoll’n and hot discourse
That ’twixt his mental and his active parts
Kingdomed Achilles in commotion rages
And batters down himself. What should I say?
He is so plaguy proud that the death-tokens of it
Cry “No recovery.”

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text:
Let Ajax go to him.—
Dear lord, go you and greet him in his tent.
’Tis said he holds you well and will be led
At your request a little from himself.

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
O Agamemnon, let it not be so!
We’ll consecrate the steps that Ajax makes
When they go from Achilles. Shall the proud lord
That bastes his arrogance with his own seam
And never suffers matter of the world
Enter his thoughts, save such as doth revolve
And ruminate himself—shall he be worshipped
Of that we hold an idol more than he?
No. This thrice-worthy and right valiant lord
Shall not so stale his palm, nobly acquired,
Nor, by my will, assubjugate his merit,
As amply titled as Achilles is,
By going to Achilles.
That were to enlard his fat-already pride
And add more coals to Cancer when he burns
With entertaining great Hyperion.
This lord go to him? Jupiter forbid
And say in thunder “Achilles, go to him.”

speaker: NESTOR
text: O, this is well; he rubs the vein of him.

speaker: DIOMEDES
text: And how his silence drinks up this applause!

speaker: AJAX
text:
If I go to him, with my armèd fist
I’ll pash him o’er the face.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: O, no, you shall not go.

speaker: AJAX
text:
An he be proud with me, I’ll feeze his pride.
Let me go to him.

speaker: ULYSSES
text: Not for the worth that hangs upon our quarrel.

speaker: AJAX
text: A paltry, insolent fellow.

speaker: NESTOR
text: How he describes himself!

speaker: AJAX
text: Can he not be sociable?

speaker: ULYSSES
text: The raven chides blackness.

speaker: AJAX
text: I’ll let his humorous blood.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text:
He will be the physician that
should be the patient.

speaker: AJAX
text: An all men were of my mind—

speaker: ULYSSES
text: Wit would be out of fashion.

speaker: AJAX
text:
—he should not bear it so; he should eat swords
first. Shall pride carry it?

speaker: NESTOR
text: An ’twould, you’d carry half.

speaker: ULYSSES
text: He would have ten shares.

speaker: AJAX
text: I will knead him; I’ll make him supple.

speaker: NESTOR
text:
He’s not yet through warm. Force him
with praises. Pour in, pour in; his ambition is dry.

speaker: ULYSSES
text: My lord, you feed too much on this dislike.

speaker: NESTOR
text: Our noble general, do not do so.

speaker: DIOMEDES
text: You must prepare to fight without Achilles.

speaker: ULYSSES
NESTOR
text:
Wherefore should you so?
He is not emulous, as Achilles is.

speaker: ULYSSES
text: Know the whole world, he is as valiant—

speaker: AJAX
text:
A whoreson dog, that shall palter with us thus!
Would he were a Trojan!

speaker: NESTOR
text: What a vice were it in Ajax now—

speaker: ULYSSES
text: If he were proud—

speaker: DIOMEDES
text: Or covetous of praise—

speaker: ULYSSES
text: Ay, or surly borne—

speaker: DIOMEDES
text: Or strange, or self-affected—

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
Thank the heavens, lord, thou art of sweet composure.
Praise him that gat thee, she that gave thee suck;
Famed be thy tutor, and thy parts of nature
Thrice famed beyond, beyond thy erudition;
But he that disciplined thine arms to fight,
Let Mars divide eternity in twain
And give him half; and for thy vigor,
Bull-bearing Milo his addition yield
To sinewy Ajax. I will not praise thy wisdom,
Which like a bourn, a pale, a shore confines
Thy spacious and dilated parts. Here’s Nestor,
Instructed by the antiquary times;
He must, he is, he cannot but be wise.—
But pardon, father Nestor, were your days
As green as Ajax’ and your brain so tempered,
You should not have the eminence of him,
But be as Ajax.

speaker: AJAX
text: Shall I call you father?

speaker: NESTOR
text: Ay, my good son.

speaker: DIOMEDES
text: Be ruled by him, Lord Ajax.

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
There is no tarrying here; the hart Achilles
Keeps thicket. Please it our great general
To call together all his state of war.
Fresh kings are come to Troy. Tomorrow
We must with all our main of power stand fast.
And here’s a lord—come knights from east to west
And cull their flower, Ajax shall cope the best.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text:
Go we to council. Let Achilles sleep.
Light boats sail swift, though greater hulks draw deep.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Friend, you, pray you, a word. Do you not
follow the young Lord Paris?

speaker: MAN
text: Ay, sir, when he goes before me.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: You depend upon him, I mean.

speaker: MAN
text: Sir, I do depend upon the Lord.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
You depend upon a notable gentleman. I
must needs praise him.

speaker: MAN
text: The Lord be praised!

speaker: PANDARUS
text: You know me, do you not?

speaker: MAN
text: Faith, sir, superficially.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Friend, know me better. I am the Lord
Pandarus.

speaker: MAN
text: I hope I shall know your Honor better.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: I do desire it.

speaker: MAN
text: You are in the state of grace?

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Grace? Not so, friend. “Honor” and “Lordship”
are my titles. What music is this?

speaker: MAN
text: I do but partly know, sir. It is music in parts.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Know you the musicians?

speaker: MAN
text: Wholly, sir.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Who play they to?

speaker: MAN
text: To the hearers, sir.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: At whose pleasure, friend?

speaker: MAN
text: At mine, sir, and theirs that love music.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Command, I mean, friend.

speaker: MAN
text: Who shall I command, sir?

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Friend, we understand not one another. I
am too courtly and thou art too cunning. At whose
request do these men play?

speaker: MAN
text:
That’s to ’t indeed, sir. Marry, sir, at the request of
Paris my lord, who is there in person; with him the
mortal Venus, the heart blood of beauty, love’s visible
soul.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Who, my cousin Cressida?

speaker: MAN
text:
No, sir, Helen. Could not you find out that by her
attributes?

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
It should seem, fellow, that thou hast not
seen the Lady Cressid. I come to speak with Paris
from the Prince Troilus. I will make a complimental
assault upon him, for my business seethes.

speaker: MAN
text: Sodden business! There’s a stewed phrase indeed.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Fair be to you, my lord, and to all this fair
company! Fair desires in all fair measure fairly
guide them!—Especially to you, fair queen, fair
thoughts be your fair pillow!

speaker: HELEN
text: Dear lord, you are full of fair words.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
You speak your fair pleasure, sweet
queen.—Fair prince, here is good broken music.

speaker: PARIS
text:
You have broke it, cousin, and, by my life, you
shall make it whole again; you shall piece it out
with a piece of your performance.

speaker: HELEN
text: He is full of harmony.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Truly, lady, no.

speaker: HELEN
text: O, sir—

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Rude, in sooth; in good sooth, very rude.

speaker: PARIS
text: Well said, my lord; well, you say so in fits.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
I have business to my lord, dear queen.—
My lord, will you vouchsafe me a word?

speaker: HELEN
text:
Nay, this shall not hedge us out. We’ll hear you
sing, certainly.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Well, sweet queen, you are pleasant with
me.—But, marry, thus, my lord: my dear lord and
most esteemed friend, your brother Troilus—

speaker: HELEN
text: My Lord Pandarus, honey-sweet lord—

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Go to, sweet queen, go to—commends himself
most affectionately to you—

speaker: HELEN
text:
You shall not bob us out of our melody. If you
do, our melancholy upon your head!

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Sweet queen, sweet queen, that’s a sweet
queen, i’ faith—

speaker: HELEN
text: And to make a sweet lady sad is a sour offence.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Nay, that shall not serve your turn, that
shall it not, in truth, la. Nay, I care not for such
words, no, no.—And, my lord, he desires you that
if the King call for him at supper, you will make his
excuse.

speaker: HELEN
text: My Lord Pandarus—

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
What says my sweet queen, my very, very
sweet queen?

speaker: PARIS
text: What exploit’s in hand? Where sups he tonight?

speaker: HELEN
text: Nay, but, my lord—

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
What says my sweet queen? My cousin will
fall out with you.

speaker: HELEN
text: You must not know where he sups.

speaker: PARIS
text: I’ll lay my life, with my disposer Cressida.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
No, no, no such matter; you are wide.
Come, your disposer is sick.

speaker: PARIS
text: Well, I’ll make ’s excuse.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Ay, good my lord. Why should you say Cressida?
No, your poor disposer’s sick.

speaker: PARIS
text: I spy.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
You spy? What do you spy?—Come, give me
an instrument.
Now, sweet queen.

speaker: HELEN
text: Why, this is kindly done.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
My niece is horribly in love with a thing you
have, sweet queen.

speaker: HELEN
text:
She shall have it, my lord, if it be not my Lord
Paris.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
He? No, she’ll none of him. They two are
twain.

speaker: HELEN
text:
Falling in after falling out may make them
three.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Come, come, I’ll hear no more of this. I’ll
sing you a song now.

speaker: HELEN
text:
Ay, ay, prithee. Now, by my troth, sweet lord,
thou hast a fine forehead.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Ay, you may, you may.

speaker: HELEN
text:
Let thy song be love. “This love will undo us all.”
O Cupid, Cupid, Cupid!

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Love? Ay, that it shall, i’ faith.

speaker: PARIS
text: Ay, good now, “Love, love, nothing but love.”

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
In good troth, it begins so.
Love, love, nothing but love, still love, still more!
For, O, love’s bow
Shoots buck and doe.
The shaft confounds
Not that it wounds
But tickles still the sore.
These lovers cry “O ho!” they die,
Yet that which seems the wound to kill
Doth turn “O ho!” to “Ha ha he!”
So dying love lives still.
“O ho!” awhile, but “Ha ha ha!”
“O ho!”groans out for “ha ha ha!”—Hey ho!

speaker: HELEN
text: In love, i’ faith, to the very tip of the nose.

speaker: PARIS
text:
He eats nothing but doves, love, and that breeds
hot blood, and hot blood begets hot thoughts, and
hot thoughts beget hot deeds, and hot deeds is love.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Is this the generation of love? Hot blood,
hot thoughts, and hot deeds? Why, they are vipers.
Is love a generation of vipers? Sweet lord, who’s
afield today?

speaker: PARIS
text:
Hector, Deiphobus, Helenus, Antenor, and all the
gallantry of Troy. I would fain have armed today,
but my Nell would not have it so. How chance my
brother Troilus went not?

speaker: HELEN
text:
He hangs the lip at something.—You know all,
Lord Pandarus.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Not I, honey sweet queen. I long to hear how
they sped today.—You’ll remember your brother’s
excuse?

speaker: PARIS
text: To a hair.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Farewell, sweet queen.

speaker: HELEN
text: Commend me to your niece.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: I will, sweet queen.

speaker: PARIS
text:
They’re come from the field. Let us to Priam’s hall
To greet the warriors. Sweet Helen, I must woo you
To help unarm our Hector. His stubborn buckles,
With these your white enchanting fingers touched,
Shall more obey than to the edge of steel
Or force of Greekish sinews. You shall do more
Than all the island kings: disarm great Hector.

speaker: HELEN
text:
’Twill make us proud to be his servant, Paris.
Yea, what he shall receive of us in duty
Gives us more palm in beauty than we have,
Yea, overshines ourself.

speaker: PARIS
text: Sweet, above thought I love thee.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
How now? Where’s thy master? At my
cousin Cressida’s?

speaker: MAN
text: No, sir, he stays for you to conduct him thither.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: O, here he comes.—How now, how now?

speaker: TROILUS
text: Sirrah, walk off.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Have you seen my cousin?

speaker: TROILUS
text:
No, Pandarus. I stalk about her door
Like a strange soul upon the Stygian banks
Staying for waftage. O, be thou my Charon,
And give me swift transportance to those fields
Where I may wallow in the lily beds
Proposed for the deserver! O, gentle Pandar,
From Cupid’s shoulder pluck his painted wings
And fly with me to Cressid!

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Walk here i’ th’ orchard. I’ll bring her
straight.

speaker: TROILUS
text:
I am giddy; expectation whirls me round.
Th’ imaginary relish is so sweet
That it enchants my sense. What will it be
When that the wat’ry palate taste indeed
Love’s thrice-repurèd nectar? Death, I fear me,
Swooning destruction, or some joy too fine,
Too subtle-potent, tuned too sharp in sweetness
For the capacity of my ruder powers.
I fear it much; and I do fear besides
That I shall lose distinction in my joys,
As doth a battle when they charge on heaps
The enemy flying.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
She’s making her ready; she’ll come straight.
You must be witty now. She does so blush and
fetches her wind so short as if she were frayed with
a spirit. I’ll fetch her. It is the prettiest villain. She
fetches her breath as short as a new-ta’en sparrow.

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Even such a passion doth embrace my bosom.
My heart beats thicker than a feverous pulse,
And all my powers do their bestowing lose,
Like vassalage at unawares encount’ring
The eye of majesty.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Come, come, what need you
blush? Shame’s a baby.—Here she is now. Swear
the oaths now to her that you have sworn to me.
What, are you gone again?
You must be watched ere you be made tame, must
you? Come your ways; come your ways. An you
draw backward, we’ll put you i’ th’ thills.—Why
do you not speak to her?—Come, draw this curtain
and let’s see your picture.
Alas the day, how loath you are to offend daylight!
An ’twere dark, you’d close sooner.—So, so, rub on,
and kiss the mistress. ) How now? A
kiss in fee-farm? Build there, carpenter; the air is
sweet. Nay, you shall fight your hearts out ere I
part you. The falcon as the tercel, for all the ducks
i’ th’ river. Go to, go to.

speaker: TROILUS
text: You have bereft me of all words, lady.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Words pay no debts; give her deeds. But
she’ll bereave you o’ th’ deeds too, if she call your
activity in question.) What, billing
again? Here’s “In witness whereof the parties
interchangeably—.” Come in, come in. I’ll go get a fire.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: Will you walk in, my lord?

speaker: TROILUS
text: O Cressid, how often have I wished me thus!

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
“Wished,” my lord? The gods grant—O, my
lord!

speaker: TROILUS
text:
What should they grant? What makes this
pretty abruption? What too-curious dreg espies
my sweet lady in the fountain of our love?

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: More dregs than water, if my fears have eyes.

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Fears make devils of cherubins; they never
see truly.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Blind fear, that seeing reason leads, finds
safer footing than blind reason, stumbling without
fear. To fear the worst oft cures the worse.

speaker: TROILUS
text:
O, let my lady apprehend no fear. In all
Cupid’s pageant there is presented no monster.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: Nor nothing monstrous neither?

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Nothing but our undertakings, when we vow
to weep seas, live in fire, eat rocks, tame tigers,
thinking it harder for our mistress to devise imposition
enough than for us to undergo any difficulty
imposed. This is the monstruosity in love, lady, that
the will is infinite and the execution confined, that
the desire is boundless and the act a slave to limit.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
They say all lovers swear more performance
than they are able and yet reserve an ability that
they never perform, vowing more than the perfection
of ten and discharging less than the tenth part
of one. They that have the voice of lions and the
act of hares, are they not monsters?

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Are there such? Such are not we. Praise us as
we are tasted, allow us as we prove; our head shall
go bare till merit crown it. No perfection in reversion
shall have a praise in present. We will not
name desert before his birth, and, being born, his
addition shall be humble. Few words to fair faith.
Troilus shall be such to Cressid as what envy can
say worst shall be a mock for his truth, and what
truth can speak truest not truer than Troilus.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: Will you walk in, my lord?

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
What, blushing still? Have you not done
talking yet?

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Well, uncle, what folly I commit I dedicate
to you.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
I thank you for that. If my lord get a boy of
you, you’ll give him me. Be true to my lord. If he
flinch, chide me for it.

speaker: TROILUS
text:
You know now your hostages:
your uncle’s word and my firm faith.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Nay, I’ll give my word for her too. Our kindred,
though they be long ere they be wooed, they
are constant being won. They are burrs, I can tell
you; they’ll stick where they are thrown.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Boldness comes to me now and brings me heart.
Prince Troilus, I have loved you night and day
For many weary months.

speaker: TROILUS
text: Why was my Cressid then so hard to win?

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Hard to seem won; but I was won, my lord,
With the first glance that ever—pardon me;
If I confess much, you will play the tyrant.
I love you now, but till now not so much
But I might master it. In faith, I lie;
My thoughts were like unbridled children grown
Too headstrong for their mother. See, we fools!
Why have I blabbed? Who shall be true to us
When we are so unsecret to ourselves?
But though I loved you well, I wooed you not;
And yet, good faith, I wished myself a man;
Or that we women had men’s privilege
Of speaking first. Sweet, bid me hold my tongue,
For in this rapture I shall surely speak
The thing I shall repent. See, see, your silence,
Cunning in dumbness, from my weakness draws
My very soul of counsel! Stop my mouth.

speaker: TROILUS
text: And shall, albeit sweet music issues thence.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Pretty, i’ faith!

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
My lord, I do beseech you pardon me.
’Twas not my purpose thus to beg a kiss.
I am ashamed. O heavens, what have I done!
For this time will I take my leave, my lord.

speaker: TROILUS
text: Your leave, sweet Cressid?

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Leave? An you take leave till tomorrow
morning—

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: Pray you, content you.

speaker: TROILUS
text: What offends you, lady?

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: Sir, mine own company.

speaker: TROILUS
text: You cannot shun yourself.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Let me go and try.
I have a kind of self resides with you,
But an unkind self that itself will leave
To be another’s fool. I would be gone.
Where is my wit? I know not what I speak.

speaker: TROILUS
text: Well know they what they speak that speak so wisely.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Perchance, my lord, I show more craft than love
And fell so roundly to a large confession
To angle for your thoughts. But you are wise,
Or else you love not; for to be wise and love
Exceeds man’s might. That dwells with gods above.

speaker: TROILUS
text:
O, that I thought it could be in a woman—
As, if it can, I will presume in you—
To feed for aye her lamp and flames of love,
To keep her constancy in plight and youth,
Outliving beauty’s outward, with a mind
That doth renew swifter than blood decays!
Or that persuasion could but thus convince me
That my integrity and truth to you
Might be affronted with the match and weight
Of such a winnowed purity in love;
How were I then uplifted! But, alas,
I am as true as truth’s simplicity
And simpler than the infancy of truth.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: In that I’ll war with you.

speaker: TROILUS
text:
O virtuous fight,
When right with right wars who shall be most right!
True swains in love shall in the world to come
Approve their truth by Troilus. When their rhymes,
Full of protest, of oath and big compare,
Wants similes, truth tired with iteration—
“As true as steel, as plantage to the moon,
As sun to day, as turtle to her mate,
As iron to adamant, as Earth to th’ center”—
Yet, after all comparisons of truth,
As truth’s authentic author to be cited,
“As true as Troilus” shall crown up the verse
And sanctify the numbers.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Prophet may you be!
If I be false or swerve a hair from truth,
When time is old and hath forgot itself,
When water drops have worn the stones of Troy
And blind oblivion swallowed cities up,
And mighty states characterless are grated
To dusty nothing, yet let memory,
From false to false, among false maids in love,
Upbraid my falsehood! When they’ve said “as false
As air, as water, wind or sandy earth,
As fox to lamb, or wolf to heifer’s calf,
Pard to the hind, or stepdame to her son,”
Yea, let them say, to stick the heart of falsehood,
“As false as Cressid.”

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Go to, a bargain made. Seal it, seal it. I’ll be
the witness. Here I hold your hand, here my
cousin’s. If ever you prove false one to another, since
I have taken such pains to bring you together, let
all pitiful goers-between be called to the world’s
end after my name: call them all panders. Let all
constant men be Troiluses, all false women Cressids,
and all brokers-between panders. Say “Amen.”

speaker: TROILUS
text: Amen.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: Amen.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Amen. Whereupon I will show you a chamber
with a bed, which bed, because it shall not
speak of your pretty encounters, press it to death.
Away.
And Cupid grant all tongue-tied maidens here
Bed, chamber, pander to provide this gear.

speaker: CALCHAS
text:
Now, princes, for the service I have done you,
Th’ advantage of the time prompts me aloud
To call for recompense. Appear it to your mind
That, through the sight I bear in things to come,
I have abandoned Troy, left my possessions,
Incurred a traitor’s name, exposed myself,
From certain and possessed conveniences,
To doubtful fortunes, sequest’ring from me all
That time, acquaintance, custom, and condition
Made tame and most familiar to my nature,
And here, to do you service, am become
As new into the world, strange, unacquainted.
I do beseech you, as in way of taste,
To give me now a little benefit
Out of those many regist’red in promise,
Which you say live to come in my behalf.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: What wouldst thou of us, Trojan, make demand?

speaker: CALCHAS
text:
You have a Trojan prisoner called Antenor
Yesterday took. Troy holds him very dear.
Oft have you—often have you thanks therefor—
Desired my Cressid in right great exchange,
Whom Troy hath still denied; but this Antenor,
I know, is such a wrest in their affairs
That their negotiations all must slack,
Wanting his manage; and they will almost
Give us a prince of blood, a son of Priam,
In change of him. Let him be sent, great princes,
And he shall buy my daughter; and her presence
Shall quite strike off all service I have done
In most accepted pain.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text:
Let Diomedes bear him,
And bring us Cressid hither. Calchas shall have
What he requests of us. Good Diomed,
Furnish you fairly for this interchange.
Withal, bring word if Hector will tomorrow
Be answered in his challenge. Ajax is ready.

speaker: DIOMEDES
text:
This shall I undertake, and ’tis a burden
Which I am proud to bear.

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
Achilles stands i’ th’ entrance of his tent.
Please it our General pass strangely by him
As if he were forgot, and, princes all,
Lay negligent and loose regard upon him.
I will come last. ’Tis like he’ll question me
Why such unplausive eyes are bent, why turned on him.
If so, I have derision medicinable
To use between your strangeness and his pride,
Which his own will shall have desire to drink.
It may do good; pride hath no other glass
To show itself but pride, for supple knees
Feed arrogance and are the proud man’s fees.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text:
We’ll execute your purpose and put on
A form of strangeness as we pass along;
So do each lord, and either greet him not
Or else disdainfully, which shall shake him more
Than if not looked on. I will lead the way.

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
What, comes the General to speak with me?
You know my mind: I’ll fight no more ’gainst Troy.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: What says Achilles? Would he aught with us?

speaker: NESTOR
text: Would you, my lord, aught with the General?

speaker: ACHILLES
text: No.

speaker: NESTOR
text: Nothing, my lord.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: The better.

speaker: ACHILLES
text: Good day, good day.

speaker: MENELAUS
text: How do you? How do you?

speaker: ACHILLES
text: What, does the cuckold scorn me?

speaker: AJAX
text: How now, Patroclus?

speaker: ACHILLES
text: Good morrow, Ajax.

speaker: AJAX
text: Ha?

speaker: ACHILLES
text: Good morrow.

speaker: AJAX
text: Ay, and good next day too.

speaker: ACHILLES
text: What mean these fellows? Know they not Achilles?

speaker: PATROCLUS
text:
They pass by strangely. They were used to bend,
To send their smiles before them to Achilles,
To come as humbly as they use to creep
To holy altars.

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
What, am I poor of late?
’Tis certain, greatness, once fall’n out with Fortune,
Must fall out with men too. What the declined is
He shall as soon read in the eyes of others
As feel in his own fall, for men, like butterflies,
Show not their mealy wings but to the summer,
And not a man, for being simply man,
Hath any honor, but honor for those honors
That are without him—as place, riches, and favor,
Prizes of accident as oft as merit,
Which, when they fall, as being slippery slanders,
The love that leaned on them, as slippery too,
Doth one pluck down another and together
Die in the fall. But ’tis not so with me.
Fortune and I are friends. I do enjoy,
At ample point, all that I did possess,
Save these men’s looks, who do, methinks, find out
Something not worth in me such rich beholding
As they have often given. Here is Ulysses.
I’ll interrupt his reading.—How now, Ulysses?

speaker: ULYSSES
text: Now, great Thetis’ son—

speaker: ACHILLES
text: What are you reading?

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
A strange fellow here
Writes me that man, how dearly ever parted,
How much in having, or without or in,
Cannot make boast to have that which he hath,
Nor feels not what he owes, but by reflection;
As when his virtues, shining upon others,
Heat them, and they retort that heat again
To the first giver.

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
This is not strange, Ulysses.
The beauty that is borne here in the face
The bearer knows not, but commends itself
To others’ eyes; nor doth the eye itself,
That most pure spirit of sense, behold itself,
Not going from itself, but eye to eye opposed
Salutes each other with each other’s form.
For speculation turns not to itself
Till it hath traveled and is mirrored there
Where it may see itself. This is not strange at all.

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
I do not strain at the position—
It is familiar—but at the author’s drift,
Who in his circumstance expressly proves
That no man is the lord of anything—
Though in and of him there be much consisting—
Till he communicate his parts to others;
Nor doth he of himself know them for aught
Till he behold them formed in the applause
Where they’re extended; who, like an arch, reverb’rate
The voice again or, like a gate of steel
Fronting the sun, receives and renders back
His figure and his heat. I was much rapt in this
And apprehended here immediately
Th’ unknown Ajax. Heavens, what a man is there!
A very horse, that has he knows not what!
Nature, what things there are
Most abject in regard, and dear in use,
What things again most dear in the esteem
And poor in worth! Now shall we see tomorrow—
An act that very chance doth throw upon him—
Ajax renowned. O, heavens, what some men do
While some men leave to do!
How some men creep in skittish Fortune’s hall,
Whiles others play the idiots in her eyes!
How one man eats into another’s pride,
While pride is fasting in his wantonness!
To see these Grecian lords—why, even already
They clap the lubber Ajax on the shoulder
As if his foot were on brave Hector’s breast
And great Troy shrieking.

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
I do believe it, for they passed by me
As misers do by beggars, neither gave to me
Good word nor look. What, are my deeds forgot?

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
Time hath, my lord, a wallet at his back
Wherein he puts alms for oblivion,
A great-sized monster of ingratitudes.
Those scraps are good deeds past, which are devoured
As fast as they are made, forgot as soon
As done. Perseverance, dear my lord,
Keeps honor bright. To have done is to hang
Quite out of fashion like a rusty mail
In monumental mock’ry. Take the instant way,
For honor travels in a strait so narrow
Where one but goes abreast. Keep, then, the path,
For Emulation hath a thousand sons
That one by one pursue. If you give way
Or turn aside from the direct forthright,
Like to an entered tide they all rush by
And leave you hindmost;
Or, like a gallant horse fall’n in first rank,
Lie there for pavement to the abject rear,
O’errun and trampled on. Then what they do in present,
Though less than yours in past, must o’ertop yours;
For Time is like a fashionable host
That slightly shakes his parting guest by th’ hand
And, with his arms outstretched as he would fly,
Grasps in the comer. Welcome ever smiles,
And Farewell goes out sighing. Let not virtue seek
Remuneration for the thing it was,
For beauty, wit,
High birth, vigor of bone, desert in service,
Love, friendship, charity are subjects all
To envious and calumniating Time.
One touch of nature makes the whole world kin,
That all, with one consent, praise newborn gauds,
Though they are made and molded of things past,
And give to dust that is a little gilt
More laud than gilt o’erdusted.
The present eye praises the present object.
Then marvel not, thou great and complete man,
That all the Greeks begin to worship Ajax,
Since things in motion sooner catch the eye
Than what stirs not. The cry went once on thee,
And still it might, and yet it may again,
If thou wouldst not entomb thyself alive
And case thy reputation in thy tent,
Whose glorious deeds but in these fields of late
Made emulous missions ’mongst the gods themselves
And drave great Mars to faction.

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
Of this my privacy,
I have strong reasons.

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
But ’gainst your privacy
The reasons are more potent and heroical.
’Tis known, Achilles, that you are in love
With one of Priam’s daughters.

speaker: ACHILLES
text: Ha? Known?

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
Is that a wonder?
The providence that’s in a watchful state
Knows almost every grain of Pluto’s gold,
Finds bottom in the uncomprehensive deep,
Keeps place with thought and almost, like the gods,
Do thoughts unveil in their dumb cradles.
There is a mystery—with whom relation
Durst never meddle—in the soul of state,
Which hath an operation more divine
Than breath or pen can give expressure to.
All the commerce that you have had with Troy
As perfectly is ours as yours, my lord;
And better would it fit Achilles much
To throw down Hector than Polyxena.
But it must grieve young Pyrrhus now at home
When Fame shall in our islands sound her trump,
And all the Greekish girls shall tripping sing
“Great Hector’s sister did Achilles win,
But our great Ajax bravely beat down him.”
Farewell, my lord. I as your lover speak.
The fool slides o’er the ice that you should break.

speaker: PATROCLUS
text:
To this effect, Achilles, have I moved you.
A woman impudent and mannish grown
Is not more loathed than an effeminate man
In time of action. I stand condemned for this.
They think my little stomach to the war,
And your great love to me, restrains you thus.
Sweet, rouse yourself, and the weak wanton Cupid
Shall from your neck unloose his amorous fold
And, like a dewdrop from the lion’s mane,
Be shook to air.

speaker: ACHILLES
text: Shall Ajax fight with Hector?

speaker: PATROCLUS
text: Ay, and perhaps receive much honor by him.

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
I see my reputation is at stake;
My fame is shrewdly gored.

speaker: PATROCLUS
text:
O, then, beware!
Those wounds heal ill that men do give themselves.
Omission to do what is necessary
Seals a commission to a blank of danger,
And danger, like an ague, subtly taints
Even then when they sit idly in the sun.

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
Go call Thersites hither, sweet Patroclus.
I’ll send the fool to Ajax and desire him
T’ invite the Trojan lords after the combat
To see us here unarmed. I have a woman’s longing,
An appetite that I am sick withal,
To see great Hector in his weeds of peace,
To talk with him, and to behold his visage,
Even to my full of view.
A labor saved.

speaker: THERSITES
text: A wonder!

speaker: ACHILLES
text: What?

speaker: THERSITES
text:
Ajax goes up and down the field, asking for
himself.

speaker: ACHILLES
text: How so?

speaker: THERSITES
text:
He must fight singly tomorrow with Hector
and is so prophetically proud of an heroical cudgeling
that he raves in saying nothing.

speaker: ACHILLES
text: How can that be?

speaker: THERSITES
text:
Why, he stalks up and down like a peacock—
a stride and a stand; ruminates like an hostess
that hath no arithmetic but her brain to set
down her reckoning; bites his lip with a politic regard,
as who should say “There were wit in this
head an ’twould out”—and so there is, but it lies
as coldly in him as fire in a flint, which will not
show without knocking. The man’s undone forever,
for if Hector break not his neck i’ th’ combat,
he’ll break ’t himself in vainglory. He knows not
me. I said “Good morrow, Ajax,” and he replies
“Thanks, Agamemnon.” What think you of this
man that takes me for the General? He’s grown a
very land-fish, languageless, a monster. A plague of
opinion! A man may wear it on both sides, like a
leather jerkin.

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
Thou must be my ambassador to him,
Thersites.

speaker: THERSITES
text:
Who, I? Why, he’ll answer nobody. He professes
not answering; speaking is for beggars; he
wears his tongue in ’s arms. I will put on his presence.
Let Patroclus make his demands to me. You
shall see the pageant of Ajax.

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
To him, Patroclus. Tell him I humbly desire
the valiant Ajax to invite the most valorous Hector
to come unarmed to my tent, and to procure safe-conduct
for his person of the magnanimous and
most illustrious, six-or-seven-times-honored captain
general of the Grecian army, Agamemnon,
et cetera. Do this.

speaker: PATROCLUS
text:
Jove
bless great Ajax.

speaker: THERSITES
text: Hum!

speaker: PATROCLUS
text: I come from the worthy Achilles—

speaker: THERSITES
text: Ha?

speaker: PATROCLUS
text:
Who most humbly desires you to invite
Hector to his tent—

speaker: THERSITES
text: Hum!

speaker: PATROCLUS
text:
And to procure safe-conduct from
Agamemnon.

speaker: THERSITES
text: Agamemnon?

speaker: PATROCLUS
text: Ay, my lord.

speaker: THERSITES
text: Ha!

speaker: PATROCLUS
text: What say you to ’t?

speaker: THERSITES
text: God b’ wi’ you, with all my heart.

speaker: PATROCLUS
text: Your answer, sir.

speaker: THERSITES
text:
If tomorrow be a fair day, by eleven of the
clock it will go one way or other. Howsoever, he
shall pay for me ere he has me.

speaker: PATROCLUS
text: Your answer, sir.

speaker: THERSITES
text: Fare you well with all my heart.

speaker: ACHILLES
text: Why, but he is not in this tune, is he?

speaker: THERSITES
text:
No, but he’s out of tune thus. What music
will be in him when Hector has knocked out his
brains I know not. But I am sure none, unless the
fiddler Apollo get his sinews to make catlings on.

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
Come, thou shalt bear a letter to him
straight.

speaker: THERSITES
text:
Let me bear another to his horse, for that’s
the more capable creature.

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
My mind is troubled, like a fountain stirred,
And I myself see not the bottom of it.

speaker: THERSITES
text:
Would the fountain of your mind were clear
again, that I might water an ass at it. I had rather
be a tick in a sheep than such a valiant ignorance.

speaker: PARIS
text: See, ho! Who is that there?

speaker: DEIPHOBUS
text: It is the Lord Aeneas.

speaker: AENEAS
text:
Is the Prince there in person?—
Had I so good occasion to lie long
As you, Prince Paris, nothing but heavenly business
Should rob my bedmate of my company.

speaker: DIOMEDES
text: That’s my mind too.—Good morrow, Lord Aeneas.

speaker: PARIS
text:
A valiant Greek, Aeneas; take his hand.
Witness the process of your speech, wherein
You told how Diomed a whole week by days
Did haunt you in the field.

speaker: AENEAS
text:
Health to you, valiant sir,
During all question of the gentle truce;
But when I meet you armed, as black defiance
As heart can think or courage execute.

speaker: DIOMEDES
text:
The one and other Diomed embraces.
Our bloods are now in calm, and, so long, health;
But when contention and occasion meet,
By Jove, I’ll play the hunter for thy life
With all my force, pursuit, and policy.

speaker: AENEAS
text:
And thou shalt hunt a lion that will fly
With his face backward. In human gentleness,
Welcome to Troy. Now, by Anchises’ life,
Welcome indeed. By Venus’ hand I swear
No man alive can love in such a sort
The thing he means to kill more excellently.

speaker: DIOMEDES
text:
We sympathize. Jove, let Aeneas live,
If to my sword his fate be not the glory,
A thousand complete courses of the sun!
But in mine emulous honor let him die
With every joint a wound and that tomorrow.

speaker: AENEAS
text: We know each other well.

speaker: DIOMEDES
text: We do, and long to know each other worse.

speaker: PARIS
text:
This is the most despiteful gentle greeting,
The noblest hateful love, that e’er I heard of.
What business, lord, so early?

speaker: AENEAS
text: I was sent for to the King, but why I know not.

speaker: PARIS
text:
His purpose meets you. ’Twas to bring this Greek
To Calchas’ house, and there to render him,
For the enfreed Antenor, the fair Cressid.
Let’s have your company, or, if you please,
Haste there before us. I constantly believe—
Or, rather, call my thought a certain knowledge—
My brother Troilus lodges there tonight.
Rouse him, and give him note of our approach,
With the whole quality whereof. I fear
We shall be much unwelcome.

speaker: AENEAS
text:
That I assure you.
Troilus had rather Troy were borne to Greece
Than Cressid borne from Troy.

speaker: PARIS
text:
There is no help.
The bitter disposition of the time
Will have it so.—On, lord, we’ll follow you.

speaker: AENEAS
text: Good morrow, all.

speaker: PARIS
text:
And tell me, noble Diomed, faith, tell me true,
Even in the soul of sound good-fellowship,
Who, in your thoughts, deserves fair Helen best,
Myself or Menelaus?

speaker: DIOMEDES
text:
Both alike.
He merits well to have her that doth seek her,
Not making any scruple of her soilure,
With such a hell of pain and world of charge;
And you as well to keep her that defend her,
Not palating the taste of her dishonor,
With such a costly loss of wealth and friends.
He, like a puling cuckold, would drink up
The lees and dregs of a flat tamèd piece;
You, like a lecher, out of whorish loins
Are pleased to breed out your inheritors.
Both merits poised, each weighs nor less nor more;
But he as he, the heavier for a whore.

speaker: PARIS
text: You are too bitter to your countrywoman.

speaker: DIOMEDES
text:
She’s bitter to her country. Hear me, Paris:
For every false drop in her bawdy veins
A Grecian’s life hath sunk; for every scruple
Of her contaminated carrion weight
A Trojan hath been slain. Since she could speak,
She hath not given so many good words breath
As for her Greeks and Trojans suffered death.

speaker: PARIS
text:
Fair Diomed, you do as chapmen do,
Dispraise the thing that they desire to buy.
But we in silence hold this virtue well:
We’ll not commend that not intend to sell.
Here lies our way.

speaker: TROILUS
text: Dear, trouble not yourself. The morn is cold.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Then, sweet my lord, I’ll call mine uncle down.
He shall unbolt the gates.

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Trouble him not.
To bed, to bed! Sleep kill those pretty eyes
And give as soft attachment to thy senses
As infants’ empty of all thought!

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: Good morrow, then.

speaker: TROILUS
text: I prithee now, to bed.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: Are you aweary of me?

speaker: TROILUS
text:
O Cressida! But that the busy day,
Waked by the lark, hath roused the ribald crows,
And dreaming night will hide our joys no longer,
I would not from thee.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: Night hath been too brief.

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Beshrew the witch! With venomous wights she stays
As tediously as hell, but flies the grasps of love
With wings more momentary-swift than thought.
You will catch cold and curse me.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Prithee, tarry. You men will never tarry.
O foolish Cressid! I might have still held off,
And then you would have tarried. Hark, there’s one up.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: What’s all the doors open here?

speaker: TROILUS
text: It is your uncle.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
A pestilence on him! Now will he be mocking.
I shall have such a life!

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
How now, how now? How go maidenheads?
Here, you maid! Where’s my Cousin Cressid?

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Go hang yourself, you naughty mocking uncle.
You bring me to do—and then you flout me too.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
To do what, to do what?—Let her say
what.—What have I brought you to do?

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Come, come, beshrew your heart! You’ll ne’er be good
Nor suffer others.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Ha, ha! Alas, poor wretch! Ah, poor capocchia!
Has ’t not slept tonight? Would he not—a
naughty man—let it sleep? A bugbear take him!

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Did not I tell you? Would he were knocked i’ th’ head!
Who’s that at door?—Good uncle, go and see.—
My lord, come you again into my chamber.
You smile and mock me, as if I meant naughtily.

speaker: TROILUS
text: Ha, ha!

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Come, you are deceived. I think of no such thing.
How earnestly they knock! Pray you, come in.
I would not for half Troy have you seen here.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Who’s there? What’s the matter? Will you
beat down the door?
How now? What’s the matter?

speaker: AENEAS
text: Good morrow, lord, good morrow.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Who’s there? My Lord Aeneas? By my troth,
I knew you not. What news with you so early?

speaker: AENEAS
text: Is not Prince Troilus here?

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Here? What should he do here?

speaker: AENEAS
text:
Come, he is here, my lord. Do not deny him.
It doth import him much to speak with me.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Is he here, say you? It’s more than I know,
I’ll be sworn. For my own part, I came in late.
What should he do here?

speaker: AENEAS
text:
Ho, nay, then! Come, come, you’ll do him
wrong ere you are ware. You’ll be so true to him to
be false to him. Do not you know of him, but yet go
fetch him hither. Go.

speaker: TROILUS
text: How now? What’s the matter?

speaker: AENEAS
text:
My lord, I scarce have leisure to salute you,
My matter is so rash. There is at hand
Paris your brother and Deiphobus,
The Grecian Diomed, and our Antenor
Delivered to us; and for him forthwith,
Ere the first sacrifice, within this hour,
We must give up to Diomedes’ hand
The Lady Cressida.

speaker: TROILUS
text: Is it so concluded?

speaker: AENEAS
text:
By Priam and the general state of Troy.
They are at hand and ready to effect it.

speaker: TROILUS
text:
How my achievements mock me!
I will go meet them. And, my Lord Aeneas,
We met by chance; you did not find me here.

speaker: AENEAS
text:
Good, good, my lord; the secrets of nature
Have not more gift in taciturnity.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Is ’t possible? No sooner got but lost? The
devil take Antenor! The young prince will go mad.
A plague upon Antenor! I would they had broke ’s
neck!

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: How now? What’s the matter? Who was here?

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Ah, ah!

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Why sigh you so profoundly? Where’s my lord?
Gone? Tell me, sweet uncle, what’s the matter?

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Would I were as deep under the earth as I
am above!

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: O the gods! What’s the matter?

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Pray thee, get thee in. Would thou hadst
ne’er been born! I knew thou wouldst be his death.
O, poor gentleman! A plague upon Antenor!

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Good uncle, I beseech you, on my knees I
beseech you, what’s the matter?

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Thou must be gone, wench; thou must be
gone. Thou art changed for Antenor. Thou must to
thy father and be gone from Troilus. ’Twill be his
death; ’twill be his bane. He cannot bear it.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: O you immortal gods! I will not go.

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Thou must.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
I will not, uncle. I have forgot my father.
I know no touch of consanguinity,
No kin, no love, no blood, no soul so near me
As the sweet Troilus. O you gods divine,
Make Cressid’s name the very crown of falsehood
If ever she leave Troilus! Time, force, and death
Do to this body what extremes you can,
But the strong base and building of my love
Is as the very center of the Earth,
Drawing all things to it. I’ll go in and weep—

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Do, do.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Tear my bright hair, and scratch my praisèd cheeks,
Crack my clear voice with sobs, and break my heart
With sounding “Troilus.” I will not go from Troy.

speaker: PARIS
text:
It is great morning, and the hour prefixed
For her delivery to this valiant Greek
Comes fast upon. Good my brother Troilus,
Tell you the lady what she is to do
And haste her to the purpose.

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Walk into her house.
I’ll bring her to the Grecian presently;
And to his hand when I deliver her,
Think it an altar and thy brother Troilus
A priest there off’ring to it his own heart.

speaker: PARIS
text:
I know what ’tis to love,
And would, as I shall pity, I could help.—
Please you walk in, my lords?

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Be moderate, be moderate.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
Why tell you me of moderation?
The grief is fine, full, perfect that I taste,
And violenteth in a sense as strong
As that which causeth it. How can I moderate it?
If I could temporize with my affection
Or brew it to a weak and colder palate,
The like allayment could I give my grief.
My love admits no qualifying dross;
No more my grief in such a precious loss.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Here, here, here he comes. Ah, sweet
ducks!

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: O Troilus, Troilus!

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
What a pair of spectacles is here! Let me
embrace too. “O heart,” as the goodly saying is,
O heart, heavy heart,
Why sigh’st thou without breaking?
where he answers again,
Because thou canst not ease thy smart
By friendship nor by speaking.
There was never a truer rhyme. Let us cast away
nothing, for we may live to have need of such a
verse. We see it, we see it. How now, lambs?

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Cressid, I love thee in so strained a purity
That the blest gods, as angry with my fancy—
More bright in zeal than the devotion which
Cold lips blow to their deities—take thee from me.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: Have the gods envy?

speaker: PANDARUS
text: Ay, ay, ay, ay, ’tis too plain a case.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: And is it true that I must go from Troy?

speaker: TROILUS
text: A hateful truth.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: What, and from Troilus too?

speaker: TROILUS
text: From Troy and Troilus.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: Is ’t possible?

speaker: TROILUS
text:
And suddenly, where injury of chance
Puts back leave-taking, jostles roughly by
All time of pause, rudely beguiles our lips
Of all rejoindure, forcibly prevents
Our locked embrasures, strangles our dear vows
Even in the birth of our own laboring breath.
We two, that with so many thousand sighs
Did buy each other, must poorly sell ourselves
With the rude brevity and discharge of one.
Injurious Time now with a robber’s haste
Crams his rich thiev’ry up, he knows not how.
As many farewells as be stars in heaven,
With distinct breath and consigned kisses to them,
He fumbles up into a loose adieu
And scants us with a single famished kiss,
Distasted with the salt of broken tears.

speaker: AENEAS
text: My lord, is the lady ready?

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Hark, you are called. Some say the genius
Cries so to him that instantly must die.—
Bid them have patience. She shall come anon.

speaker: PANDARUS
text:
Where are my tears? Rain, to lay this wind,
or my heart will be blown up by the root.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: I must, then, to the Grecians?

speaker: TROILUS
text: No remedy.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
A woeful Cressid ’mongst the merry Greeks.
When shall we see again?

speaker: TROILUS
text: Hear me, my love. Be thou but true of heart—

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: I true? How now, what wicked deem is this?

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Nay, we must use expostulation kindly,
For it is parting from us.
I speak not “Be thou true” as fearing thee,
For I will throw my glove to Death himself
That there is no maculation in thy heart;
But “Be thou true,” say I, to fashion in
My sequent protestation: “Be thou true,
And I will see thee.”

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
O, you shall be exposed, my lord, to dangers
As infinite as imminent! But I’ll be true.

speaker: TROILUS
text: And I’ll grow friend with danger. Wear this sleeve.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: And you this glove. When shall I see you?

speaker: TROILUS
text:
I will corrupt the Grecian sentinels,
To give thee nightly visitation.
But yet, be true.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: O heavens! “Be true” again?

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Hear why I speak it, love.
The Grecian youths are full of quality,
Their loving well composed, with gift of nature flowing,
And swelling o’er with arts and exercise.
How novelty may move, and parts with person,
Alas, a kind of godly jealousy—
Which I beseech you call a virtuous sin—
Makes me afeard.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: O heavens, you love me not!

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Die I a villain then!
In this I do not call your faith in question
So mainly as my merit. I cannot sing,
Nor heel the high lavolt, nor sweeten talk,
Nor play at subtle games—fair virtues all,
To which the Grecians are most prompt and pregnant.
But I can tell that in each grace of these
There lurks a still and dumb-discursive devil
That tempts most cunningly. But be not tempted.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: Do you think I will?

speaker: TROILUS
text:
No.
But something may be done that we will not,
And sometimes we are devils to ourselves
When we will tempt the frailty of our powers,
Presuming on their changeful potency.

speaker: AENEAS
text: Nay, good my lord—

speaker: TROILUS
text: Come, kiss, and let us part.

speaker: PARIS
text: Brother Troilus!

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Good brother, come you hither,
And bring Aeneas and the Grecian with you.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: My lord, will you be true?

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Who, I? Alas, it is my vice, my fault.
Whiles others fish with craft for great opinion,
I with great truth catch mere simplicity.
Whilst some with cunning gild their copper crowns,
With truth and plainness I do wear mine bare.
Fear not my truth. The moral of my wit
Is “plain and true”; there’s all the reach of it.
Welcome, Sir Diomed. Here is the lady
Which for Antenor we deliver you.
At the port, lord, I’ll give her to thy hand
And by the way possess thee what she is.
Entreat her fair and, by my soul, fair Greek,
If e’er thou stand at mercy of my sword,
Name Cressid, and thy life shall be as safe
As Priam is in Ilium.

speaker: DIOMEDES
text:
Fair Lady Cressid,
So please you, save the thanks this prince expects.
The luster in your eye, heaven in your cheek,
Pleads your fair usage, and to Diomed
You shall be mistress and command him wholly.

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Grecian, thou dost not use me courteously,
To shame the zeal of my petition to thee
In praising her. I tell thee, lord of Greece,
She is as far high-soaring o’er thy praises
As thou unworthy to be called her servant.
I charge thee use her well, even for my charge,
For, by the dreadful Pluto, if thou dost not,
Though the great bulk Achilles be thy guard,
I’ll cut thy throat.

speaker: DIOMEDES
text:
O, be not moved, Prince Troilus.
Let me be privileged by my place and message
To be a speaker free. When I am hence,
I’ll answer to my lust, and know you, lord,
I’ll nothing do on charge. To her own worth
She shall be prized; but that you say “Be ’t so,”
I speak it in my spirit and honor: “no.”

speaker: TROILUS
text:
Come, to the port. I’ll tell thee, Diomed,
This brave shall oft make thee to hide thy head.—
Lady, give me your hand, and, as we walk,
To our own selves bend we our needful talk.

speaker: PARIS
text: Hark, Hector’s trumpet.

speaker: AENEAS
text:
How have we spent this morning!
The Prince must think me tardy and remiss
That swore to ride before him to the field.

speaker: PARIS
text: ’Tis Troilus’ fault. Come, come to field with him.

speaker: DEIPHOBUS
text: Let us make ready straight.

speaker: AENEAS
text:
Yea, with a bridegroom’s fresh alacrity
Let us address to tend on Hector’s heels.
The glory of our Troy doth this day lie
On his fair worth and single chivalry.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text:
Here art thou in appointment fresh and fair,
Anticipating time with starting courage.
Give with thy trumpet a loud note to Troy,
Thou dreadful Ajax, that the appallèd air
May pierce the head of the great combatant
And hale him hither.

speaker: AJAX
text:
Thou, trumpet, there’s my purse.
Now crack thy lungs and split thy brazen pipe.
Blow, villain, till thy spherèd bias cheek
Outswell the colic of puffed Aquilon.
Come, stretch thy chest, and let thy eyes spout blood.
Thou blowest for Hector.

speaker: ULYSSES
text: No trumpet answers.

speaker: ACHILLES
text: ’Tis but early days.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: Is not yond Diomed with Calchas’ daughter?

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
’Tis he. I ken the manner of his gait.
He rises on the toe; that spirit of his
In aspiration lifts him from the earth.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: Is this the Lady Cressid?

speaker: DIOMEDES
text: Even she.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: Most dearly welcome to the Greeks, sweet lady.

speaker: NESTOR
text: Our general doth salute you with a kiss.

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
Yet is the kindness but particular.
’Twere better she were kissed in general.

speaker: NESTOR
text:
And very courtly counsel. I’ll begin.
So much for Nestor.

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
I’ll take that winter from your lips, fair lady.
Achilles bids you welcome.

speaker: MENELAUS
text: I had good argument for kissing once.

speaker: PATROCLUS
text:
But that’s no argument for kissing now,
For thus popped Paris in his hardiment
And parted thus you and your argument.

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
O deadly gall and theme of all our scorns,
For which we lose our heads to gild his horns!

speaker: PATROCLUS
text:
The first was Menelaus’ kiss; this mine.
Patroclus kisses you.

speaker: MENELAUS
text: O, this is trim!

speaker: PATROCLUS
text: Paris and I kiss evermore for him.

speaker: MENELAUS
text: I’ll have my kiss, sir.—Lady, by your leave.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: In kissing, do you render or receive?

speaker: MENELAUS
text: Both take and give.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
I’ll make my match to live,
The kiss you take is better than you give.
Therefore no kiss.

speaker: MENELAUS
text: I’ll give you boot: I’ll give you three for one.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: You are an odd man. Give even, or give none.

speaker: MENELAUS
text: An odd man, lady? Every man is odd.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text:
No, Paris is not, for you know ’tis true
That you are odd, and he is even with you.

speaker: MENELAUS
text: You fillip me o’ th’ head.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: No, I’ll be sworn.

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
It were no match, your nail against his horn.
May I, sweet lady, beg a kiss of you?

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: You may.

speaker: ULYSSES
text: I do desire it.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: Why, beg two.

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
Why, then, for Venus’ sake, give me a kiss
When Helen is a maid again and his.

speaker: CRESSIDA
text: I am your debtor; claim it when ’tis due.

speaker: ULYSSES
text: Never’s my day, and then a kiss of you.

speaker: DIOMEDES
text: Lady, a word. I’ll bring you to your father.

speaker: NESTOR
text: A woman of quick sense.

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
Fie, fie upon her!
There’s language in her eye, her cheek, her lip;
Nay, her foot speaks. Her wanton spirits look out
At every joint and motive of her body.
O, these encounterers, so glib of tongue,
That give accosting welcome ere it comes
And wide unclasp the tables of their thoughts
To every tickling reader! Set them down
For sluttish spoils of opportunity
And daughters of the game.

speaker: ALL
text: The Trojan’s trumpet.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: Yonder comes the troop.

speaker: AENEAS
text:
Hail, all the state of Greece! What shall be done
To him that victory commands? Or do you purpose
A victor shall be known? Will you the knights
Shall to the edge of all extremity
Pursue each other, or shall they be divided
By any voice or order of the field?
Hector bade ask.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: Which way would Hector have it?

speaker: AENEAS
text: He cares not; he’ll obey conditions.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: ’Tis done like Hector.

speaker: ACHILLES
text:
But securely done,
A little proudly, and great deal misprizing
The knight opposed.

speaker: AENEAS
text:
If not Achilles, sir,
What is your name?

speaker: ACHILLES
text: If not Achilles, nothing.

speaker: AENEAS
text:
Therefore Achilles. But whate’er, know this:
In the extremity of great and little,
Valor and pride excel themselves in Hector,
The one almost as infinite as all,
The other blank as nothing. Weigh him well,
And that which looks like pride is courtesy.
This Ajax is half made of Hector’s blood,
In love whereof half Hector stays at home;
Half heart, half hand, half Hector comes to seek
This blended knight, half Trojan and half Greek.

speaker: ACHILLES
text: A maiden battle, then? O, I perceive you.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text:
Here is Sir Diomed.—Go, gentle knight;
Stand by our Ajax. As you and Lord Aeneas
Consent upon the order of their fight,
So be it, either to the uttermost
Or else a breath. The combatants being kin
Half stints their strife before their strokes begin.

speaker: ULYSSES
text: They are opposed already.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: What Trojan is that same that looks so heavy?

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
The youngest son of Priam, a true knight,
Not yet mature, yet matchless firm of word,
Speaking in deeds, and deedless in his tongue,
Not soon provoked, nor being provoked soon calmed,
His heart and hand both open and both free.
For what he has, he gives; what thinks, he shows;
Yet gives he not till judgment guide his bounty,
Nor dignifies an impair thought with breath;
Manly as Hector, but more dangerous,
For Hector in his blaze of wrath subscribes
To tender objects, but he in heat of action
Is more vindicative than jealous love.
They call him Troilus, and on him erect
A second hope, as fairly built as Hector.
Thus says Aeneas, one that knows the youth
Even to his inches, and with private soul
Did in great Ilium thus translate him to me.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: They are in action.

speaker: NESTOR
text: Now, Ajax, hold thine own!

speaker: TROILUS
text: Hector, thou sleep’st. Awake thee!

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: His blows are well disposed.—There, Ajax!

speaker: DIOMEDES
text: You must no more.

speaker: AENEAS
text: Princes, enough, so please you.

speaker: AJAX
text: I am not warm yet. Let us fight again.

speaker: DIOMEDES
text: As Hector pleases.

speaker: HECTOR
text:
Why, then, will I no more.—
Thou art, great lord, my father’s sister’s son,
A cousin-german to great Priam’s seed.
The obligation of our blood forbids
A gory emulation ’twixt us twain.
Were thy commixtion Greek and Trojan so
That thou couldst say “This hand is Grecian all,
And this is Trojan; the sinews of this leg
All Greek, and this all Troy; my mother’s blood
Runs on the dexter cheek, and this sinister
Bounds in my father’s,” by Jove multipotent,
Thou shouldst not bear from me a Greekish member
Wherein my sword had not impressure made
Of our rank feud. But the just gods gainsay
That any drop thou borrowd’st from thy mother,
My sacred aunt, should by my mortal sword
Be drained. Let me embrace thee, Ajax.
By him that thunders, thou hast lusty arms!
Hector would have them fall upon him thus.
Cousin, all honor to thee!

speaker: AJAX
text:
I thank thee, Hector.
Thou art too gentle and too free a man.
I came to kill thee, cousin, and bear hence
A great addition earnèd in thy death.

speaker: HECTOR
text:
Not Neoptolemus so mirable—
On whose bright crest Fame with her loud’st “Oyez”
Cries “This is he”—could promise to himself
A thought of added honor torn from Hector.

speaker: AENEAS
text:
There is expectance here from both the sides
What further you will do.

speaker: HECTOR
text:
We’ll answer it;
The issue is embracement.—Ajax, farewell.

speaker: AJAX
text:
If I might in entreaties find success,
As seld I have the chance, I would desire
My famous cousin to our Grecian tents.

speaker: DIOMEDES
text:
’Tis Agamemnon’s wish; and great Achilles
Doth long to see unarmed the valiant Hector.

speaker: HECTOR
text:
Aeneas, call my brother Troilus to me,
And signify this loving interview
To the expecters of our Trojan part;
Desire them home.
Give me thy hand, my cousin.
I will go eat with thee and see your knights.

speaker: AJAX
text: Great Agamemnon comes to meet us here.

speaker: HECTOR
AGAMEMNON
text:
Worthy all arms! As welcome as to one
That would be rid of such an enemy—
But that’s no welcome. Understand more clear:
What’s past and what’s to come is strewed with husks
And formless ruin of oblivion;
But in this extant moment, faith and troth,
Strained purely from all hollow bias-drawing,
Bids thee, with most divine integrity,
From heart of very heart, great Hector, welcome.

speaker: HECTOR
text: I thank thee, most imperious Agamemnon.

speaker: AGAMEMNON
text: My well-famed lord of Troy, no less to you.

speaker: MENELAUS
text:
Let me confirm my princely brother’s greeting:
You brace of warlike brothers, welcome hither.

speaker: HECTOR
text: Who must we answer?

speaker: AENEAS
text: The noble Menelaus.

speaker: HECTOR
text:
O, you, my lord? By Mars his gauntlet, thanks!
Mock not that I affect th’ untraded oath;
Your quondam wife swears still by Venus’ glove.
She’s well, but bade me not commend her to you.

speaker: MENELAUS
text: Name her not now, sir; she’s a deadly theme.

speaker: HECTOR
text: O, pardon! I offend.

speaker: NESTOR
text:
I have, thou gallant Trojan, seen thee oft,
Laboring for destiny, make cruel way
Through ranks of Greekish youth; and I have seen thee,
As hot as Perseus, spur thy Phrygian steed,
Despising many forfeits and subduments,
When thou hast hung thy advanced sword i’ th’ air,
Not letting it decline on the declined,
That I have said to some my standers-by
“Lo, Jupiter is yonder, dealing life!”
And I have seen thee pause and take thy breath
When that a ring of Greeks have hemmed thee in,
Like an Olympian wrestling. This have I seen.
But this thy countenance, still locked in steel,
I never saw till now. I knew thy grandsire
And once fought with him; he was a soldier good,
But, by great Mars, the captain of us all,
Never like thee! O, let an old man embrace thee;
And, worthy warrior, welcome to our tents.

speaker: AENEAS
text: ’Tis the old Nestor.

speaker: HECTOR
text:
Let me embrace thee, good old chronicle
That hast so long walked hand in hand with time.
Most reverend Nestor, I am glad to clasp thee.

speaker: NESTOR
text:
I would my arms could match thee in contention
As they contend with thee in courtesy.

speaker: HECTOR
text: I would they could.

speaker: NESTOR
text:
Ha! By this white beard, I’d fight with thee tomorrow.
Well, welcome, welcome. I have seen the time!

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
I wonder now how yonder city stands
When we have here her base and pillar by us.

speaker: HECTOR
text:
I know your favor, Lord Ulysses, well.
Ah, sir, there’s many a Greek and Trojan dead
Since first I saw yourself and Diomed
In Ilium, on your Greekish embassy.

speaker: ULYSSES
text:
Sir, I foretold you then what would ensue.
My prophecy is but half his journey yet,
For yonder walls, that pertly front your town,
Yon towers, whose wanton tops do buss the clouds,
Must kiss their own feet.

speaker: HECTOR
text:
I must not believe you.
There they stand yet, and modestly I think
The fall of every Phrygian stone will cost
A drop of Grecian blood. The end crowns all,
